6. Making the career move
You don’t need to start over. Add inference concepts to the platform skills you have, and show the work in public. The field is young, so newcomers can catch up fast.
Pick a direction
Pick the direction closest to the work you already do. Most platform engineers start in the first two and grow toward the third.
Follow a learning path
Vishakha Sadhwani’s AI Inference Engineering Roadmap 2026 is a thorough 13-stage map of the field. Coming from platform engineering, you can move through it faster, because you already own much of the infrastructure half. A shorter path:
- Learn the model, not just the container. Transformer basics, attention and the KV cache, dense versus MoE models, and how to read a model config. The goal is to estimate the memory any model needs in five minutes.
- Learn one engine deeply. Pick vLLM, learn what each core flag trades away, and measure time to first token and per-token latency yourself.
- Translate your platform skills to GPUs. Device allocation, gateways that hold long streams, autoscaling on inference signals, and observability for engines.
- Learn to judge quality and cost. Build an eval, run a capacity sweep and calculate cost per million tokens. This is where platform engineers most often have a gap, and where the role adds the most value.
Build projects that prove it
Each project below fits on a rented GPU or two, and each produces a repo with real numbers. Shut instances down between runs, and use spot capacity for batch experiments.
Show your work in public
Many inference roles fill through networks before they reach a careers board. In August 2026, Zeoli found one serving company valued at $17.5B that didn’t list any dedicated inference performance openings. Public work is how people outside those networks get found.
- Write READMEs like lab reports. State the question, the setup (model, GPU, engine version and flags), the method, the results with numbers, what surprised you, and how to reproduce it.
- Publish what failed. A clear account of a failure shows more skill than a clean demo.
- Pin versions and show cost. Results without an engine version and a price are hard to trust and harder to reuse.
- Write and speak about it. Turn each project into a short post. Submit talks to meetups, CNCF events and community live streams.
Contribute to open source
Much of what inference projects still need is platform work. Upbound’s own upstream list from Project Champagne reads like a platform backlog: configurable load balancers, certificate issuance, Recreate rollouts for exclusive devices, an honest Ready signal, engine metrics scraped out of the box, and auth that suits long-running agents.
Projects to follow include vLLM , SGLang , llm-d , KServe , NVIDIA Dynamo , Agent Router (formerly Envoy AI Gateway), the Gateway API Inference Extension , Modelplane and Crossplane . Good first contributions:
- Run it and report what breaks, with a reproduction and numbers. This is how Champagne contributed most.
- Write operator documentation: deployment, tuning and troubleshooting guides drawn from your own runs.
- Add metrics, dashboards and alerts that make silent failures loud.
- Improve manifests, Helm charts and compositions for real environments.
- Contribute benchmark recipes and tests for the hardware you have.
Read each project’s contributing guide, start with a small change, and comment on an issue before taking on a large one.
Ongoing learning
Engines add flags every few weeks, and research reaches production within months.
- Read release notes for the engine you run, every release, and re-run your benchmark when you upgrade.
- Read the core papers: Orca on continuous batching, PagedAttention , DistServe on disaggregation, the original speculative decoding paper, and FlashAttention .
- Read Philip Kiely’s Inference Engineering . The e-book is free from Baseten.
- Follow practitioners. Newsletters such as The Pragmatic Engineer , ByteByteGo and Data Gravity cover the field well. Join the community channels for the engines you use.
- Learn evals. Whether an open model can replace a hosted one is decided by evals, and few engineers can build good ones. Start with Anthropic’s Demystifying evals for AI agents and Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar’s evals FAQ .
- Learn the economics. Be able to explain cost per million tokens and cost per user session to a finance partner.
Find the roles
Don’t expect a consistent job title yet. The same work shows up as inference engineer, performance engineer, model serving engineer or ML infrastructure engineer, and sometimes as AI platform engineer, so search for all of them. Pay reflects how scarce the skills are: in August 2026, Zeoli found an Anthropic inference performance role posted at $350,000 to $850,000, and an OpenAI equivalent at $295,000 to $555,000.
You may not need to change jobs to get started, though. If your company is planning to self-host its first model, put your hand up. Your team will probably end up responsible for that project anyway, and running it is the most direct experience you can get.
Prepare for interviews
Practice answering these. Each one points to the section of this guide that covers it. Several are adapted from Lamhot Siagian’s interview pocket notes on efficient inference (Section 7).
- Prefill and decode. Why is decode usually limited by memory bandwidth rather than compute, and what changes at long context? (Section 2)
- Hardware trends. If compute keeps growing faster than memory bandwidth, will inference soon become compute-bound? (Section 2)
- Memory math. How much memory do a model and its KV cache need at a given context length and concurrency? (Section 2)
- Goodput. What is goodput, and why plan capacity with it? (Section 2)
- Prefix caching. Which applications benefit most from prefix caching? (Section 2)
- Precision. You need to serve a 70B model on two 80 GB GPUs. What precision would you choose, and why? (Sections 2 and 3.4)
- Quantization. When does weight-only quantization speed things up, and when does it not? (Section 3.4)
- Speculative decoding. When would you not use speculative decoding? (Section 3.4)
- Chunked prefill. How do long prompts slow other users’ streams, and what does chunked prefill change? (Section 3.4)
- Parallelism. Which parallelism strategy would you pick for a given model and GPU type, and when does tensor parallelism beat pipeline parallelism? (Sections 3.4 and 3.5)
- Profiling. How would you tell whether a workload is limited by compute or by memory bandwidth? (Section 3.8)
- Debugging “slow.” p99 time to first token just spiked. How do you tell queueing, hidden reasoning and slow generation apart? (Section 3.8)
- Cost. What does a million tokens cost on your GPUs, and how does that compare with a hosted API? (Section 2)
- Capacity planning. Your user count will grow 10x in six months. How do you plan capacity? (Section 3.10)
- Rollouts and SLOs. How would you roll out a new model version safely, and what SLO would you set for the service? (Sections 3.8 and 3.10)
- Failure stories. Describe one failure with real numbers. Cover what broke and how you found it, then what you changed.

articles.title: Gemini 4 Carbon is now available
articles.body:
Gemini 4 Carbon is now available
Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning.
Two weeks ago, we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program. Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon, Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops.
Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity’s WANDR, and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model.
To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change.
Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price 1 as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity, the Gemini app, and AI Mode in Search.
Higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis
Across legal, finance, and enterprise operations, Gemini 4 Carbon combines frontier visual understanding, reasoning, and exhaustive retrieval to synthesize grounded insights across large sets of dense documents and data. It follows strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports.
Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark that tests a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows. Carbon ranks #2 while being more than 6X lower in average cost per task compared to the top performing model.
In pre-release evaluations, Carbon matched the performance of the best model tested on deep financial research on Hebbia’s E2E Financial Agentic evaluation, and ranked at the top out of 23 frontier model configurations on Balyasny Asset Management’s General Financial Intelligence benchmark, spanning legal expertise, agentic tool use and execution, coding and data engineering, and perception and context understanding.
Improved agentic coding, full stack development, and 3D and UI design
Carbon performs exceptionally well on engineering tasks that require multi-agent collaboration like multi-package migrations, cross-subsystem root-cause investigations, and complex architectural redesigns. For web app development, it runs build-and-verify loops, recovers from errors, and checks both its code and the rendered UI to produce complete, working applications. Stronger visual design, spatial reasoning, and attention to environmental detail also carry over to 3D game development and creative coding.
Frontier cybersecurity capabilities
Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber delivers our strongest cybersecurity capabilities to date, giving security teams the end-to-end intelligence they need in protecting critical software. When accessed through the Fairwind Program, Carbon leads on key benchmarks across finding (SEC-bench Pro), exploiting (ExploitGym), and patching (CWE-bench v1) vulnerabilities: inspecting software, tracing how flaws can be chained together across systems, and generating verified root-cause patches.
Early testers inside and outside of Google are already seeing strong results with Carbon for cyber in practice.
- In Project Fortify, Google’s autonomous system spanning scanning, triage, and remediation, Carbon hit 100% recall on scanning and 95% precision on triage, on our internal benchmark. On Open Source code repository testing we see an over 25% relative improvement on Argon's already strong recall rate, surfacing previously undetected, real-world logic flaws. Bringing these gains across Google, one of the world’s largest users of open-source software, helps secure both our own systems and the broader ecosystem.
- Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research (CVR) team recently used Carbon to prove that two bugs in a popular open-source software were in fact exploitable vulnerabilities, comparable in severity to the recent PHP2Shell exploit. By using Carbon to build a proof of concept, CVR helped maintainers re-classify the bug as critical and swiftly issue a patch. Details will be shared after the responsible disclosure process completes.
- As part of Wiz’s Scan for Good program, the team used Carbon to assess vulnerabilities in public digital infrastructure. For example, when scanning two major SaaS providers, the model uncovered 0-day vulnerabilities in under two hours compressing weeks of vulnerability research to a single afternoon. The team partnered with the impacted organizations to remediate in record time, helping to mitigate potential impact on tens of thousands of companies.
Stronger scientific and mathematical reasoning
Gemini 4 Carbon shows strongly improved performance in reasoning across physics, math, and life sciences, synthesizing experimental data, testing hypotheses, and reasoning through multi-step domain problems. For drug toxicity research company Axiom Bio, Carbon is now the leading model in performance for translational science, finding novel mechanisms of toxicity they hadn’t found previously. Axiom is now moving their production scientific analyses and agents to both Carbon and Argon to unlock the creation of safer drugs.
Researchers across Google have been using Carbon in Google Antigravity to accelerate their work:
- Code verification: Researchers built a new agentic framework for formal verification called AlphaProof Code and put it to work on a major security challenge: mathematically proving the actual code underlying the cryptographic protocol of Signal. Using Carbon alongside other models, our researchers translated security goals to mathematical theorems. AlphaProof Code agents then used Carbon to generate millions of lines of code in Lean, a computer language for writing mathematical proofs, helping them prove key security properties in weeks — a task that historically takes expert teams years. The result indicates Carbon’s potential to unlock scalable formal verification, long considered a gold-standard approach to building secure software.
- Enzyme assay development: Provided with only lab notebooks and raw data, Carbon went beyond standard analysis to surface hard-to-interpret data anomalies, which it used to diagnose subtle wet lab experimental artifacts such as incomplete automated mixing in deep wells, leading to substantially improved reproducibility. Moreover Carbon improved methods to deconvolute chromatography peaks and caught trace sample carryover in research instruments, significantly accelerating the development of new assays and tightening the feedback loop between computation and the bench.
- Protein structure prediction: Structure prediction models like AlphaFold 3 use Multiple Sequence Alignments (MSAs) of evolutionary relatives to help infer how amino acid chains fold. As a result they often struggle on understudied, viral, microbial, and eukaryotic proteins that have very few matches in standard databases. Working in a multi-agent setup, our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon to autonomously discover remote homologs across petabase-scale unannotated sequence archives, environmental and viral sequence catalogs, and 3D structure databases. For example, across 7 low-homolog protein families from the CASP17 blind test set, Carbon increased the number of homologs retrieved by 40-fold on average, greatly increasing the information available to structure prediction models without need for retraining. While broader benchmarking is still underway, addressing this upstream search bottleneck potentially offers a promising path toward modeling hard-to-characterize regions of the proteome.
Four weeks ago, we opened applications to give 10,000 scientists access to Argon in Google Antigravity free of charge for six months to accelerate the pace of their research, and we’ve onboarded thousands of scientists already. Today, we’re expanding access to Carbon for current and future participants, and going forward, the program will continue providing access to our latest frontier models as they become available. Applications remain open and onboarding continues on a weekly rolling basis, subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection.
Progress in model safety and security
With each new model release, we continue to strengthen our safety and security mitigations, agentic misuse prevention, model alignment, and harm reduction proportionately with model capability.
Because Gemini 4 Carbon introduces stronger cyber capabilities we build on Argon’s strong safety and security stack to fortify robustness to misuse and prompt injection.
- Mitigating frontier safety misuse risks: We’ve strengthened our misuse safeguards to help ensure stronger defensive reasoning does not translate into offensive risk. In simulated cyberattack testing environments seeded with ExploitBench and CyScenarioBench, Carbon blocked 99% of attack trajectories from our adaptive red-teaming agent that can iteratively revisit its attack plans after each block. The Carbon safeguards lowered the per-attempt breach rate to just 0.8% (down from 3.1% on Argon). Our safeguards also lowered the automated cyberattack query success rate to 2.17% in Gray Swan’s testing, compared to 9.86% on Argon. And external testing by Trajectory Labs found zero new universal jailbreaks across 132 hours and over 13,000 requests.
- Promoting safe and aligned model interactions: When we announced Carbon, we showed significant improvements in alignment as measured by our monitor flag rates across the model’s lifecycle, as well as reductions in data fabrication. New results show that on our 375-task agentic honesty benchmark, it passed 92% of tasks (compared to 70% for Argon) — declining to fill in missing experimental data 98% of the time and flagging methodological flaws 68% of the time.
- Protecting users from indirect prompt injection attacks: Two weeks ago, we shared that Carbon achieved a 0% prompt injection attack success rate on the Gray Swan IPI benchmark — marking the first time that milestone has been reached. At the same time, we know that prompt injection robustness remains an area for continued improvement. Our advanced automated red teaming continues to push the limits here and has shown that models could be further improved against sophisticated attacks in some distributions. It provides the data for us to continuously advance our models’ security to the next frontier.
For more details, read the full Gemini 4 Carbon Safety and Security report.
Getting started with Gemini 4 Carbon
Starting today, Carbon joins Argon in our family of frontier models across our products:
- For developers: Build with the Gemini API paid tier in AI Studio and Android Studio, and if you’re a Google AI Ultra subscriber, you can try it in Google Antigravity and AI Studio.
- For enterprises: Try it in Gemini for business via the API or model drop down, Google Antigravity, or CodeMender.
- For everyday users: Try Carbon starting today in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search if you’re a Google AI Ultra subscriber.
- For scientists & researchers: Apply for a chance to get access to both Argon and Carbon via Google Antigravity’s highest usage tier free of charge for 6 months (onboarded on a rolling basis), subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection.
- For cybersecurity defenders: Apply to join the Fairwind Program to get access to Carbon for cyber on a rolling basis.
See the model card to learn more about Gemini 4 Carbon and to start building with it, explore our updated Gemini 4 developer guide and documentation for best practices on migrating workflows to the model.

articles.title: Compress any LLM 3x in one click,near-lossless,in under 50 MB RAM
articles.body:
01. Architectural Motivation & The Physics of the Memory Wall
To understand why generative artificial intelligence models crawl to an agonizing halt on edge devices, one must look past algorithmic abstractions and confront the underlying solid-state physics of digital silicon. Consider the typical machine learning workstation or consumer laptop. It is equipped with a modern graphics processing unit such as the NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 Ti Mobile (GA107 silicon). On paper, this processor is astonishing: it houses 2,560 CUDA cores and 80 second-generation Tensor Cores, delivering an aggregate compute density of 29.8 TFLOPS in half-precision floating-point arithmetic. In theory, it can execute nearly thirty trillion numerical calculations every second.
Yet, when an engineer attempts to deploy a modest 7-billion parameter language model in uncompressed FP16 precision, the system collapses immediately.
The root cause is the memory wall: a severe physical asymmetry where computational density on GPU dies has scaled exponentially following Moore's Law, while the external memory interface that transports numbers from dynamic random-access memory (GDDR6 VRAM) into arithmetic logic units has hit hard thermal and electrical signaling limits. On consumer silicon, that interface is typically 128 bits wide, providing an aggregate memory bandwidth of 192.0 gigabytes per second.
During autoregressive token generation, a language model emits exactly one token at a time ($M = 1$). To predict that single token, the GPU cannot reuse loaded weights across a sequence batch. It must sweep every single parameter matrix of the network from high-latency global VRAM into on-chip register files. For a single token, operational arithmetic intensity drops to approximately 1 FLOP per byte loaded.
At 192.0 GB/s, reading an uncompressed 14 GB model once requires approximately 73 milliseconds. This caps the physical theoretical ceiling of generation to less than 14 tokens per second, leaving more than 95% of the GPU's computational tensor cores completely starved of data, idling while bytes traverse copper traces.
Even worse, consumer edge GPUs feature strict physical VRAM limits, typically capped at 4GB (3,770.6 MiB addressable ceiling). Because a 14 GB or 7 GB model physically cannot fit inside 4GB of video memory, traditional execution frameworks offload layers to host system RAM across the PCIe expansion bus. A standard PCIe Gen3 x4 connection provides an effective transfer rate of roughly 3.94 GB/s. Offloading parameters across this bus causes generation speeds to crater to 0.28 tokens per second: an unusable latency for interactive speech interfaces, autonomous robotics, or real-time telecommunications.
Prior post-training quantization schemes (such as GPTQ, AWQ, and SmoothQuant) attempted to compress weights to 4-bit representations, but introduced three critical architectural bottlenecks:
- Domain-Shift Brittleness: Quantization grids calibrated on synthetic or generic text corpora (such as WikiText-2 or C4) experience catastrophic perplexity degradation when exposed to telephone speech transcripts, structured JSON schemas, medical terminology, or foreign languages.
- High Preprocessing Latency: Calculating empirical second-order Hessian statistics requires minutes to hours of forward passes over GPU hardware, making on-device dynamic compression impossible.
- Structural Incompatibility with Recurrent State-Space Models: Modern architectures featuring non-transformer layers (such as Mamba-2, ConvNet/SSM hybrids, and Liquid Neural Networks) break standard transformer calibration assumptions, resulting in severe runtime failures.
SPECTRA resolves these constraints through an architecture-agnostic framework grounded in Shannon source coding theory, calibration-free topological saliency extraction, Group-32 microscaling, and register-fused Triton GPU kernels.
Table 0: Master Architectural Taxonomy and Methodological Foundations of the SPECTRA Engine
Comprehensive taxonomy mapping SPECTRA core subsystems to mathematical principles and execution hardware.
02. Information Theory & The Mechanics of Functional Losslessness
2.1 Lossless Bitstream Entropy Bounds vs. Continuous Parameter Rate-Distortion
To understand why traditional compression formats cannot shrink neural networks below the memory wall, we examine the theoretical limits of bit-exact representation through classical information theory. Under Claude Shannon's landmark 1948 Source Coding Theorem, the minimum expected code length $L$ required to losslessly encode a discrete symbol sequence $W$ is bounded strictly by its Shannon entropy $H(W)$:
In modern foundation models, learned weight tensors are stored in IEEE 754 half-precision (FP16) or Brain Floating Point (BF16) formats. A 16-bit floating-point number factorizes into a 1-bit sign $s \in \{0, 1\}$, an $E$-bit exponent $e \in \{0, 1\}^E$, and an $M$-bit fractional significand or mantissa $m \in \{0, 1\}^M$:
Empirical entropy audits across deep parameter manifolds reveal a fundamental structural asymmetry in the information density of these fields:
- Sign Bit Entropy: Distributed near-symmetrically across positive and negative domains, exhibiting near-maximal discrete entropy: $H(s) \approx 1.0\text{ bit}$.
- Exponent Vector Entropy: Displays strong clustering around layer-specific dynamic scales, yielding low discrete entropy: $H(e) \in [1.6, 2.7]\text{ bits}$.
- Fractional Mantissa Entropy: In overparameterized neural networks, stochastic gradient updates fill the lowest-order mantissa bits with near-uniform noise. In BF16 ($M = 7$), empirical mantissa entropy is $H(m) \approx 6.8\text{ to }7.0\text{ bits}$; in FP16 ($M = 10$), it reaches $H(m) \approx 9.5\text{ to }9.9\text{ bits}$.
Summing these components demonstrates that the aggregate discrete entropy of floating-point weight tensors is approximately 10.5 bits in BF16 and 13.5 bits in FP16. Consequently, any general-purpose or floating-point lossless bitstream compressor (such as zstd, LZ4, or fpzip) is fundamentally bounded to a lossless compression ratio of:
Because lossless compression cannot exceed $1.52\times$, compression ratios between $2.80\times$ and $3.31\times$ mathematically mandate transitioning to Shannon Rate-Distortion Theory ($R(D)$). Under rate-distortion theory, continuous weight distributions are mapped to discrete microscaled states while bounding functional task distortion.
2.2 Continuous Rate-Distortion Theory and Granular vs. Clipping Distortion
To analyze non-invertible tensor compression, we examine the continuous rate-distortion function $R(D)$, which characterizes the minimal bit rate $R$ required to represent a source distribution within an expected distortion threshold $D$:
In practical uniform $b$-bit quantization parameterized by clipping threshold $\alpha$ and group step size $\Delta = \frac{2\alpha}{2^b - 1}$, total expected distortion $D(\Delta, \alpha)$ factorizes into two distinct components:
When learned weight tensors exhibit heavy tails (kurtosis $\kappa \gg 3.0$), this distortion trade-off breaks down catastrophically. Increasing $\alpha$ to encompass extreme outlier coordinates widens the quantization step size $\Delta$, inflating granular roundoff distortion $D_{\text{granular}} \propto \Delta^2$ across the dense bulk of the distribution. Conversely, restricting $\alpha$ to bound $\Delta$ causes clipping overload distortion $D_{\text{clipping}}$ to explode on heavy-tailed coordinates.
2.3 Architectural Proofs: Propositions 1, 2, and 3
We now establish the three formal mathematical propositions that govern channel outlier isolation, Group-32 reconstruction error bounds, and closed-form Gaussian noise predictions within the SPECTRA engine.
Statement: For any $K$ channel saliency values $S_1, \dots, S_K$, the population fourth-moment kurtosis satisfies $\kappa \le K$.
Formal Proof: Let $z_j = (S_j - \mu_S)/\sigma_S$ denote the standardized channel saliencies, where $\mu_S = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{j=1}^K S_j$ and $\sigma_S^2 = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{j=1}^K (S_j - \mu_S)^2$. By construction, $\sum_{j=1}^K z_j^2 = K$. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality on the vector of squared terms $(z_1^2, \dots, z_K^2)$ and the all-ones vector:
Dividing both sides by $K$ yields the population kurtosis bound:
Consequence: Under the SPECTRA adaptive rule $r = 0.01(1 + 0.15 \ln(1 + \max(0, \kappa - 3)))$, the outlier ratio satisfies $r \le 0.01(1 + 0.15 \ln(K - 2))$. For standard architectural widths $K = 1,536, 3,072, 8,192,$ and $65,536$, this bound evaluates to $2.10\%, 2.20\%, 2.35\%,$ and $2.66\%$, respectively. The $3.0\%$ hard cap is reached only when $\kappa$ exceeds approximately $6.2 \times 10^5$, establishing that the 3.0% threshold serves as an asymptotic physical safety clamp.
Statement: If a group of 32 weights contains both signs ($w_{\min} \le 0 \le w_{\max}$), every reconstructed weight $\hat{w}$ satisfies $|w - \hat{w}| \le s/2$, apart from the floating-point rounding of the scale $s$ itself to 16 bits.
Formal Proof: Because $0$ lies within $[w_{\min}, w_{\max}]$, the zero-point formula $z = \text{round}(-w_{\min}/s)$ is not clipped to the boundary. The reconstruction grid points $(q - z)s$ for 4-bit integer codes $q \in \{0, 1, \dots, 15\}$ start within $s/2$ of $w_{\min}$ (at $q = 0$) and, since the scale is defined as $s = (w_{\max} - w_{\min})/15$, terminate within $s/2$ of $w_{\max}$ (at $q = 15$). Every weight $w \in [w_{\min}, w_{\max}]$ lies between consecutive grid points spaced by $s$, ensuring:
Remark: In deep neural networks with 32 weights per group, entirely one-sided groups are exceedingly rare (requiring all 32 independent weights to possess the same sign). In empirical audits across a $512 \times 1,024$ matrix, the observed maximum error divided by scale was $0.49999s$, confirming strict adherence to the $s/2$ bound.
Statement: Suppose the 32 weights of a group are independent and Gaussian with standard deviation $\sigma$. In modern Transformer and state-space architectures, linear projection layers are situated immediately downstream from normalization layers, such as Layer Normalization or Root Mean Square Normalization (RMSNorm). 3.4 Microscaled Group-32 Quantization with Marlin-Interleaved Layout Once outlier coordinates are isolated, the dense residual tensor $W_{\text{dense}}$ contains exclusively bounded Gaussian variance. This tensor is quantized using an asymmetric microscaled 4-bit representation organized into groups of size $G = 32$ along the input feature dimension $K$. For each group $g \in \{0, \dots, (K/G) - 1\}$ in row $i \in \{0, \dots, N - 1\}$, local min and max parameters are extracted: Asymmetric Group-32 Microscaling Formulas$$w_{\min}^{(i,g)} = \min_{k \in [0, G-1]} W_{\text{dense}}[i, gG + k], \qquad w_{\max}^{(i,g)} = \max_{k \in [0, G-1]} W_{\text{dense}}[i, gG + k]$$$$s^{(i,g)} = \max\left(\frac{w_{\max}^{(i,g)} - w_{\min}^{(i,g)}}{15.0}, 10^{-8}\right), \qquad z^{(i,g)} = \text{clamp}\left(\text{round}\left(-\frac{w_{\min}^{(i,g)}}{s^{(i,g)}}\right), 0, 15\right)$$ To optimize execution on modern Ampere architectures, SPECTRA packs these values into a Marlin-interleaved layout. Instead of packing consecutive adjacent elements ($2k, 2k + 1$) into single bytes, Marlin interleaving maps coordinate $k \in [0, 15]$ into the lower nibble (bits $[3:0]$) and coordinate $k + 16 \in [16, 31]$ into the upper nibble (bits $[7:4]$) of byte $k$ within each 32-element group: Marlin Coordinate Nibble Interleaving$$\text{PackedByte}[i, g, k] = \left(q_k^{(i,g)} \ \& \ 0x0F\right) \ | \ \left(\left(q_{k+16}^{(i,g)} \ \& \ 0x0F\right) \ll 4\right), \qquad \forall k \in [0, 15]$$

Under sustained 10-minute generation runs, GPU clock frequencies throttle to maintain thermal equilibrium, stabilizing decoding at 12.08 tokens per second. Even under steady-state thermal throttling, SPECTRA sustains real-time conversational speeds (exceeding human reading speeds of 4-5 tok/s by more than 2.4x) within an acoustically quiet 35W power envelope. 08. Technical Appendices & Deep-Dive Specifications Appendix A: Complete Mathematical Proofs (Propositions 1, 2, and 3) + Proposition 1: Kurtosis is Bounded by Matrix Width Theorem: For any sequence of $K$ real channel saliencies $S_1, \dots, S_K$, the population fourth standardized moment (kurtosis) satisfies $\kappa \le K$. Full Proof: Define the sample mean $\mu_S = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^K S_j$ and sample variance $\sigma_S^2 = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^K (S_j - \mu_S)^2$. Define standardized variables $z_j = (S_j - \mu_S)/\sigma_S$. By algebraic definition: $$\sum_{j=1}^K z_j = 0, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^K z_j^2 = K$$ Apply the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in $\mathbb{R}^K$ to the vectors $u = (z_1^2, \dots, z_K^2)^T$ and $v = (1, \dots, 1)^T$: $$\sum_{j=1}^K z_j^4 = \|u\|_2^2 \le \left(\sum_{j=1}^K z_j^2\right)^2 = K^2$$ The population kurtosis is defined as $\kappa = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^K z_j^4$. Dividing by $K$: $$\kappa = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^K z_j^4 \le \frac{K^2}{K} = K$$ This bound is tight and attained if and only if $K-1$ of the standardized terms equal $-1/\sqrt{K-1}$ and one term equals $\sqrt{K-1}$. $\blacksquare$ 
Proposition 2: Group-32 Reconstruction Error Bound Theorem: For any group of $G = 32$ real weights spanning zero ($w_{\min} \le 0 \le w_{\max}$), under uniform 4-bit asymmetric quantization with scale $s = (w_{\max} - w_{\min})/15$ and zero point $z = \text{round}(-w_{\min}/s)$, every reconstructed weight satisfies $|w - \hat{w}| \le s/2$. Full Proof: Since $w_{\min} \le 0 \le w_{\max}$, we have $-w_{\min}/s \in [0, 15]$. Therefore, $z = \text{round}(-w_{\min}/s)$ satisfies $z \in \{0, 1, \dots, 15\}$ without boundary saturation. Reconstructed grid coordinates are given by: $$\hat{w}(q) = (q - z)s, \qquad q \in \{0, 1, \dots, 15\}$$ For $q = 0$, $\hat{w}(0) = -zs$. By rounding bounds, $|-w_{\min}/s - z| \le 1/2$, which implies $|\hat{w}(0) - w_{\min}| \le s/2$. For $q = 15$: $$\hat{w}(15) = (15 - z)s = 15s - zs = w_{\max} - w_{\min} - zs = w_{\max} - (w_{\min} + zs)$$ Because $|w_{\min} + zs| \le s/2$, it follows that $|\hat{w}(15) - w_{\max}| \le s/2$. Because grid intervals have constant spacing $s$, any real weight $w \in [w_{\min}, w_{\max}]$ is at most $s/2$ away from its nearest integer code $q = \text{clamp}(\text{round}(w/s + z), 0, 15)$. Hence, $|w - \hat{w}| \le s/2$. $\blacksquare$ 
Proposition 3: Closed-Form Gaussian Group Noise Prediction Theorem: For 32 independent Gaussian weights $w_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, sample range $d \approx 4.14$, expected scale $s = d\sigma/15$, and uniform error variance $\sigma_{\text{err}}^2 = s^2/12$: $$\text{Relative Frobenius Error} = \frac{d}{15\sqrt{12}} = \frac{4.14}{51.9615} \approx 7.97\%$$ $$\text{Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)} = 20 \log_{10}\left(\frac{15\sqrt{12}}{d}\right) \approx 21.97\text{ dB}$$ $$\text{Cosine Similarity} \approx 1 - \frac{\epsilon^2}{2} = 1 - \frac{(0.0797)^2}{2} \approx 0.99682$$ Empirical Agreement: Across synthetic Gaussian tests, empirical error is $8.08\%$ and SNR is $21.85\text{ dB}$, matching theoretical predictions within 0.11 percentage points and 0.12 dB. $\blacksquare$ Appendix B: TRDC4B01 Binary Layout Specification & Memory Geometry + The TRDC (Tensor Reconstruction Data Container) binary format ensures zero-copy, zero-host-RAM-spike ingestion across consumer systems. Below is the C-struct definition and file memory geometry: typedef struct __attribute__((packed)) {
    char     magic[8];        /* Must equal "TRDC4B01" (0x5452444334423031) */
    uint64_t version;         /* Format specification version (currently 1) */
    uint64_t meta_length;     /* Byte length of trailing metadata JSON manifest */
} TRDCHeader;
/* Ingestion Pipeline (POSIX mmap):
 * 1. fd = open("model.trdc", O_RDONLY);
 * 2. ptr = mmap(NULL, file_size, PROT_READ, MAP_SHARED, fd, 0);
 * 3. Validate header: memcmp(ptr->magic, "TRDC4B01", 8) == 0;
 * 4. Read trailing JSON manifest at offset: file_size - ptr->meta_length;
 * 5. Stream contiguous tensor payloads directly to pinned CUDA DMA buffers.
 */ Appendix C: Microarchitectural Roofline & GA107 Hardware Telemetry + Microarchitectural hardware counters measured on the GA107 GPU die during sustained single-token decoding ($M = 1$): Appendix D: In-Depth Methodological Comparison with Prior Art + Detailed technical comparison against specific historical milestones: 
  - Vs. GPTQ: GPTQ requires calculating $(X X^T)^{-1}$ over hours of GPU forward passes. SPECTRA derives channel sensitivity directly from LayerNorm/RMSNorm scale parameters $\gamma$ in less than 50 milliseconds without calibration text.
  - Vs. AWQ: AWQ performs grid searches across candidate scale factors to protect top-1% channels. SPECTRA analytically scales Group-32 microscaled blocks and adaptively modulates outlier budgets ($r \le 3.0\%$) using fourth-moment kurtosis.
  - Vs. SpQR: SpQR relies on sparse matrix multiplications ($SpMM$), causing severe thread divergence and cache misses on consumer GPUs. SPECTRA gathers and accumulates outliers directly inside register files within the fused GEMV kernel.
  - Vs. QuIP# / QuaRot: QuIP# requires multiplying activations by dense randomized Hadamard matrices at runtime, adding compute latency. SPECTRA avoids online rotations entirely, relying on Group-32 microscaling.
Appendix E: Developer Quickstart & Python CLI Guide + 
            The open-source SPECTRA repository provides a comprehensive command-line interface (cli.py) and local streaming server (server.py):
# Clone the open-source repository
git clone https://github.com/NeuraCryption/SPECTRA.git
cd SPECTRA
# Install dependencies (requires PyTorch >= 2.2 and Triton)
pip install -r requirements.txt
# Compress any Hugging Face model without calibration data
python -m spectra.cli compress \
    --model-id deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B \
    --output ./models/deepseek-r1-1.5b-spectra.trdc \
    --mode pure-group32
# Run real-time streaming inference on edge hardware
python -m spectra.cli run \
    --model-path ./models/deepseek-r1-1.5b-spectra.trdc \
    --prompt "Explain quantum decoherence in simple terms:" \
    --max-tokens 512
# Launch OpenAI-compatible local server
python -m spectra.server --model-path ./models/deepseek-r1-1.5b-spectra.trdc --port 8080 Appendix F: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) + Q: What is the core innovation of SPECTRA?
A: SPECTRA combines calibration-free AST parameter sensitivity analysis with Group-32 microscaling and in-register fused Triton GPU kernels, achieving 3.31x model compression and 82.53 tok/s decoding on 4GB consumer silicon without calibration data or loss of reasoning.
Q: Why does Group-32 microscaling outperform sparse outlier extraction?
A: Under extreme value theory, partitioning weights into groups of 32 limits expected maximum parameter variance by 35.5% compared to large groups. Microscaling absorbs heavy-tailed outliers locally without introducing the quantization boundary friction caused by decoupling outliers into sparse matrices.
Q: How does the AST pre-scanner eliminate calibration data?
A: In normalized networks, learned affine scale parameters $\gamma$ directly reflect the diagonal Hessian curvature ($F_{jj} \propto |\gamma_j|^2$). Extracting $\gamma$ from the model structure identifies channel sensitivity analytically with zero calibration passes.
Q: Can SPECTRA be deployed on non-NVIDIA GPUs?
A: The core SPECTRA engine is written in OpenAI Triton, which supports NVIDIA GPUs (CUDA) and AMD GPUs (ROCm). A fallback PyTorch reference implementation is also provided for CPU and edge NPU environments.
Q: Where can I review the peer-reviewed research paper?
A: The full 40-page research publication is permanently archived on Zenodo under DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24058202.

articles.title: Palantir hires a former Democratic senator as it faces scrutiny in new Congress
articles.body:
Palantir hires a former Democratic senator as it faces scrutiny in new Congress
By Luke Garrett
Monday, November 9, 2026 • 5:00 AM EST
Heard on Morning Edition
Tech companies are expecting a wave of scrutiny from Democrats for the industry's ties with the Trump administration when they take over Congress in January. In anticipation, many are hiring former Democratic lawmakers and aides to make their case to the incoming House and Senate majorities.
Related Story: NPR
Among the latest to make that move is Palantir, which has hired former Sen. Jon Tester, a colorful Montana Democrat who's also an organic farmer.
"My agreement with Palantir is advisory in nature, it is not lobbying," Tester, who lost reelection to the Senate in 2024, told NPR in an interview.
The secretive American software and artificial intelligence company has drawn the ire of Democrats in Congress during President Trump's second term. Palantir — named by billionaire founder Peter Theil after the mythical "seeing stone" from J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings — has been accused of abetting mass surveillance on Americans and immigrants.
"Perception is reality in Washington, D.C. and in politics in general," said Tester. "But the fact is, I think Palantir has got a good story to tell, and they need to tell it. And hopefully folks will be receptive to it."
Palantir has long denied claims it aids mass surveillance on the American public — saying it doesn't gather or manipulate data at all, but instead creates tools for government agencies and private companies to organize and optimize their own information. The company has said it is committed to "protecting privacy and upholding liberal democratic values."
Earlier this year, while in the minority, Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., along with 30 other Democratic lawmakers demanded answers about Palantir's contracts with the Department of Homeland Security and whether its tools are part of efforts by the federal government to surveil Americans. Palantir denied the accusation and said it is "neither conducting nor enabling mass surveillance of American citizens," but Wyden wasn't fully satisfied with its response, according to his Senate office.
"Senator Wyden has a number of questions about Palantir's work to facilitate the Trump-Vance abuse of government data that he intends to ask again as chairman of the Finance Committee," Wyden's staff wrote in a statement to NPR. "If Palantir is not responsive next year, compulsory processes will be on the table."
It's not a coincidence that tech companies are turning to Democrats to help burnish their reputation, said Aya Ibrahim, a senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and a former State Department official.
"I think at the end of the day, these companies have an inordinate amount of money and they will try and put it wherever they can in order to stave off any real accountability," Ibrahim said.
Related Story: NPR
During Trump's second term, Palantir's CEO and co-founder Alex Karp — a self-described liberal — has been highly critical of Democrats on issues like immigration and AI.
"I would say to my Democratic friends, also of which I still have, I hope many," Karp said in an interview with Axios in 2025 specifically referencing his support for much more restrictive immigration policies. "You have to grow a spine because a lot of these people actually agree with me in private."
During his 18 years in the Senate, Tester was an outspoken critic of the PATRIOT Act that passed shortly after the 9/11 attacks that expanded the Justice Department's surveillance powers. When asked whether his concerns over government surveillance remain and whether he has the same concerns with his new employer, Tester said Palantir is different and that the company doesn't build "big databases" or trade in private data.
"I wanted to do away with the Patriot Act because it was about privacy," Tester said. "It was about making sure that I am not being watched by anybody, including Big Brother. And by the way, I've talked to many people within Palantir. They believe the same way I do. This is an organization that believes in privacy."
Related Story: NPR
Last year, over a dozen former Palantir employees criticized the company over its $30 million contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to create a tool that provides "near real-time visibility" into the movement of migrants. The former employees argued the company violated its own code of conduct by working with the Trump administration on such products.
Related Story: NPR
Valued at over $350 billion, Palantir currently holds $2 billion worth of federal contracts, according to government records. The lion's share are with the Departments of Defense, Homeland Security and State — but the software firm also works with the Departments of Agriculture, Veterans Affairs and Health and Human Services.
Tester said he'll be focused on the government services side of Palantir's work.
The former Montana senator called the midterm election results a blue "tidal wave" after two years of a Congress that gave him "great disappointment."
"It is going to make a difference as far as the policies that are being advocated for," Tester said of the upcoming Congress. "I don't think you're going to see the kind of aggressive tactics that were taken forth by ICE moving forward."
Transcript
LEILA FADEL, HOST:
The tech industry is bracing for a new Democrat-controlled Congress. A company that is likely to face scrutiny has just hired a prominent Democrat. NPR's Luke Garrett reports.
LUKE GARRETT, BYLINE: Palantir is a secretive software firm with $2 billion worth of contracts across the federal government. The majority are with the departments of Defense and Homeland Security. Last year, former employees told NPR the company's products gave DHS near-real-time visibility into the movements of migrants in the U.S. Now some Democrats have vowed to investigate Palantir's work with the Trump administration and whether it's helping the government conduct mass surveillance. Jon Tester, who was a Democratic senator for 18 years, has been hired to advise the company.
JON TESTER: You know, a perception is reality in Washington, D.C. and in politics in general. But the fact is that I think Palantir's got a good story to tell, and they need to tell it. And hopefully folks will be receptive to it.
GARRETT: The company was founded by billionaire investor Peter Thiel, who named Palantir after the mythical seeing stone from "The Lord Of The Rings." Its CEO, Alex Karp, is a self-described liberal who has worked closely with the Trump administration, and he's been highly critical of Democrats on issues like immigration. Here's Karp on "The Axios Show" last year.
(SOUNDBITE OF TV SHOW, "THE AXIOS SHOW")
ALEX KARP: I would say to my Democratic friends, also of which I still have, I hope, many, there - you have to grow a spine because a lot of these people actually agree with me in private.
GARRETT: Tester tells NPR he'll be focused on Palantir's work streamlining government services for farmers and veterans.
TESTER: And I think that's what it's about. I mean, it's about saving money. It's about making sure government works for people.
GARRETT: As a senator, Tester aggressively opposed the Bush-era PATRIOT Act, which expanded government surveillance. When asked if he had the same surveillance concerns about Palantir, Tester said he didn't.
TESTER: I've talked to many people within Palantir. They believe the same way I do. This is an organization that believes in privacy.
GARRETT: Tester's employment at Palantir comes as other tech companies have also gone on a hiring spree of former Democratic lawmakers and aides in anticipation of changing power in Washington. Senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and former State Department official Aya Ibrahim says that's not a coincidence.
AYA IBRAHIM: I think, at the end of the day, these companies have an inordinate amount of money. And they will try and put it wherever they can in order to stave off any real accountability.
GARRETT: Ibrahim says the midterm results are an opportunity to check the growing power of the tech industry.
Luke Garrett, NPR News, Washington.

"I wanted to do away with the Patriot Act because it was about privacy," Tester said. "It was about making sure that I am not being watched by anybody, including Big Brother. And by the way, I've talked to many people within Palantir. They believe the same way I do. This is an organization that believes in privacy."
Related Story: NPR
Last year, over a dozen former Palantir employees criticized the company over its $30 million contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to create a tool that provides "near real-time visibility" into the movement of migrants. The former employees argued the company violated its own code of conduct by working with the Trump administration on such products.
Related Story: NPR
Valued at over $350 billion, Palantir currently holds $2 billion worth of federal contracts, according to government records. The lion's share are with the Departments of Defense, Homeland Security and State — but the software firm also works with the Departments of Agriculture, Veterans Affairs and Health and Human Services.
Tester said he'll be focused on the government services side of Palantir's work.
The former Montana senator called the midterm election results a blue "tidal wave" after two years of a Congress that gave him "great disappointment."
"It is going to make a difference as far as the policies that are being advocated for," Tester said of the upcoming Congress. "I don't think you're going to see the kind of aggressive tactics that were taken forth by ICE moving forward."
Transcript
LEILA FADEL, HOST:
The tech industry is bracing for a new Democrat-controlled Congress. A company that is likely to face scrutiny has just hired a prominent Democrat. NPR's Luke Garrett reports.
LUKE GARRETT, BYLINE: Palantir is a secretive software firm with $2 billion worth of contracts across the federal government. The majority are with the departments of Defense and Homeland Security. Last year, former employees told NPR the company's products gave DHS near-real-time visibility into the movements of migrants in the U.S. Now some Democrats have vowed to investigate Palantir's work with the Trump administration and whether it's helping the government conduct mass surveillance. Jon Tester, who was a Democratic senator for 18 years, has been hired to advise the company.
JON TESTER: You know, a perception is reality in Washington, D.C. and in politics in general. But the fact is that I think Palantir's got a good story to tell, and they need to tell it. And hopefully folks will be receptive to it.
GARRETT: The company was founded by billionaire investor Peter Thiel, who named Palantir after the mythical seeing stone from "The Lord Of The Rings." Its CEO, Alex Karp, is a self-described liberal who has worked closely with the Trump administration, and he's been highly critical of Democrats on issues like immigration. Here's Karp on "The Axios Show" last year.
(SOUNDBITE OF TV SHOW, "THE AXIOS SHOW")
ALEX KARP: I would say to my Democratic friends, also of which I still have, I hope, many, there - you have to grow a spine because a lot of these people actually agree with me in private.
GARRETT: Tester tells NPR he'll be focused on Palantir's work streamlining government services for farmers and veterans.
TESTER: And I think that's what it's about. I mean, it's about saving money. It's about making sure government works for people.
GARRETT: As a senator, Tester aggressively opposed the Bush-era PATRIOT Act, which expanded government surveillance. When asked if he had the same surveillance concerns about Palantir, Tester said he didn't.
TESTER: I've talked to many people within Palantir. They believe the same way I do. This is an organization that believes in privacy.
GARRETT: Tester's employment at Palantir comes as other tech companies have also gone on a hiring spree of former Democratic lawmakers and aides in anticipation of changing power in Washington. Senior fellow at the AI Now Institute and former State Department official Aya Ibrahim says that's not a coincidence.
AYA IBRAHIM: I think, at the end of the day, these companies have an inordinate amount of money. And they will try and put it wherever they can in order to stave off any real accountability.
GARRETT: Ibrahim says the midterm results are an opportunity to check the growing power of the tech industry.
Luke Garrett, NPR News, Washington.

articles.title: What's new in the .NET 11 runtime
articles.body:
Note
Access to this page requires authorization. You can try signing in or changing directories.
Access to this page requires authorization. You can try changing directories.
This article describes new features in the .NET runtime for .NET 11. It was last updated for release candidate 2 (RC 2).
Updated minimum hardware requirements
The minimum hardware requirements for .NET 11 have been updated to require more modern instruction sets on both x86/x64 and Arm64 architectures. Additionally, the ReadyToRun (R2R) compilation targets have been updated to take advantage of newer hardware capabilities.
Arm64 requirements
For Apple, there's no change to the minimum hardware or the ReadyToRun target. The Apple M1 chips are approximately equivalent to armv8.5-a and provide support for at least the AdvSimd (NEON), CRC, DOTPROD, LSE, RCPC, RCPC2, and RDMA instruction sets.
For Linux, there's no change to the minimum hardware. .NET continues to support devices such as Raspberry Pi that might only provide support for the AdvSimd instruction set. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to include the LSE instruction set, which might result in additional jitting overhead if you launch an application.
For Windows, the baseline is updated to require the LSE instruction set. This is required by Windows 11 and by all Arm64 CPUs officially supported by Windows 10. Additionally, it's inline with the Arm SBSA (Server Base System Architecture) requirements. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to be armv8.2-a + RCPC, which provides support for at least AdvSimd, CRC, LSE, RCPC, and RDMA, and covers the majority of hardware officially supported.
x86/x64 requirements
For all three operating systems (Apple, Linux, and Windows), the baseline is updated from x86-64-v1 to x86-64-v2. This changes the hardware from only guaranteeing CMOV, CX8, SSE, and SSE2 to also guaranteeing CX16, POPCNT, SSE3, SSSE3, SSE4.1, and SSE4.2. This guarantee is required by Windows 11 and by all x86/x64 CPUs officially supported on Windows 10. It includes all chips still officially supported by Intel and AMD, with the last older chips having gone out of support around 2013.
The ReadyToRun target has been updated to x86-64-v3 for Windows and Linux, which additionally includes the AVX, AVX2, BMI1, BMI2, F16C, FMA, LZCNT, and MOVBE instruction sets. The ReadyToRun target for Apple remains unchanged.
Impact
Starting with .NET 11, .NET fails to run on older hardware and might print a message similar to the following:
The current CPU is missing one or more of the baseline instruction sets.
For ReadyToRun-capable assemblies, there might be additional startup overhead on some supported hardware that doesn't meet the expected support for a typical device.
Reason for change
.NET supports a broad range of hardware, often above and beyond the minimum hardware requirements put in place by the underlying operating system. This support adds significant complexity to the codebase, particularly for much older hardware that's unlikely to still be in use. Additionally, it defines a "lowest common denominator" that AOT targets must default to, which can, in some scenarios, lead to reduced performance.
The update to the minimum baseline was made to reduce the maintenance complexity of the codebase and to better align with the documented (and often enforced) hardware requirements of the underlying operating system.
For more information, see Minimum hardware requirements updated.
Runtime Async
.NET 11 introduces runtime-native async (Runtime Async V2), a significant step toward replacing compiler-generated async state machines with runtime-managed suspension and resumption. Instead of the compiler emitting state-machine classes, the runtime itself tracks async execution, producing cleaner stack traces, better debuggability, and lower overhead.
Runtime Async is a preview feature. To opt in, add the following property to your project file:
<PropertyGroup>
  <Features>runtime-async=on</Features>
</PropertyGroup>
A net11.0 project no longer requires <EnablePreviewFeatures>true</EnablePreviewFeatures> to use Runtime Async.
The .NET runtime libraries themselves are compiled with runtime-async=on. The runtime libraries no longer contain compiler-generated state machines and rely entirely on runtime-provided async. This makes it possible to migrate an entire app (with only library dependencies) to the new model, and it provides broad functional and performance validation of the feature. The product team welcomes any reports—positive or negative—about throughput and library size changes you observe.
.NET 11 also includes two additional improvements:
- Covariant Task → Task<T> overrides: When a derived class returns Task<T> for a base method that returns Task, the runtime now generates a void-returning thunk that bridges the calling convention difference, so virtual dispatch works for both flavors. The same fix applies to NativeAOT.
- Inlining in crossgen2: Restrictions that prevented runtime-async methods from being inlined during ReadyToRun (R2R) compilation have been removed. All async tests pass with both crossgen2 and composite R2R, and inlining of await-less async calls (the synchronous fast path) is confirmed end-to-end.
Note
The DOTNET_RuntimeAsync and UNSUPPORTED_RuntimeAsync environment variables that previously controlled runtime-async behavior have been removed. To opt out of runtime-async per project, set <UseRuntimeAsync>false</UseRuntimeAsync> in your project file instead of relying on the environment variable.
Cleaner live stack traces
The most visible improvement is in live stack traces—what profilers, debuggers, and new StackTrace() see during execution. With compiler-generated async, each async method produces multiple frames from state-machine infrastructure. With Runtime Async, the actual methods appear directly on the call stack.
// To enable runtime async, add the following to your .csproj:
//   <Features>runtime-async=on</Features>
await OuterAsync();
static async Task OuterAsync()
{
    await Task.CompletedTask;
    await MiddleAsync();
}
static async Task MiddleAsync()
{
    await Task.CompletedTask;
    await InnerAsync();
}
static async Task InnerAsync()
{
    await Task.CompletedTask;
    Console.WriteLine(new StackTrace(fNeedFileInfo: true));
}
Without runtime-async—13 frames, state-machine infrastructure visible:
   at Program.<<Main>$>g__InnerAsync|0_2() in Program.cs:line 24
   at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...)
   at Program.<<Main>$>g__InnerAsync|0_2()
   at Program.<<Main>$>g__MiddleAsync|0_1() in Program.cs:line 14
   at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...)
   at Program.<<Main>$>g__MiddleAsync|0_1()
   at Program.<<Main>$>g__OuterAsync|0_0() in Program.cs:line 8
   at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...)
   at Program.<<Main>$>g__OuterAsync|0_0()
   at Program.<Main>$(String[] args) in Program.cs:line 3
   at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...)
   at Program.<Main>$(String[] args)
   at Program.<Main>(String[] args)
With runtime-async—5 frames, the real call chain:
   at Program.<<Main>$>g__InnerAsync|0_2() in Program.cs:line 24
   at Program.<<Main>$>g__MiddleAsync|0_1() in Program.cs:line 14
   at Program.<<Main>$>g__OuterAsync|0_0() in Program.cs:line 8
   at Program.<Main>$(String[] args) in Program.cs:line 3
   at Program.<Main>(String[] args)
Note
Exception stack traces (from catch (Exception ex)) already look the same with or without Runtime Async, because existing ExceptionDispatchInfo cleanup in compiler-generated code handles that case. The improvement is in what you see during live execution.
This improvement benefits anything that inspects the live execution stack, including profiling tools, diagnostic logging, and the debugger call stack window.
NativeAOT and ReadyToRun support
Runtime Async supports NativeAOT and ReadyToRun compilation. This extends the feature beyond JIT-compiled code to ahead-of-time compiled scenarios. The runtime also reuses continuation objects more aggressively and avoids saving unchanged locals, reducing allocation pressure in async-heavy code.
Debugging improvements
Breakpoints now bind correctly inside runtime-async methods, and the debugger can step through await boundaries without jumping into compiler-generated infrastructure.
Runtime Async performance improvements
Runtime Async includes several performance improvements:
- JIT async support: The JIT compiles a dedicated runtime-async version of a synchronous, task-returning method rather than delegating through a thunk. The JIT turns the method's tail calls into runtime-async calls and awaits the task that would otherwise be returned, eliminating an extra layer of indirection.
- Tail-merged suspension points: The JIT tail-merges async suspension points so generated code is smaller.
- Cached continuations: Continuations used for runtime-async callable task thunks are cached and reused.
- Pooled methods opt out: Methods that are already pooled opt out of runtime-async, avoiding redundant work.
- Tiered async compilation: Async versions now flow through tiered compilation, so hot async methods get tier 1 optimizations after warm-up.
- Task and ValueTask factory intrinsics: The JIT recognizes common factories, such as Task.FromResult, Task.CompletedTask, and ValueTask.FromResult, and folds them into faster async paths.
- Tail-await optimizations: Implicit tailcalls from async methods are enabled again when the method directly returns another async result, and await Task.Yield() avoids extra allocations in runtime-async paths.
Async continuations without ExecutionContext
Async continuations can now opt out of ExecutionContext capture and restore. ExecutionContext carries ambient state—such as AsyncLocal<T> values—across await points. Every Task continuation previously captured a snapshot of the context and restored it before running, even when no AsyncLocal<T> state was in use and the restore was a no-op.
The runtime now detects when a continuation has nothing to restore and skips the capture/restore cycle entirely. Task, Task<T>, ValueTask, and ValueTask<T> all benefit from this change, as does the runtime-async implementation path. Applications that use ConfigureAwait(false) and AsyncLocal<T> sparingly see reduced overhead in high-throughput async code paths.
JIT improvements
- Bounds check elimination: The just-in-time (JIT) compiler now eliminates bounds checks for the common pattern where an index plus a constant is compared against a length, such as i + cns < len. It also eliminates more redundant bounds checks for index-from-end access (for example, values[^1]). These improvements reduce redundant checks in tight loops and improve throughput for array and span operations.
- Redundant checked context removal: The JIT can now prove and remove redundant checked arithmetic contexts—for example, when a value is already known to be in range. This optimization eliminates unnecessary overflow checks in generated code.
- Switch expression folding: Multi-target switch expressions now fold into simpler branchless checks when the targets are a small set of constants, for example x is 0 or 1 or 2 or 3 or 4.
- Faster uint-to-float/double casts: Casting uint to float or double is faster on pre-AVX-512 x86 hardware.
- SVE2 intrinsics: New Arm SVE2 (Scalable Vector Extension 2) intrinsics are available: ShiftRightLogicalNarrowingSaturate(Even|Odd). These expand the set of vectorized operations available on Arm hardware that supports SVE2.
- Math.BigMul on x64: Math.BigMul(long, long, out long) is now significantly faster on x64. The JIT generates a single MUL r/m64 instruction when both operands are 64-bit values and the caller requests the high half of the result, eliminating the previous helper call.
- Single-IG prolog restriction removed: The JIT no longer requires the function prolog to fit in a single instruction group (IG). Complex prologues with many saved registers, large stack allocations, or runtime-async state setup no longer trigger fallback paths.
- SELECT(cond, cns, cns) folding: The JIT now folds conditional selects whose two branches both produce the same constant into just that constant—for example, condition ? 42 : 42 becomes 42. This fold eliminates unnecessary comparisons that can appear after earlier optimizations unify branches.
- AVX-VNNI-512 intrinsics: System.Runtime.Intrinsics.X86.AvxVnni.V512 exposes 512-bit forms of the AVX-VNNI multiply-add intrinsics on CPUs with AVX512-VNNI support.
- Saturating floating-point conversions: Unchecked float and double conversions to small integer types now saturate to type bounds instead of wrapping through intermediate truncation.
- ARM64 Vector<T> by reference for SVE: When the runtime is compiled with ARM SVE support, Vector<T> values are passed by reference rather than by value, aligning with the ARM calling convention for scalable types and enabling better code generation for SVE-intensive code.
For better performance and code quality, .NET 11 adds several more JIT optimizations:
Constant-folding SequenceEqual
The JIT can now fold a string.Equals or ReadOnlySpan<T>.SequenceEqual call whose operands are both compile-time constants, replacing the byte-by-byte comparison with the constant true or false result. This matters most after inlining, when a caller passes another literal to a helper that compares against a known string. When IsAdmin is inlined into a caller that passes "Guest", the JIT sees "Guest" == "Admin" and folds it to false:
static bool IsAdmin(string role) => role == "Admin";
The optimization applies to string literals, const string fields, and UTF-8 literals (for example, "PNG"u8).
Devirtualization improvements
The JIT can now devirtualize generic virtual methods, including non-shared generic virtual methods and shared generic virtual methods that don't require a runtime lookup. Default interface methods declared on generic interfaces can now be devirtualized as well.
In addition, the result of Activator.CreateInstance<T>() is now treated as having an exact type, allowing the JIT to devirtualize subsequent calls made on the returned object.
These improvements unlock further downstream optimizations such as inlining and constant folding, reducing runtime dispatch overhead and improving performance. For example:
IfaceGeneric<string> caller = new Caller<string>();
Iface obj = Activator.CreateInstance<Impl>();
caller.DefaultImpl(obj, "test"); // Can be optimized down to Console.WriteLine("test")
interface Iface
{
    void GenericMethod<T>(T value);
}
interface IfaceGeneric<T>
{
    void DefaultImpl(Iface obj, T value) => obj.GenericMethod(value);
}
class Impl : Iface
{
    public void GenericMethod<T>(T value) => Console.WriteLine(value);
}
class Caller<T> : IfaceGeneric<T>
{
}
Here the JIT can determine the exact implementation behind both interface calls, devirtualize them, inline through the call chain, and ultimately fold the code down to the equivalent of Console.WriteLine("test").
Eliminating bounds checks after an empty-span guard
The JIT now picks up the length != 0 assertion from an empty-span check and uses it to prove the bounds check on the first element succeeds:
if (!span.IsEmpty && span[0] == value)
{
    // The bounds check on span[0] is now eliminated.
}
Redundant branch and test elimination
When an outer predicate is already implied by an inner branch, the JIT now removes the redundant outer check. Similarly, when code assigns a value in a conditional and then immediately tests it, the second test is eliminated:
if (x > 0)
{
    if (x > 1) S();  // The outer x > 0 check is folded away.
}
int y = condition ? 1 : 2;
if (y == 1) A(); else B();  // The y == 1 test is eliminated;
                             // each branch of the ternary goes directly to A() or B().
These optimizations are most visible after inlining, where guards from different methods land in the same compiled body.
Hardware intrinsics and code generation
.NET 11 includes several new hardware intrinsics and code generation improvements:
- Hardware FP16 instructions for Half arithmetic and conversions: The JIT uses hardware FP16 instructions for Half arithmetic and conversions when the processor supports them. On x64, arithmetic uses AVX10.1, while conversions between Half and float can use F16C (available on most AVX2-capable hardware). On Arm64, arithmetic uses the optional FP16 instruction set, while conversions between Half and float or double use baseline Arm64 instructions. The optimization requires no application changes and preserves the existing ABI representation of Half.
- Better cost modeling for x86/x64 SIMD: The JIT's floating-point execution and size costs previously reflected x87-era assumptions. Updated costs that reflect modern SSE/AVX hardware let the JIT make better decisions about hoisting and common subexpression elimination (CSE) around SIMD code.
- Faster DotProduct on AVX: Lowering for Vector128.Dot-style operations now emits a mul + permute + add sequence instead of vdpps/vdppd when AVX is available, which is consistently faster.
- Faster IndexOfAnyAsciiSearcher on Arm64: Arm64 versions of Vector*.Count, IndexOf, and LastIndexOf no longer route through ExtractMostSignificantBits, yielding a 5–50% improvement in workloads that use these APIs in their core loop.
- Arm64 ToScalar for 64-bit integers: ToScalar on Vector*<long> and Vector*<ulong> now uses fmov instead of umov, which is shorter and faster on most cores.
- SVE CreateWhile API expansion: CreateWhile gains signed, double, and single variants alongside the existing unsigned ones, completing the predicate-generation surface for SVE loops.
- New SVE2 and Arm64 instruction-set detection: The runtime now reports SVE_AES, SVE_SHA3, SVE_SM4, SHA3, and SM4 as separate instruction sets, allowing Sve2*.IsSupported queries for those features on capable hardware.
- AVX10 detection fix: The CPUID-bit cache for AVX10 was being overwritten by a later query, which could cause AVX10 to be misreported on capable hardware. This is now fixed.
ReadyToRun improvements
Comparer<T>.Default and EqualityComparer<T>.Default are now specialized in ReadyToRun (R2R) images. Previously, the default comparers used reflection that R2R couldn't see ahead of time, causing callers to fall back to the JIT. R2R now generates a specialized helper in the image—mirroring the NativeAOT approach—and benchmarks show up to a 20× improvement for collections operations that rely on the default comparer.
VM improvements
- Cached interface dispatch on non-JIT platforms: On platforms that lack JIT support, such as iOS, interface dispatch was falling back to an expensive generic fixup path. Cached dispatch yields up to 200x improvements in interface-heavy code on these targets.
- Guid.NewGuid() on Linux: Guid.NewGuid() on Linux now uses the getrandom() syscall with batch caching instead of reading from /dev/urandom, yielding approximately 12% throughput improvement for GUID generation.
WebAssembly improvements
Browser and WebAssembly support has several improvements:
- WebCIL payload loading: The runtime can now load WebCIL payloads directly, improving compatibility with browser-based deployment scenarios.
- Better debugging symbols: Symbol and stack trace quality for WebAssembly debugging has improved, making it easier to diagnose issues in browser-hosted .NET apps.
- float[], Span<float>, and ArraySegment<float> marshaling: float[], Span<float>, and ArraySegment<float> are now marshaled more directly across JavaScript boundaries, reducing overhead for interop-heavy code.
.NET includes improvements to CoreCLR-on-WebAssembly:
- WebCIL V1 is the default for CoreCLR WASM builds: The shared WebCIL header gains a TableBase field (28 → 32 bytes). Both Mono and CoreCLR readers accept V0 and V1. Crossgen2's WasmObjectWriter produces V1 directly, and CoreCLR-flavored WASM SDK builds default WasmWebcilVersion to V1.
- Native re-link works for CoreCLR WASM apps: A full Emscripten-based pipeline replaces the previous stub targets. Re-linking dotnet.native.wasm from the runtime pack and including custom native code via NativeFileReference now works.
- JavaScript minification in Release builds: Browser CoreCLR Release builds ship minified JavaScript.
- NativeAOT publish for WASM no longer drops package satellites: Satellite assemblies from NuGet packages are now passed to ILC and pruned from the publish output, fixing localization for AOT-published apps that depend on packages such as System.CommandLine.
CoreCLR on WebAssembly now runs the libraries test suite end to end.
Platform support for more than 1024 CPUs
The .NET runtime can now initialize on machines with more than 1024 logical processors. Previously, sched_getaffinity was called with the default cpu_set_t (capped at 1024), causing initialization to fail on high-core-count servers. The runtime now allocates the CPU set dynamically. The GC retains its 1024-heap limit, but the CPU count limit is removed.
In-process crash report logging
A new in-process crash reporting mechanism captures diagnostic information from within the crashing process before it terminates. Previously, crash diagnostics were collected by an out-of-process monitor. While the out-of-process approach is safe, it can miss information that's only available inside the dying process. The new in-process path logs the managed stack trace, module list, and key runtime state to a well-known path before the process exits.
This capability originated on mobile platforms and is now also available on Linux and macOS. When DOTNET_DbgEnableMiniDump isn't enabled, set DOTNET_EnableCrashReport=1 or DOTNET_EnableCrashReportOnly=1 to select the in-process reporter. Existing createdump behavior remains in place when minidumps are enabled.
NativeAOT: faster interface dispatch
NativeAOT now uses a dispatch helper for interface method calls. Instead of a direct fat-pointer call sequence, the runtime routes interface dispatch through a shared helper that can be patched to the correct implementation after the call site warms up. This reduces the binary size of interface call sites and improves throughput on workloads with many interface method calls.
Generic virtual method dispatch also uses the shared dispatch-cell infrastructure, which improves both monomorphic and polymorphic call performance. In addition, Assembly.GetCallingAssembly() now works on NativeAOT when stack trace data is available.
SIMD lane construction and composition
System.Runtime.Intrinsics now includes lane construction and composition APIs for hardware vector types. The new APIs let you construct a vector from individually specified lanes and extract or reorder lanes between vectors. This enables precise, portable control over SIMD vector element placement without falling back to platform-specific intrinsics.
The new methods fall into a few families:
- Patterned construction: CreateGeometricSequence, CreateAlternatingSequence, and CreateHarmonicSequence build a vector from a starting value and a rule.
- Interleave and de-interleave: Zip, ZipLower/ZipUpper, Unzip, UnzipEven/UnzipOdd.
- Rearrange: The Concat family (ConcatLowerLower, ConcatLowerUpper, ConcatUpperLower, ConcatUpperUpper) and Reverse.
using System.Runtime.Intrinsics;
// {1, 2, 4, 8} — each lane is the previous lane times two
Vector128<int> powers = Vector128.CreateGeometricSequence(1, 2);
// Interleave two vectors lane-by-lane
(Vector128<int> lower, Vector128<int> upper) =
    Vector128.Zip(Vector128.Create(1), Vector128.Create(2));
These APIs are available on Vector128<T>, Vector256<T>, Vector512<T>, Vector64<T>, and Vector<T>. They're building blocks for image processing, audio digital signal processing (DSP), and other SIMD-intensive workloads that need fine-grained control over vector element layout.
File locking on iOS and tvOS
On iOS and tvOS, including simulators, CoreCLR now disables advisory file locking by default. A FileStream that acquired an advisory lock could cause the operating system to terminate an app when the app entered the background while it held the lock. As a result, FileShare restrictions are no longer enforced by those locks on iOS and tvOS, including between handles in the same process. Mac Catalyst and other platforms keep their existing defaults.
If your app relies on FileShare enforcement and you accept the risk of suspension-related termination, restore file locking by using either of the following settings:
- Set the DOTNET_SYSTEM_IO_DISABLEFILELOCKING environment variable to 0.
- Set the System.IO.DisableFileLocking runtime configuration property to false. For example, in the runtimeconfig.json file:
{
  "configProperties": {
    "System.IO.DisableFileLocking": false
  }
}
Reliability fixes
The runtime includes fixes for the following issues:
- On Linux, the SDK no longer crashes on Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8 on Arm64, and the runtime correctly traverses cgroup v2 memory limits at the root of the hierarchy.
- Generic virtual method dispatch no longer hangs after repeated AssemblyLoadContext unloads.
- TryDequeue no longer spuriously reports an empty queue while a segment freezes during growth. TryPeek has the same reliability fix.
- On Windows, garbage collection works correctly on machines with multiple CPU groups.
Runtime diagnostics
The async profiler now instruments both runtime-async methods and compiler-generated async state-machine methods, so tools receive one consistent event model regardless of async implementation style. The runtime also adds improved interpreter perf-map logging support, and fixes parsing of CORECLR_NOTIFICATION_PROFILERS lists that don't end with a semicolon.
