- carousel: Build a carousel component that displays a set of items in a horizontal or vertical layout.
- checkbox: Style checkboxes, including custom icons, layout, colors, check/uncheck animations, while preserving native functionality and accessibility.
- copy-button: Build a copy button that copies text from arbitrary elements to the clipboard.
- dark-mode-toggle: Build a dark mode toggle component that allows users to override their system color scheme preference for the current site.
- dialog: Build a modal or non-modal dialog component that is accessible, manages focus appropriately, and can be dismissed the way users expect on each platform.
- hovercard: Build a hovercard component that displays an interactive structured preview of the page a certain type of link (e.g. a user profile) will navigate to when hovered over.
- menu: Build a menu component that displays a list of options or actions, with support for nested submenus.
- navbar: Build a site navigation bar that adapts across screen sizes and indicates the current page.
- navigation-drawer: Create a navigation drawer component that, when triggered from a menu button, slides in from the side overlaid on top of existing page content, and slides out when dismissed (by swiping away, tapping outside, or pressing escape).
- persistent-app-tours: Create persistent onboarding walkthroughs using tethered native overlays that stay open during user interaction.
- persistent-toast-notifications: Create non-intrusive toast and overlay notifications for persistent, stackable messaging and state communication.
- progress: Build a styled progress bar that communicates completion of a task or process, in both determinate and indeterminate states.
- progress-ring: Build a progress ring component that visually represents the completion status of a task or process, with support for content in the center and brand-consistent styling.
- scrollspy: Highlight the currently visible section of a page in a navigation menu
- spinner: Build a loading spinner that communicates busy state to all users, respects reduced-motion preferences, and animates efficiently.
- stack-drill-down: Build full-screen hierarchical navigation that lets users drill down into nested views and swipe or navigate back to return, with browser history kept in sync.
- tabs: Build a responsive tabbed interface with good UX when not all tabs fit on screen.
- toolbar: Build a toolbar component that displays a set of controls for performing actions.
- content-first-noise-reduction: Maximize content and reduce noise by removing blocking popups, keeping persistent navigation compact, and moving secondary content behind on-demand disclosure.

- custom-text-decorations: Add text decorations such as underlines, overlines, strikethroughs, or entirely custom shapes, with reveal animations, custom offsets and end insets, and flexible ink skipping.

- dark-mode: Implement dark mode support in a way that respects the user's light/dark theme preference and adapts browser UI (e.g. scrollbars, form controls, etc)

- webmcp: Use this guide to implement WebMCP in browser applications, exposing client-side functionality as tools to AI agents via declarative or imperative APIs.
- Progressive Enhancement & Nuanced Fallbacks: We distinguish between purely additive enhancements (like speculative preloading) which are safe to let older browsers silently ignore, and critical behaviors (like dialog controls or network beacons) where we write highly considered, low-overhead fallbacks.
- Responsible Fallbacks: We prioritize lightweight, case-specific custom fallbacks (<50 LOC) or conditionally-loaded polyfills instead of heavy third-party bundles.
- Gotchas & Quirks: We document hidden platform limitations, such as the 64KB payload quota for fetchLater() or macOS-specific scrollbar behaviors.
- Baseline-Aware Integration: We leverage real-time compatibility data from the Baseline project so agents dynamically adapt to current browser support.
- Origin Trial & Volatile Feature Gates: Guides covering experimental Origin Trial APIs or volatile features (single-engine features shipped within the last 3 months or still stabilizing) remain discoverable via search, but are gated on retrieve so agents do not adopt unstable APIs without explicit developer consent.
Configure Origin Trial and volatile feature opt-ins for a repository with an optional .mwgrc JSON file in your project root (or ~/.mwgrc as a user-level fallback), which you can commit to share across your team:
- Activation: The coding agent activates the modern-web-guidance skill because of a relevant task. The agent is instructed to use the modern-web-guidance CLI for web platform queries.
- Local Semantic Search: The agent runs modern-web-guidance search "<query>". The tool matches the query to the best guide using an offline, zero-dependency embedding model and BM25 search engine (no network calls, no API keys).
- Guide Fetch: The agent retrieves the guide via modern-web-guidance retrieve <guide-id>, inserting targeted code patterns, gotchas, and fallbacks directly into its context window.
Tip
Note: We use npx to ensure the content doesn't go stale, but the CLI works offline, completely private and local.
The npm package is self-contained, with no extra dependencies to ensure both low-latency and supply-chain security.
Vercel Skills CLI (aka npx skills)
npx skills add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance
GitHub CLI
gh skill install GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance
Google Antigravity
agy plugin install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance
GitHub Copilot CLI
/plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance
/plugin install modern-web-guidance@googlechrome
Claude Code Plugin
/plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance
/plugin install modern-web-guidance@googlechrome
/plugin  # Select GoogleChrome marketplace, press enter, enable AutoUpdate
/reload-plugins
Grok Build CLI
grok plugin install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance --trust
Kimi Code
/plugins install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance
OpenAI Codex
codex plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance
codex plugin add modern-web-guidance@googlechrome
If you installed the skill using npx modern-web-guidance@latest install, you can update with: npx modern-web-guidance@latest update.
Otherwise, consult your agent's documentation for updating plugins and skills.
We developed a robust eval harness to ensure that the content is empirically proven and continuously calibrated so AI agents write better code. We run automated evaluations using a closed-loop validation pipeline:
  [ Expert-authored guidance and demo ]
            │
            ▼
  [ Target generation ] ──> Tasks on real webapps, Golden solutions, Playwright graders
            │
            ▼
  [ Calibration loop ] ───> Runs Grader on Golden Solutions (Must Pass 100%)
            │               Runs Grader on Unmodified Base App (Must Fail 100%)
            ▼
  [ E2E agent evals ] ────> Runs coding agents in guided vs. unguided modes
                            Compares pass rates and accessibility w/ and w/o the skill
- Simulated Developer Tasks: We define realistic developer prompts against full base applications (daily-grind, devtools-times) that mimic real-world requests (e.g., "make my images load faster"). Prompts avoid naming APIs or features, testing whether the agent can naturally discover and apply the right guides.
- Static & Browser-Based Assertions: Playwright graders verify that each implementation requirement was followed—checking source patterns, computed styles, runtime DOM behaviors, and accessibility states.
- Self-Healing Calibration: Graders are calibrated against multi-agent (Claude/Codex/AGY) golden solutions (100% pass target) and an unmodified baseline application (0% pass target).
- E2E Testing: We measure coding agent performance on real tasks with and without guidance. The opportunity (100% - unguided pass rate) and uplift (guided - unguided pass rate) are key: if models already succeed without guidance, we prune redundant advice; where agents struggle, we refine guides to maximize uplift.
Explore full per-agent and per-guide breakdowns on the Eval Dashboard.
You can customize which skill packs are installed using the --choose flag:
npx modern-web-guidance@latest install --choose
- modern-web-guidance (~205 tokens): Comprehensive guidance on modern browser APIs, layouts, and performance.
- chrome-extensions (~175 tokens): Guidance on Manifest V3, background workers, extension APIs, and Chrome Web Store publishing.
Google collects anonymous usage information to improve the tool's reliability, relevance, and performance. Collected information includes installation counts, the calling agent name, guide retrieval IDs, and CLI tool search queries generated by the agent (e.g. "dark mode scrollbar color-scheme"). Raw user prompts are not collected. You can inspect what is collected in modern-web.ts.
Tip
To Opt-Out: set the DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 env variable in your shell profile (e.g., .bashrc or .zshrc):
export DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1
Google handles this data in accordance with the Google Privacy Policy.
Found a bug, outdated pattern, or missing web platform feature? Open an issue or see CONTRIBUTING.md in the source repository (GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src).
Huge thanks to everyone who has contributed!

Portions of the documentation in this project are derived from MDN Web Docs by Mozilla Contributors and W3C, WHATWG, and IETF specifications.

articles.title: Cyberattacks threaten to make open source AI a little less open, Hugging Face exec warns
articles.body:
The very qualities that make open AI platforms valuable, like open doors and rich data, might also make them vulnerable to more hacks, Irene Solaiman, chief policy officer and SVP of strategy at Hugging Face, said on a recent episode of the Equity podcast.
The October attack on OpenCode, which targeted users’ third-party API keys and caused financial damage, is the latest example. It follows an incident this summer in which an OpenAI agent swarm breached Hugging Face in an apparent attempt to cover its tracks after accessing answers to cybersecurity evaluations.
The risks aren’t limited to platforms that invite open community contributions. On Monday, AI infrastructure startup Fireworks, which helps developers run and train open AI models, disclosed that attackers had accessed some customers’ model weights, datasets, and billing information. The company temporarily disabled certain self-service dataset functions as it investigates. While the attack isn’t necessarily due to Fireworks’ openness, it highlights how much valuable information is concentrated within AI infrastructure providers.
“The things I worry about making an open community targeted are also what makes it special,” Solaiman said on Equity. “We are necessarily permissive. We want the average hobbyist in their basement who doesn’t have an institutional affiliation to be able to contribute.”
“You want people to be able to just submit pull requests and allow anybody without a valid affiliation to contribute … but then you have some losers who ruin it for the rest,” she added in a separate conversation.
That permissiveness isn’t the only thing drawing attackers. The wealth of information open platforms host also makes them targets. Hugging Face became a temptation for OpenAI’s agent swarm because of the evaluation datasets it holds, whereas OpenCode’s target in this case came from its “juicy third-party API keys,” per Solaiman.
“The combination of that makes us prime targets,” Solaiman told TechCrunch in a separate conversation. She added that there’s a “danger of open source really closing down at a time when we’ve gotten so much public support.”
Much of the industry has come out recently in support of open AI models, including heavy hitters like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. And increasingly, governments, enterprises, and startups are relying on open models to build.
So what would a pullback actually look like? It could theoretically mean restrictions on who can upload models or datasets, more stringent identity verification, or additional vetting of developers before they can access certain features. While these moves could protect platforms from attackers, it could also make it more difficult for independent researchers and hobbyists to participate in communities they would have been welcomed in before.
For now, Hugging Face is trying to avoid that route. Solaiman said the company has been beefing up monitoring tools to catch hacks, as well as taking steps to prevent them. But monitoring can be expensive to maintain, she noted, and not every platform will be able to afford it.
“Administrative access tokens were part of what gave that agent swarm better access, so we just rotate them a lot more frequently than we used to,” Solaiman said. “We also now have stricter network controls.”
In other words, the credentials that give admins broad access to Hugging Face’s systems now get changed more often, which means a stolen token would be useful for less time.
Other parts of the open source ecosystem are dealing with similar security-related trade-offs. GitHub, the world’s largest host for open source projects, has been fighting off attackers who inject malicious code into projects to quickly spread malware. The company began tightening security requirements for publishing packages to the npm registry, revoking older authentication tokens, and limiting how long new ones remain valid.
Zach Steindler, an engineer at GitHub who handles software supply chain security, told TechCrunch via email that while security measures can disrupt established workflows, the platforms can become more secure without fundamentally restricting participation.
“It’s less about limiting functionality and more about going and fixing things that weren’t secure in the first place,” Steindler said. He noted that npm install scripts have existed for years, but recent attacks highlighted how dangerous they could be. GitHub worked with OpenJS — a nonprofit that hosts critical open source projects built with JavaScript — on a safer approach.
The same logic applies to where security teams put their effort, per Steindler: “Security is all about maximizing impact with the resources we have, and I would much rather invest in detecting suspicious behavior and containment capabilities: things that cover all accounts and access methods. Suspicious behavior is suspicious regardless of who is exhibiting it.”

articles.title: .NET 11
articles.body:
Today, we’re excited to announce the release of .NET 11! This year’s release makes building modern applications faster, more productive, and has improvements across C# 15, ASP.NET Core, .NET MAUI, and Windows development. With hundreds of runtime optimizations, more responsive SDK tooling, and less overhead in everyday commands, you can spend less time waiting and more time creating. Build richer web and cross-platform applications, take advantage of new C# language features, and explore AI-powered development with improved tools and agentic capabilities.
.NET 11 support
.NET 11 is a Standard Term Support (STS) release with two years of support under the .NET support policy. STS and Long Term Support (LTS) releases have the same quality and servicing policies; the difference is the length of support. .NET 10 remains a supported LTS option. Stay current with servicing updates whichever release you choose.
Join us at .NET Conf, November 10-13
Explore .NET 11 with the product teams and community at .NET Conf 2026. The conference includes product team sessions on November 10 and 11, followed by two days of community sessions.
Watch the Day 1 livestream, including the keynote, or browse the conference session playlist.
What’s new in .NET 11
Some of the changes we’re most excited for you to try:
- C# 15 union types and closed hierarchies help you express the possible states of your application and handle them with compiler-checked patterns.
- A Native AOT CLI host and a warm MSBuild server reduce overhead in everyday developer workflows.
- ASP.NET Core brings asynchronous validation, OpenAPI 3.2, and new capabilities for Blazor and SignalR applications. Experimental Blazor AI components integrate with the Agent User Interaction Protocol (AG-UI) for advanced agentic web experiences.
- Build AI-powered, agentic applications with Microsoft.Extensions.AI (MEAI) for model access, MCP for tool integration, and Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) for agents and workflows.
- Put agentic development tools to work with .NET Skills for .NET-specific guidance, .NET MAUI DevFlow for inspecting and testing running apps, and the .NET Upgrade canvas for reviewing modernization progress.
- .NET MAUI adopts CoreCLR as its default runtime and improves XAML iteration and native controls.
- The libraries add built-in Zstandard compression, simpler process execution, richer JSON support, and new ways to work with in-memory data without copying it first.
The what’s new in .NET 11 overview links to the full details. Here are the changes behind those headlines and how to start using them.
Languages
C# 15
C# 15 is the default language version for projects targeting .NET 11. Union types are one of its biggest additions: a value can be one of a declared set of case types, with conversions from those types and exhaustiveness checking in switch expressions.
Consider a product lookup that either finds a product or reports that it wasn’t found:
ProductLookup result = new Product(42, "Mechanical keyboard");
string message = result switch
{
    Product product => $"Found {product.Name}",
    ProductNotFound missing => $"No product with ID {missing.Id}",
};
Console.WriteLine(message);
public sealed record Product(int Id, string Name);
public sealed record ProductNotFound(int Id);
public union ProductLookup(Product, ProductNotFound);
The result type tells a caller which outcomes it needs to handle. There’s no need to use object or an unrelated base class just to put those outcomes behind one return type.
C# 15 also adds closed hierarchies. A closed class limits direct derivation to its declaring assembly, giving the compiler the information it needs to check patterns over the hierarchy. Unions are useful when you want to combine existing types; closed hierarchies fit models where you own the inheritance relationship.
Smaller language features help with everyday code, too. Collection expression arguments let you pass constructor or factory arguments without giving up collection expression syntax:
HashSet<string> names =
    [with(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), "Alice", "ALICE", "Bob"];
Console.WriteLine(names.Count);
This prints 2: the comparer controls equality, so "Alice" and "ALICE" are one entry.
Other additions include extension indexers and labeled break and continue. These features don’t require the preview language version. The separate memory safety work remains in preview; see the C# 15 feature documentation for its opt-in requirements.
F# 11
F# 11 improves compiler memory use and reduces allocations in FSharp.Core collection operations. It also adds ways to bound concurrent asynchronous work, useful when a collection operation would otherwise start more work than a service or machine can handle comfortably.
The F# release notes distinguish the default-language updates from preview capabilities, including Runtime Async support for custom computation-expression builders.
Platform
SDK
The SDK now enables a Native AOT CLI host by default. Commands such as help and version queries can run without starting the managed CLI, and tool launches can avoid that startup path too. Commands that need managed execution still use it.
The MSBuild server also stays warm between CLI invocations by default, reducing repeated startup work. SDK installers on Linux and macOS are smaller through assembly deduplication.
File-based apps can grow across source files with #:include, and solution filters can be created and edited from the CLI. dotnet watch adds Aspire app-host integration, crash recovery, and device selection for mobile projects.
For teams using Microsoft.Testing.Platform, dotnet test gains run-level timeouts, failure limits, clearer progress reporting, and per-module results directories. The test runner matters: these switches aren’t interchangeable with the VSTest command-line options.
Container publishing adds reproducible image digests through SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH and avoids redundant layer uploads when the target manifest already exists. NuGet source configuration gains a minimum package publication age setting, which lets teams wait before newly published package versions become eligible for selection. This is an additional policy control, not a replacement for vulnerability checks or reviewing dependencies.
See what’s new in the SDK and tooling for command examples and configuration.
Runtime and performance
Performance work in .NET 11 reaches both the code you deploy and the tools you use to develop it. Stephen Toub’s Performance Improvements in .NET 11 takes a detailed tour through hundreds of runtime and library optimizations, with benchmarks and code examples.
The just-in-time (JIT) compiler improvements remove more redundant bounds checks and branches, improve devirtualization, and fold more operations into constants. For example, the JIT can optimize additional SequenceEqual calls when it knows the inputs at compile time. These changes improve generated code without requiring you to rewrite the corresponding application logic.
Native AOT interface dispatch uses a shared helper that reduces the code needed at interface call sites and improves throughput for interface-heavy workloads. Hardware support also expands, including FP16 instructions for Half operations on supported x64 and Arm64 hardware and new vector construction and composition APIs.
There’s useful work on diagnostics, too. In-process crash report logging can capture a managed stack trace, module information, and runtime state before a process exits. Previously available on mobile platforms, this reporting path now also supports Linux and macOS.
As always, measure the effect on your own application. Throughput, startup time, memory use, and deployment size depend on the workload and publishing options you choose.
Runtime Async has been a recurring theme throughout the .NET 11 previews. It moves asynchronous suspension and resumption into the runtime instead of relying on compiler-generated state machines.
One especially useful result is a clearer live call stack. Profilers and debuggers can show the asynchronous methods themselves instead of the infrastructure used to execute them. This is a distinction from exception stack traces, which already hide much of that infrastructure.
Runtime Async remains a preview feature. To try it in a project targeting net11.0, add:
<PropertyGroup>
  <Features>runtime-async=on</Features>
</PropertyGroup>
You don’t need to enable EnablePreviewFeatures for this scenario. The .NET runtime libraries themselves are built with Runtime Async, but opting your application’s code into the new compilation model is a separate choice. See the Runtime Async documentation for its behavior and current guidance, and test your application’s dependencies and diagnostics before adopting it.
AI libraries and tools
The .NET 11 SDK includes an MCP server template. MCP gives AI applications a common way to discover and call tools and services. The template uses the official MCP C# SDK and includes a working sample tool, so you can start exposing your own functionality without first installing a separate template package:
dotnet new mcpserver -o MyMcpServer
For applications that consume AI services, Microsoft.Extensions.AI (MEAI) provides abstractions such as IChatClient and IEmbeddingGenerator. These libraries let you compose model access with dependency injection, caching, and OpenTelemetry using familiar .NET patterns. They’re available as NuGet packages, rather than features that require you to move all of your application code to a new framework version.
Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) builds on these abstractions with agents that call tools and maintain conversation state, plus workflows that coordinate agents and application code. Connect agents to MCP tools to give them access to your application’s capabilities, and expose an agent through an ASP.NET Core AG-UI endpoint to build an interactive Blazor experience. The AG-UI hosting integration is currently prerelease.
For hands-on examples, start with .NET AI Essentials: The Core Building Blocks Explained and continue with our Microsoft Agent Framework walkthrough.
Libraries
The .NET libraries add capabilities that previously required extra setup, intermediate buffers, or custom helpers.
The Process API expansion includes one-shot methods to run a process and capture its output and exit status. More advanced APIs give you control over inherited handles, suspended starts, and process signaling. Build tools and developer utilities can spend less code on process plumbing while still inspecting how a child process finished. See Process API Improvements in .NET 11 for examples.
Zstandard compression joins the existing compression formats in System.IO.Compression. New span-based compression APIs support callers that manage their own buffers, and ZIP improvements include CRC32 validation when reading entries.
Four new in-memory stream adapters bridge existing data to APIs that accept a Stream: ReadOnlyMemoryStream, WritableMemoryStream, ReadOnlySequenceStream, and StringStream. For example, a pipeline’s segmented ReadOnlySequence<byte> can be read as a stream without first flattening it into a new contiguous buffer.
System.Text.Json adds support for C# unions, F# discriminated unions, and JSON Lines output from asynchronous sequences. F# union support uses reflection and doesn’t support source generation, trimming, or Native AOT, so check the documented limits before choosing it for a trimmed application.
LINQ adds FullJoin, which preserves unmatched elements from both inputs. This is useful for reconciliation work, such as comparing two inventories where you need to see missing items on either side.
The libraries also expand numeric types, DNS resolution, cryptography, and tracing configuration. The library overview covers the complete set of changes and marks APIs that remain experimental.
Entity Framework Core 11
Entity Framework Core 11 improves how your model becomes a query and how that query becomes SQL.
EF Core removes unnecessary joins in more reference-navigation and split-query scenarios, improves GroupBy translation, and translates the new LINQ FullJoin operator on relational providers that support it. These changes can simplify generated SQL while letting more queries stay in LINQ.
Complex types and JSON columns can now be used on entities mapped with table-per-type or table-per-concrete-type inheritance. Other improvements include migrations tooling and additional provider-specific JSON capabilities.
For SQL Server applications, EF Core adds support for vector indexes and approximate vector search. The SQL Server features and corresponding EF APIs are experimental. See the vector search documentation and limitations before evaluating them.
EF Core 11 requires .NET 11. When upgrading, check your database provider’s compatibility and the EF Core 11 breaking changes as well as the runtime changes.
Developer tools
The new dotnetup toolchain manager lets you install and update .NET SDKs and runtimes in your user account. It’s currently in public preview and helps you manage side-by-side versions and keep up with servicing updates.
.NET Skills gives coding agents task-specific guidance from the .NET team. Our .NET Skills introduction explains how to add these skills to your coding agent.
The experimental .NET MAUI DevFlow toolkit exposes a running app’s visual tree, screenshots, and interaction tools, so an agent can inspect and test the UI rather than work only from source code.
For modernization, the .NET Upgrade canvas gives you a visual view of a GitHub Copilot upgrade session. Review assessment findings and dependency compatibility, follow implementation tasks, and monitor failures and progress as the upgrade agent works. Our modernization walkthrough in the GitHub Copilot app covers the workflow from assessment through execution.
Workloads
Web: ASP.NET Core and Blazor
Application types are most useful when the rest of the stack understands them. ASP.NET Core supports C# unions wherever it uses System.Text.Json, including JSON request and response bodies in Minimal APIs and MVC. Generated OpenAPI documents describe the union’s alternatives with an anyOf schema.
This support applies to JSON bodies, not to route, query, header, or form binding. When multiple union cases have the same JSON shape, configure a classifier so deserialization can distinguish them. The ASP.NET Core union documentation explains those boundaries.
Validation also becomes more practical for rules that need to do I/O. Asynchronous validation works with the new asynchronous DataAnnotations APIs, so a validator can await a database lookup or a remote call instead of blocking a thread. Minimal APIs and Blazor forms can use this support.
OpenAPI 3.2 is now the default for generated documents. Among other improvements, it lets the document describe the per-event payload of a server-sent event stream. If a client generator or another part of your toolchain doesn’t yet support 3.2, you can explicitly select an earlier document version.
For long-lived connections, SignalR authentication refresh lets a connection refresh authentication without reconnecting. Blazor Interactive Server components can receive the updated identity and react when claims change.
Blazor adds capabilities for both statically rendered pages and interactive applications.
The new CacheView component caches the rendered output of a component subtree during static server-side rendering. On a cache hit, Blazor replays the markup without creating those child components or running their lifecycle methods. That gives you a smaller unit of caching for expensive, mostly static sections of a page.
Interactive Server apps can opt into automatic circuit pause when a browser tab becomes inactive. After a configurable delay, pausing frees the server memory and SignalR connection held by an inactive user. The feature requires an additional package and explicit configuration; upgrading doesn’t silently change your application’s circuit behavior.
Forms gain client-side validation for static server rendering and asynchronous validation support. QuickGrid and Virtualize add ways to move to a particular item, useful when returning a user to their place in a large collection.
Blazor also adds components for agentic user interfaces. The new Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.AI package includes components for streaming chat, tool rendering, approval flows, and shared UI state. Basic chat works with any IChatClient. For advanced experiences with a remote agent, the AG-UI .NET integration carries streamed responses, tool events, approval requests, and shared-state updates between an ASP.NET Core agent endpoint and the Blazor UI.
The Blazor AI components package is experimental and remains prerelease throughout .NET 11. It’s an opportunity to try the direction and give feedback, not a stable part of the ASP.NET Core shared framework. See the Blazor AI components documentation.
The AG-UI .NET SDK introduction covers the protocol’s client and server APIs. Build Agentic UI with the new Blazor AI components puts them together in a working app.
See what’s new in ASP.NET Core for the Blazor features, configuration examples, and compatibility details.
Client: .NET MAUI
.NET MAUI in .NET 11 makes CoreCLR the default runtime across its platforms. The move to CoreCLR brings mobile and desktop apps onto the same runtime foundation as other .NET workloads. On Apple platforms that don’t allow JIT compilation, the runtime uses precompiled code and the interpreter rather than generating native code at runtime.
Native AOT is an opt-in publishing alternative; its Android support remains experimental. Review the platform-specific runtime guidance and test your app’s libraries when choosing a deployment model.
The UI development loop gets attention, too:
- XAML Incremental Hot Reload is a preview feature in .NET 11. It updates live instances of pages and controls, including supported structural edits, without requiring you to navigate away and back. It’s enabled by default in Debug builds.
- Implicit XAML namespace declarations remove the need to repeat the standard namespace declarations at the root of every file.
- Windows uses the new CollectionView2 handler by default, while Android Shell adopts a handler-based architecture.
- New mobile test templates and dotnet test device selection bring testing into the CLI workflow.
These are meaningful runtime and handler changes, so exercise navigation, custom handlers, and trimmed publishing as part of your upgrade. The optional Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility package no longer ships; apps that still reference it need to migrate off it.
.NET MAUI follows its own support policy, separate from the .NET runtime’s STS and LTS lifecycle.
Windows: WinUI, Windows Forms, and WPF
For new Windows desktop apps, WinUI 3 is the recommended native UI framework, pairing C# and XAML with modern controls and the Fluent Design System. It’s delivered through the Windows App SDK, which also makes modern Windows APIs available to existing WPF and Windows Forms apps.
To add UI tests, see UWP and WinUI 3 apps: UI testing with MSTest.
Windows Forms in .NET 11 adds an opt-in modern visual styles mode that you can select at the application or control level. It also adds ways to react to system visual and accessibility settings, defer revealing a form until it’s ready, and suspend painting during bulk updates.
These controls let you introduce refreshed rendering where it makes sense for your application instead of treating a framework upgrade as an automatic visual redesign.
WPF updates focus on reliability, including fixes for Fluent window backdrops, window manager failures, and weak-event cleanup. Self-contained Windows publishing also includes a native dependency needed by apps that load mixed-mode WPF assemblies.
Get started and plan your upgrade
Install the .NET 11 SDK. Use a compatible, up-to-date Visual Studio 2026 installation, or Visual Studio Code with C# Dev Kit.
To create and run a console app:
dotnet new console -n HelloDotnet11 -f net11.0
dotnet run --project HelloDotnet11
You can replace the generated program with either of the C# examples above to try the new language features.
For an existing application, plan the upgrade across your development and deployment environments:
- Update the SDK selection in global.json if your repository pins it, and install the matching SDK on development machines and build agents.
- Update target frameworks to .NET 11, preserving platform-specific target framework suffixes where applicable. Update packages and workloads to compatible versions.
- Review the .NET 11 breaking changes, including the updated minimum CPU requirements. Installing a new SDK alone doesn’t retarget your app.
- Run your tests and measure the application under a representative workload. Validate your actual publishing mode, container base images, native dependencies, and deployment hosts.
Upgrading from .NET 8 or .NET 9
.NET 8 and .NET 9 reach end of support on November 10, 2026. Move to a supported release to continue receiving fixes. Choose .NET 11 for the latest capabilities, or .NET 10 if its LTS lifecycle fits your requirements better. See the .NET support policy for dates and servicing requirements.
If you’re upgrading from a .NET 11 release candidate, update to the final SDK, runtime, and compatible package and workload versions rather than staying on a prerelease build.
Thank you for building .NET with us
.NET 11 is the work of over 7,000 contributors. Thank you to everyone who contributed code, tested previews, reported issues, and helped us make better design decisions throughout the year. Your feedback across the previews and release candidates helped shape what we’re shipping today.
The .NET ecosystem continues to grow, with more than 589,000 unique packages on NuGet and over 1.1 trillion package downloads.
Download .NET 11, try it with an application you know well, and join us at .NET Conf to learn directly from the people building it. Share your results and questions in the .NET GitHub discussions.

Languages
C# 15
C# 15 is the default language version for projects targeting .NET 11. Union types are one of its biggest additions: a value can be one of a declared set of case types, with conversions from those types and exhaustiveness checking in switch expressions.
Consider a product lookup that either finds a product or reports that it wasn’t found:
ProductLookup result = new Product(42, "Mechanical keyboard");
string message = result switch
{
    Product product => $"Found {product.Name}",
    ProductNotFound missing => $"No product with ID {missing.Id}",
};
Console.WriteLine(message);
public sealed record Product(int Id, string Name);
public sealed record ProductNotFound(int Id);
public union ProductLookup(Product, ProductNotFound);
The result type tells a caller which outcomes it needs to handle. There’s no need to use object or an unrelated base class just to put those outcomes behind one return type.
C# 15 also adds closed hierarchies. A closed class limits direct derivation to its declaring assembly, giving the compiler the information it needs to check patterns over the hierarchy. Unions are useful when you want to combine existing types; closed hierarchies fit models where you own the inheritance relationship.
Smaller language features help with everyday code, too. Collection expression arguments let you pass constructor or factory arguments without giving up collection expression syntax:
HashSet<string> names =
    [with(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), "Alice", "ALICE", "Bob"];
Console.WriteLine(names.Count);
This prints 2: the comparer controls equality, so "Alice" and "ALICE" are one entry.
Other additions include extension indexers and labeled break and continue. These features don’t require the preview language version. The separate memory safety work remains in preview; see the C# 15 feature documentation for its opt-in requirements.
F# 11
F# 11 improves compiler memory use and reduces allocations in FSharp.Core collection operations. It also adds ways to bound concurrent asynchronous work, useful when a collection operation would otherwise start more work than a service or machine can handle comfortably.
The F# release notes distinguish the default-language updates from preview capabilities, including Runtime Async support for custom computation-expression builders.
Platform
SDK
The SDK now enables a Native AOT CLI host by default. Commands such as help and version queries can run without starting the managed CLI, and tool launches can avoid that startup path too. Commands that need managed execution still use it.
The MSBuild server also stays warm between CLI invocations by default, reducing repeated startup work. SDK installers on Linux and macOS are smaller through assembly deduplication.
File-based apps can grow across source files with #:include, and solution filters can be created and edited from the CLI. dotnet watch adds Aspire app-host integration, crash recovery, and device selection for mobile projects.
For teams using Microsoft.Testing.Platform, dotnet test gains run-level timeouts, failure limits, clearer progress reporting, and per-module results directories. The test runner matters: these switches aren’t interchangeable with the VSTest command-line options.
Container publishing adds reproducible image digests through SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH and avoids redundant layer uploads when the target manifest already exists. NuGet source configuration gains a minimum package publication age setting, which lets teams wait before newly published package versions become eligible for selection. This is an additional policy control, not a replacement for vulnerability checks or reviewing dependencies.
See what’s new in the SDK and tooling for command examples and configuration.
Runtime and performance
Performance work in .NET 11 reaches both the code you deploy and the tools you use to develop it. Stephen Toub’s Performance Improvements in .NET 11 takes a detailed tour through hundreds of runtime and library optimizations, with benchmarks and code examples.
The just-in-time (JIT) compiler improvements remove more redundant bounds checks and branches, improve devirtualization, and fold more operations into constants. For example, the JIT can optimize additional SequenceEqual calls when it knows the inputs at compile time. These changes improve generated code without requiring you to rewrite the corresponding application logic.
Native AOT interface dispatch uses a shared helper that reduces the code needed at interface call sites and improves throughput for interface-heavy workloads. Hardware support also expands, including FP16 instructions for Half operations on supported x64 and Arm64 hardware and new vector construction and composition APIs.
There’s useful work on diagnostics, too. In-process crash report logging can capture a managed stack trace, module information, and runtime state before a process exits. Previously available on mobile platforms, this reporting path now also supports Linux and macOS.
As always, measure the effect on your own application. Throughput, startup time, memory use, and deployment size depend on the workload and publishing options you choose.
Runtime Async has been a recurring theme throughout the .NET 11 previews. It moves asynchronous suspension and resumption into the runtime instead of relying on compiler-generated state machines.
One especially useful result is a clearer live call stack. Profilers and debuggers can show the asynchronous methods themselves instead of the infrastructure used to execute them. This is a distinction from exception stack traces, which already hide much of that infrastructure.
Runtime Async remains a preview feature. To try it in a project targeting net11.0, add:
<PropertyGroup>
  <Features>runtime-async=on</Features>
</PropertyGroup>
You don’t need to enable EnablePreviewFeatures for this scenario. The .NET runtime libraries themselves are built with Runtime Async, but opting your application’s code into the new compilation model is a separate choice. See the Runtime Async documentation for its behavior and current guidance, and test your application’s dependencies and diagnostics before adopting it.
AI libraries and tools
The .NET 11 SDK includes an MCP server template. MCP gives AI applications a common way to discover and call tools and services. The template uses the official MCP C# SDK and includes a working sample tool, so you can start exposing your own functionality without first installing a separate template package:
dotnet new mcpserver -o MyMcpServer
For applications that consume AI services, Microsoft.Extensions.AI (MEAI) provides abstractions such as IChatClient and IEmbeddingGenerator. These libraries let you compose model access with dependency injection, caching, and OpenTelemetry using familiar .NET patterns. They’re available as NuGet packages, rather than features that require you to move all of your application code to a new framework version.
Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) builds on these abstractions with agents that call tools and maintain conversation state, plus workflows that coordinate agents and application code. Connect agents to MCP tools to give them access to your application’s capabilities, and expose an agent through an ASP.NET Core AG-UI endpoint to build an interactive Blazor experience. The AG-UI hosting integration is currently prerelease.
For hands-on examples, start with .NET AI Essentials: The Core Building Blocks Explained and continue with our Microsoft Agent Framework walkthrough.
Libraries
The .NET libraries add capabilities that previously required extra setup, intermediate buffers, or custom helpers.
The Process API expansion includes one-shot methods to run a process and capture its output and exit status. More advanced APIs give you control over inherited handles, suspended starts, and process signaling. Build tools and developer utilities can spend less code on process plumbing while still inspecting how a child process finished. See Process API Improvements in .NET 11 for examples.
Zstandard compression joins the existing compression formats in System.IO.Compression. New span-based compression APIs support callers that manage their own buffers, and ZIP improvements include CRC32 validation when reading entries.
Four new in-memory stream adapters bridge existing data to APIs that accept a Stream: ReadOnlyMemoryStream, WritableMemoryStream, ReadOnlySequenceStream, and StringStream. For example, a pipeline’s segmented ReadOnlySequence<byte> can be read as a stream without first flattening it into a new contiguous buffer.
System.Text.Json adds support for C# unions, F# discriminated unions, and JSON Lines output from asynchronous sequences. F# union support uses reflection and doesn’t support source generation, trimming, or Native AOT, so check the documented limits before choosing it for a trimmed application.
LINQ adds FullJoin, which preserves unmatched elements from both inputs. This is useful for reconciliation work, such as comparing two inventories where you need to see missing items on either side.
The libraries also expand numeric types, DNS resolution, cryptography, and tracing configuration. The library overview covers the complete set of changes and marks APIs that remain experimental.
Entity Framework Core 11
Entity Framework Core 11 improves how your model becomes a query and how that query becomes SQL.
EF Core removes unnecessary joins in more reference-navigation and split-query scenarios, improves GroupBy translation, and translates the new LINQ FullJoin operator on relational providers that support it. These changes can simplify generated SQL while letting more queries stay in LINQ.
Complex types and JSON columns can now be used on entities mapped with table-per-type or table-per-concrete-type inheritance. Other improvements include migrations tooling and additional provider-specific JSON capabilities.
For SQL Server applications, EF Core adds support for vector indexes and approximate vector search. The SQL Server features and corresponding EF APIs are experimental. See the vector search documentation and limitations before evaluating them.
EF Core 11 requires .NET 11. When upgrading, check your database provider’s compatibility and the EF Core 11 breaking changes as well as the runtime changes.
Developer tools
The new dotnetup toolchain manager lets you install and update .NET SDKs and runtimes in your user account. It’s currently in public preview and helps you manage side-by-side versions and keep up with servicing updates.
.NET Skills gives coding agents task-specific guidance from the .NET team. Our .NET Skills introduction explains how to add these skills to your coding agent.
The experimental .NET MAUI DevFlow toolkit exposes a running app’s visual tree, screenshots, and interaction tools, so an agent can inspect and test the UI rather than work only from source code.
For modernization, the .NET Upgrade canvas gives you a visual view of a GitHub Copilot upgrade session. Review assessment findings and dependency compatibility, follow implementation tasks, and monitor failures and progress as the upgrade agent works. Our modernization walkthrough in the GitHub Copilot app covers the workflow from assessment through execution.
Workloads
Web: ASP.NET Core and Blazor
Application types are most useful when the rest of the stack understands them. ASP.NET Core supports C# unions wherever it uses System.Text.Json, including JSON request and response bodies in Minimal APIs and MVC. Generated OpenAPI documents describe the union’s alternatives with an anyOf schema.
This support applies to JSON bodies, not to route, query, header, or form binding. When multiple union cases have the same JSON shape, configure a classifier so deserialization can distinguish them. The ASP.NET Core union documentation explains those boundaries.
Validation also becomes more practical for rules that need to do I/O. Asynchronous validation works with the new asynchronous DataAnnotations APIs, so a validator can await a database lookup or a remote call instead of blocking a thread. Minimal APIs and Blazor forms can use this support.
OpenAPI 3.2 is now the default for generated documents. Among other improvements, it lets the document describe the per-event payload of a server-sent event stream. If a client generator or another part of your toolchain doesn’t yet support 3.2, you can explicitly select an earlier document version.
For long-lived connections, SignalR authentication refresh lets a connection refresh authentication without reconnecting. Blazor Interactive Server components can receive the updated identity and react when claims change.
Blazor adds capabilities for both statically rendered pages and interactive applications.
The new CacheView component caches the rendered output of a component subtree during static server-side rendering. On a cache hit, Blazor replays the markup without creating those child components or running their lifecycle methods. That gives you a smaller unit of caching for expensive, mostly static sections of a page.
Interactive Server apps can opt into automatic circuit pause when a browser tab becomes inactive. After a configurable delay, pausing frees the server memory and SignalR connection held by an inactive user. The feature requires an additional package and explicit configuration; upgrading doesn’t silently change your application’s circuit behavior.
Forms gain client-side validation for static server rendering and asynchronous validation support. QuickGrid and Virtualize add ways to move to a particular item, useful when returning a user to their place in a large collection.
Blazor also adds components for agentic user interfaces. The new Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.AI package includes components for streaming chat, tool rendering, approval flows, and shared UI state. Basic chat works with any IChatClient. For advanced experiences with a remote agent, the AG-UI .NET integration carries streamed responses, tool events, approval requests, and shared-state updates between an ASP.NET Core agent endpoint and the Blazor UI.
The Blazor AI components package is experimental and remains prerelease throughout .NET 11. It’s an opportunity to try the direction and give feedback, not a stable part of the ASP.NET Core shared framework. See the Blazor AI components documentation.
The AG-UI .NET SDK introduction covers the protocol’s client and server APIs. Build Agentic UI with the new Blazor AI components puts them together in a working app.
See what’s new in ASP.NET Core for the Blazor features, configuration examples, and compatibility details.
Client: .NET MAUI
.NET MAUI in .NET 11 makes CoreCLR the default runtime across its platforms. The move to CoreCLR brings mobile and desktop apps onto the same runtime foundation as other .NET workloads. On Apple platforms that don’t allow JIT compilation, the runtime uses precompiled code and the interpreter rather than generating native code at runtime.
Native AOT is an opt-in publishing alternative; its Android support remains experimental. Review the platform-specific runtime guidance and test your app’s libraries when choosing a deployment model.
The UI development loop gets attention, too:
- XAML Incremental Hot Reload is a preview feature in .NET 11. It updates live instances of pages and controls, including supported structural edits, without requiring you to navigate away and back. It’s enabled by default in Debug builds.
- Implicit XAML namespace declarations remove the need to repeat the standard namespace declarations at the root of every file.
- Windows uses the new CollectionView2 handler by default, while Android Shell adopts a handler-based architecture.
- New mobile test templates and dotnet test device selection bring testing into the CLI workflow.
These are meaningful runtime and handler changes, so exercise navigation, custom handlers, and trimmed publishing as part of your upgrade. The optional Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility package no longer ships; apps that still reference it need to migrate off it.
.NET MAUI follows its own support policy, separate from the .NET runtime’s STS and LTS lifecycle.
Windows: WinUI, Windows Forms, and WPF
For new Windows desktop apps, WinUI 3 is the recommended native UI framework, pairing C# and XAML with modern controls and the Fluent Design System. It’s delivered through the Windows App SDK, which also makes modern Windows APIs available to existing WPF and Windows Forms apps.
To add UI tests, see UWP and WinUI 3 apps: UI testing with MSTest.
Windows Forms in .NET 11 adds an opt-in modern visual styles mode that you can select at the application or control level. It also adds ways to react to system visual and accessibility settings, defer revealing a form until it’s ready, and suspend painting during bulk updates.
These controls let you introduce refreshed rendering where it makes sense for your application instead of treating a framework upgrade as an automatic visual redesign.
WPF updates focus on reliability, including fixes for Fluent window backdrops, window manager failures, and weak-event cleanup. Self-contained Windows publishing also includes a native dependency needed by apps that load mixed-mode WPF assemblies.
Get started and plan your upgrade
Install the .NET 11 SDK. Use a compatible, up-to-date Visual Studio 2026 installation, or Visual Studio Code with C# Dev Kit.
To create and run a console app:
dotnet new console -n HelloDotnet11 -f net11.0
dotnet run --project HelloDotnet11
You can replace the generated program with either of the C# examples above to try the new language features.
For an existing application, plan the upgrade across your development and deployment environments:
- Update the SDK selection in global.json if your repository pins it, and install the matching SDK on development machines and build agents.
- Update target frameworks to .NET 11, preserving platform-specific target framework suffixes where applicable. Update packages and workloads to compatible versions.
- Review the .NET 11 breaking changes, including the updated minimum CPU requirements. Installing a new SDK alone doesn’t retarget your app.
- Run your tests and measure the application under a representative workload. Validate your actual publishing mode, container base images, native dependencies, and deployment hosts.
Upgrading from .NET 8 or .NET 9
.NET 8 and .NET 9 reach end of support on November 10, 2026. Move to a supported release to continue receiving fixes. Choose .NET 11 for the latest capabilities, or .NET 10 if its LTS lifecycle fits your requirements better. See the .NET support policy for dates and servicing requirements.
If you’re upgrading from a .NET 11 release candidate, update to the final SDK, runtime, and compatible package and workload versions rather than staying on a prerelease build.
Thank you for building .NET with us
.NET 11 is the work of over 7,000 contributors. Thank you to everyone who contributed code, tested previews, reported issues, and helped us make better design decisions throughout the year. Your feedback across the previews and release candidates helped shape what we’re shipping today.
The .NET ecosystem continues to grow, with more than 589,000 unique packages on NuGet and over 1.1 trillion package downloads.
Download .NET 11, try it with an application you know well, and join us at .NET Conf to learn directly from the people building it. Share your results and questions in the .NET GitHub discussions.

articles.title: ClickHouse Acquires Xata
articles.body:
Xata is joining ClickHouse
By:
Monica Sarbu
Published:
Reading time:
6 min read
Today, we're excited to announce that Xata is joining ClickHouse to bring agentic capabilities to ClickHouse Managed Postgres.
Together with ClickHouse, we're building a Postgres platform designed for modern applications and AI agents, combining high-performance production workloads on local NVMe storage with Xata’s technology for instant database provisioning, instant copy-on-write branching, and scale-to-zero compute.
Nothing changes for Xata customers in the short term and we continue to accept new sign-ups. In parallel, we're working on bringing branching and an agentic tier to ClickHouse Managed Postgres. We will eventually migrate Xata customers to ClickHouse Managed Postgres. You can also read ClickHouse's announcement.
What is Xata
It’s undeniable that this year software development has changed forever, with agents and software factories now doing the grunt work. However, the increase in coding output has uncovered new bottlenecks. For many companies the database workflows are now the bottleneck: every pull request and every agent run needs a safe, isolated database with production-like data.
Traditionally, creating a copy of a production database is a slow and expensive process, especially when dealing with terabytes of data. Creating a database for every pull request or agent run simply doesn't scale with traditional cloning. With copy-on-write branching, however, there's no need to copy the data, making it possible to create a new branch with production data in seconds.
This is exactly what we’ve built at Xata. Even if a database has multiple terabytes of data, creating a branch takes only around 3 seconds. This means the schema and the data appear as if they were instantly copied to the child branch. At the same time, the child branch is fully independent: it has its own compute, running on a different physical node, and nothing that happens on the child branch impacts the parent database.
The key capabilities are:
- Instant database provisioning: Create a new, fully functional Postgres database instantly.
- Instant copy-on-write branching: Create database branches in seconds, without duplicating the underlying data. You only pay for the diff: create 50 branches of a 1TB database and you’re billed for something much closer to 1TB than 50TB.
- Scale-to-zero compute: Automatically suspend idle databases and wake them on the next connection, in about one second, minimizing costs.
- Anonymized production data: Remove sensitive information before data leaves production, so developers and agents can safely work with database branches.
Together, these capabilities make it remarkably cheap to run a branch per PR, per agent run, or even per SQL session. AI-native customers like Sapien, Enginy, David AI, Runner AI, and LoopAI each create thousands of database branches every week.
You might also know Xata from our open-source projects in the Postgres ecosystem, including pgstream, for logical replication with anonymization and DDL support, and pgroll, for zero-downtime, reversible schema changes.
Why ClickHouse
Earlier this year, ClickHouse launched ClickHouse Managed Postgres, which became generally available today. Built on local NVMe storage, it's currently the fastest Postgres service out there, and not by a small margin.
When we started talking with the ClickHouse Managed Postgres team, it quickly became clear just how complementary the two services are: ClickHouse Managed Postgres is optimized for high-throughput, long-lived production workloads, while Xata is designed to provision large numbers of small, short-lived databases in seconds, with production-like data and capabilities like instant branching and scale-to-zero that are particularly well suited for agentic workloads.
Both platforms run unmodified vanilla Postgres and share a strong focus on reliability and stability. The common foundation puts us in a great position to move quickly on integrating the two platforms. In fact, David AI is an example of a customer that already uses ClickHouse Managed Postgres and Xata together and they shared the following with us:
As an AI company working with large volumes of data, we need reliable infrastructure that help us move fast. We moved from Neon to ClickHouse Managed Postgres for better reliability and performance, and our users immediately noticed how much faster everything felt. Xata’s branching has been a great fit for our devs (and AI coding agents!), making it easy to build and test in parallel. Bringing both together means high-performance Postgres and instant branching in a single platform, simplifying our infrastructure and giving our team more time to build.
Best-in-class OLTP and OLAP
By almost any measure, Postgres is the most popular OLTP database and ClickHouse is the most popular OLAP database. Combining the two is something teams have been stitching together themselves for years. The Postgres team at ClickHouse has been making that integration first-class: very fast replication from Postgres into ClickHouse and a unified query layer to build applications.
An integrated transactional and analytical data platform is something we've wanted to build since Xata's early days, when our first product paired Postgres with a search and analytics engine.
On a personal level, we've long admired ClickHouse and already knew the founders and many of the engineers, which gives us confidence that together we can take this vision much further.
What Xata enables
A database branch for every pull request and agent run
The GitHub integration enables automatically creating an isolated database branch for every pull request. These branches can be integrated into CI/CD pipelines, allowing code changes to be safely tested before merging into production. Since they are only needed for testing, branches are often scaling to zero after only a few minutes, minimizing costs.
The same approach applies to coding agents, where every agent run can have its own isolated database to develop and test changes without affecting production.
For details on the branch-per-PR use case and the cost savings it provides, see this blog post.
Powering AI platforms
AI platforms that embed Postgres are seeing an explosion in demand: first thousands, then hundreds of thousands, and eventually millions of databases per week. There are two main use cases: instant database provisioning for every new application, and a database branch for every deployment preview, allowing code changes to be tested safely against production data.
Because unused databases scale to zero, platforms can run very large fleets of small, mostly idle databases at a fraction of the cost, while keeping full compatibility, since it's simply vanilla Postgres.
How it works
Two key technologies enable fast branching and short wake-up times: our Xatastor storage engine and warm pools for compute instances.
Xatastor is our storage engine, which provides separation of storage and compute, high multi-tenancy, copy-on-write branching, compression, thin provisioning, and more. It exposes ZFS zvols over the network using the NVMe/TCP protocol. Because it works at the block-device level, we can run unmodified vanilla PostgreSQL. For a deep-dive into the Xatastor architecture, see this dedicated blog post.
We use warm pools of compute instances to obtain super fast provisioning, wake-up after scale-to-zero, and branching times. This removes the actual node and pod provisioning from the hot path of making a new database or branch available. You can find more information about how this works in this blog post.
What's next
Building Xata has been an incredible journey over the last five years. We're extremely proud of the technology we've built, and even more proud of the team behind it, which is now joining ClickHouse.
We've tackled some really difficult engineering challenges, and it's been incredibly rewarding to see developers and customers embrace these capabilities, creating exponentially more branches as they expand their usage.
What excites us most about this next chapter is that the vision behind Xata is more relevant than ever, and as part of ClickHouse, we're in the best possible position to bring it to fruition.
What this means for you:
- If you're a Xata customer: you can continue using it as usual. We'll integrate Xata's features into ClickHouse Managed Postgres, and once there's feature parity, we'll migrate customers as smoothly as possible, ideally with no impact on the service.
- If you're a ClickHouse Managed Postgres customer: branching, scale-to-zero and an agentic tier are coming to ClickHouse Managed Postgres
- If you're new to both: you can get started with ClickHouse Managed Postgres or sign up for Xata today.
We're excited about what we can build together with ClickHouse, and this is just the beginning.
Give every agentic workload its own Postgres branch
Create instant database clones with production-like data for every agent, workflow, and CI/CD pipeline.
Related Posts
A thousand Postgres branches for $1
See how we reduced branching times from 20+ seconds to around a second and what use-cases these speed improvements enable.
Inside Xatastor: ZFS + NVMe-oF for millions of Postgres databases
Read the technical details of our new distributed storage system, which is the key to scaling to a huge number of Postgres instances.
