Large-Scale Measurement and Real-World Mitigation of Web Browser Fingerprinting in the Wild
1Mozilla Corporation · 2University of Toronto · 3UC San Diego
This is the companion site to a study Mozilla ran on browser fingerprinting. With the help of almost 25 million Firefox release users, we measured how identifiable browsers really are, found which characteristics make them unique, and used that to design the fingerprinting protections that shipped in Firefox 143. Here you can read the paper and its key findings, browse the full appendix data the PDF had no room for, download the privacy-preserving aggregate data and analysis code, learn how the data was collected, and run an interactive test that compares your own browser against the measured population. If you have a question the data could answer, there is also a discussion board for proposing follow-up research.
Browser fingerprinting is a known tracking mechanism on the modern web, but its real-world effectiveness toward users has been hard to measure. To build robust protections, we measured uniqueness across a large, unbiased population, to determined what individual metrics cause users to be unique. These measurements used multiple privacy preserving technologies, like OHTTP, to ensure that no individual users can be identified or tracked across the web. The protections we built into Firefox avoid web compatibility problems while dropping the percentage of uniquely identifiable users from 75% to 46%.
Paper abstract
Web browser fingerprinting has become a key tracking mechanism on the modern web, yet its real-world effectiveness and which of the existing mitigations offer value at scale remain insufficiently understood.
In this paper, we present a large-scale study of browser fingerprinting based on real-world telemetry from almost 25 million Firefox release users. This dataset enables us to quantify user uniqueness at population scale and identify which characteristics contribute most to this uniqueness.
Our analysis shows fingerprintability is largely driven by a small set of high-impact characteristics and their combinations, rather than the accumulation of many independent measurements. Building on these insights, we propose and evaluate fingerprinting protections based on their impact on uniqueness and cohort structure, and design data-driven mitigations.
These protections, shipped in Firefox 143, reduce the fraction of uniquely identifiable users from 75% to 46% while maintaining web compatibility, demonstrating that practical reductions in fingerprintability are achievable in a mainstream browser.
Our key findings
Here's what we want to present to you with this paper and the broader scope of our work.
- Uniqueness is caused by a small number of metrics - not one or thirty
- Fingerprinting test sites have a seemingly endless list of measurements they can pull from your browser. If a user has a unique fingerprint, it is typically not because of a single measurement, but it is also not because of 20 or 30 measurements. It is a small number of metrics that make users unique. In fact, it's very close to the 80/20 rule. Specifically, of all the users seen as unique by Fingerprint Pro (the most discerning fingerprinter we model) - 80% of them are unique after only 8 metrics - while the fingerprinter collects a total of over 50 metrics. Signifyd collects more metrics, but identifies fewer users as unique: 80% of the users it sees as unique will be identified after 9 metrics despite collecting over 80.
- The numbers only mean anything per operating system
- Whenever someone cites a single percentage when describing "How many users are unique" - you should be suspicious. Because this collapses multiple different populations that behave very differently. Firstly, as a baseline, your operating system is always going to be exposed to a fingerprinter. We are always working within the constraint of web compatibility, and lying about the user's operating system breaks shortcut keys and gives you the wrong downloads among other problems. So if we know the website is going to learn your real OS anyway, we can use it to segment the population and analyze it separately. And when you do you see that each operating system behaves differently because they have different important metrics. Admittedly, it's very difficult to give a concise summary of work and also provide four sets of numbers - so even we fall prey to the trap of providing a single number, as we did in the prior paragraph. But every time we have a single percentage, somewhere we have that number broken down by operating system, and in doing so, you will see that each behaves differently.
- Entropy is not the measurement you want
- It's so, so easy to take all the results for a metric and just calculate Shannon entropy - it's a standard yardstick in this literature. But as we show - a high Shannon entropy does not reliably predict fingerprinting impact.
- Cohort size, not just uniqueness
- Previous analyses calculated how many people were unique, but they did not analyze the other people - the ones who weren't. All those other people might be 1 million users who share one fingerprint or 500,000 distinct fingerprints shared by 2 people each - that's quite the difference. We use the Simpson Index (aka the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index) to quantify that difference and compare different sets of cohorts (shared fingerprints). This lets us compare how effective different fingerprinting defenses are based not just on how much uniqueness they eliminate but how much they collapse groups of users into each other. For example, two different protections can each lower the share of unique users by about 2.1 percentage points. But one improves the cohort score by 56%, while another raises it by only 13%. Judged on uniqueness alone, two defenses can look equally effective; while the cohort improvement varies significantly.
- The same protection performs very differently per platform
- Protections are not uniformly impactful, and the variation is not small. As an example, clamping the available screen resolution takes 25.3 percentage points off cumulative macOS uniqueness but between 0 and 3 points off the other three platforms. Averaged across all users, that 25-point drop shrinks to 3.5 - a protection that matters enormously to one platform can look marginal in the aggregate. This is yet another reason why it's so important to segment and analyze data on a per-operating-system basis.
- Standardization and randomization go hand-in-hand
- Making users report the same values makes them look more alike, but it never makes everyone look the same. Some users will still stand out, and that gets worse on websites with small visitor populations. Standardization improves the situation, but it should still be paired with randomization. Randomization is very strong when it works, but can always be detected and bypassed. Neither can carry the burden of providing privacy on its own.
- The data shows why values differ, not just that they do
- Correlating fingerprinting values with users' hardware and other characteristics let us identify why certain measurements differed between users. Knowing the root cause lets us build protections that reach much further, and protect small groups of users who would otherwise stand out as a minority. Addressing these differences has already produced more consistent outputs for image rendering, Web Audio, and mathematical operations on Android, with more root causes being investigated.
- Users don't connect website breakage to the setting
- Breakage from a strict mode is delayed, and the delay hides the cause. Turning on a stricter mode is a one-time act - but the broken website arrives later and nothing connects the two. From the user's perspective, this website doesn't work in Firefox and they have no idea why and are frustrated. Report after report we see people posting for help, confused - despite having taken specific action to enable a hidden setting opting them into strict fingerprinting protections.
- Protections that ship have to keep the web working
- Users don't realize that a setting they changed caused the breakage, and don't know how to fix it - so a protection that breaks the web breaks the browser along with it. We selected and tuned mitigations on both measured impact and compatibility. For a default, compatibility isn't a trade-off against privacy - it's a precondition for it.
- The hard part is finding what breaks
- The web is vast, and even the most innocuous change is likely to break something somewhere. Some breakage can be anticipated, which helps design, testing, and detection. The other breakage gets fixed only if a chain of luck holds: someone has to recognize the breakage, report it, reproduce it on the right hardware, and get it to the right person.
- We are deliberately not publishing everything we could
- Commercial fingerprinters evolve continuously, and they borrow openly from the community that studies them. Sites built to teach people about fingerprinting - CreepJS among them - get picked up and used outright by fingerprinting products. So we have been deliberately conservative. There are analyses this dataset would support that we have not run, data we could have released that we have not, and offensive angles on this work that we have not pursued. That is a choice rather than an oversight: we would rather leave a question open than make it easier to build a better fingerprinter.
Test your own browser
This interactive test re-implements individual measurements as close as possible to how Firefox's own collection code performed them, runs in your browser, and compares each result against the published aggregate data. For every characteristic you can see your value and how many of the ~25 million measured browsers share it - overall and within your operating system.
The test runs entirely in your browser. All comparisons happen locally, against our static reference files. No data is stored or submitted to us.
If the test, or anything else on this site, looks wrong, please report it as an issue on GitHub. For a problem with the test, include the diagnostics from its Copy diagnostics button, or, if you would rather not post your measured values publicly, email them to tom@ritter.vg.
Paper
The extended version of the paper is available as a PDF.
Full appendix data
The paper's appendices contain a wealth of data locked behind a reasonable page limit and PDF formatting. This full data page carries all of it - every rank for every operating system and all three modeled services, the complete protection chains, and the paper's figures regenerated at print resolution.
Data collection
      Our measurements come from Firefox telemetry, specifically the 
      user-characteristics ping, a dedicated telemetry ping.
      Unlike normal telemetry pings that are sent regularly, this ping
      must be explicitly enabled (which has happened twice, once in 2025
      and once in 2026), and sends one data report before becoming dormant
      again.
    
This ping carries no client ID, only a UUID unique to the ping used to de-duplicate users. It cannot be keyed to any other telemetry submissions. It is submitted over Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP): a relay operated independently of Mozilla forwards the encrypted submission, so the relay can see the sender's IP address but not the contents, and Mozilla receives the contents but not the IP address. Access to the collected data was restricted to four authorized Mozilla employees. The data was retained for 90 days and has since been deleted.
Aggregate data & analysis code
We release four types of data:
- A list of fingerprints generated for different phases of protections, per modeled fingerprinter, with the user's OS and locale unmasked.
- Aggregate tables of the frequency of value per metric, split by OS
- Aggregate tables of the frequency of value per metric, correlated by other metrics' values, again split by OS
- A detailed analysis of rendered canvas images that allows comparison
In the fingerprint lists, the fingerprints cannot be recreated from a website measuring user characteristics, due to the way the telemetry was collected. After being generated, the files were shuffled to a new ordering, and any locale occurring fewer than 100 times was anonymized.
In the aggregate tables, any value observed fewer than 100 times within a single per-OS population is withheld - so the published data describes cohorts, never individuals.
In the canvas comparison, raw canvas renderings are provided, but they are devoid of any connection to other user data. Any unique canvas rendering is not provided; only the hash.
For verification and exploration, the code used to process the data and perform different analyses is available for review. It additionally contains the specific fingerprinting scripts captured, reverse engineered, and modeled for the paper.
Future Research
Far more can be asked of this dataset than we have asked. Some of it we chose not to pursue, some of it we simply did not think of, and some of it is a better fit for someone who is not us.
There is a discussion board for proposing follow-up analyses. Two kinds are worth posting:
- Answerable from the published aggregate data. Anyone can run these - the per-operating-system distributions are released, and the analysis toolkit is open. Post the question anyway, so the work is not duplicated and so the result lands somewhere others can find it.
- Needs the raw data. These we would have to run ourselves, since the underlying ping data is not something we can ever release. Describe what you want to know and why! To be clear, we do not have the raw data anymore but it is possible we will perform a re-collection in the future which we could analyze. We cannot promise to run everything, and some questions we will decline because we do not wish to help build a better fingerprinter.

articles.title: X-energy gets green light to build its first small modular nuclear reactors
articles.body:
Nuclear startup X-energy announced Monday that it had been given the go-ahead from federal officials to build its first four commercial reactors.
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approved the construction permit application for four of X-energy’s Xe-100 reactors at a Dow chemical plant in Texas. Each reactor will be capable of generating 80 megawatts of electricity and 200 megawatts of heat. X-energy says the approval is the first for an advanced nuclear reactor at an industrial site in the United States.
The U.S. nuclear industry has pinned its hopes on small modular reactors — or SMRs — like those being developed by X-energy. By shrinking the reactor, proponents say it will speed construction and reduce costs, though those advantages have yet to be proven. No SMR is currently in operation in the U.S., and X-energy says Dow’s reactors won’t be operational until the early 2030s.
X-energy claims that its reactor design, which flows helium gas over uranium-containing fuel pellets, is safer than many existing reactors, but the Union of Concerned Scientists questioned the claim and the speed with which X-energy received the permit.
“The NRC only accomplished this feat by pushing consideration of critical safety questions to a later date—issues the NRC should’ve fully resolved before green lighting construction,” Edwin Lyman, director of nuclear power safety for the organization, said in a statement.
The nuclear industry has benefited from strong interest from hyperscalers and data center developers, who are desperate for any and all sources of electricity. Amazon’s Climate Pledge Fund led X-energy’s $500 million Series C-1, and the big tech company has also committed to buying 5 gigawatts of capacity from the nuclear startup.
X-energy rode that wave of excitement earlier this year when its April initial public offering raised $1 billion. But since then, investors’ optimism has tempered.
The hesitancy isn’t surprising: Nuclear power plants are expensive to build and can take years to complete. Eventually, X-energy hopes to rein in both time and cost, but its first reactors are likely to be pricey.
The new permit approval gave X-energy a small jolt yesterday, though it was only enough to recover last week’s losses. The company’s shares are trading at less than half their initial offering price.

articles.title: Show HN: A 15 MB self-hosted Netflix and Spotify for your media server
articles.body:
English · 简体中文 · हिन्दी · Español · Français · العربية · Português · Русский · 日本語 · Deutsch · 한국어 · Italiano · Polski · Nederlands · Türkçe · Українська
HolyArrs is one self-hosted app for your shows, movies and music.
Browse like a streaming app, ask for what you want, and it handles the rest.
About 15 MB to download · about 140 MB of RAM idle with 10,000 titles · amd64, arm64, armv7
The six apps it replaces download 718.2 MB together.
Quick start · Why · What it does · Moving from other apps · The manual · Help
Save this as docker-compose.yml in a new folder on a local disk:
name: holyarrs
services:
  holyarrs:
    image: holyarrs/holyarrs:latest
    container_name: holyarrs
    environment:
      - PUID=1000
      - PGID=1000
      - TZ=America/New_York
    volumes:
      - /your/local/path:/config
      - /path/to/movies:/movies #optional
      - /path/to/tv:/tv #optional
      - /path/to/music:/music #optional
      - /path/to/downloads:/downloads #optional
    ports:
      - 6262:6262
    restart: unless-stoppeddocker compose up -d
Open http://your-server:6262 and make the owner account. A short setup walks you through folders, a downloader and a Source.
No API keys to hunt down. No second container. Every setting is explained in the manual further down.
A normal media server runs six apps: Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, Bazarr, Prowlarr and Seerr.
That's six logins, six ports, six update cycles and six API keys to copy between them. When a show doesn't land, you check six places to find out why.
I wanted one app. One login, one port, one place to look.
So I built it.
About 48 times smaller. Compressed registry download, linuxserver.io images, amd64, measured 2026-11-08. Idle RAM measured with 10,000 titles and 55,000 movies and episodes.
Someone asks for a title. HolyArrs searches your Sources, picks the best release with your Pick rules, sends it to your downloader and files it in your library. Your media server hears about it when it lands.
See every page in motion
- Downloaders: qBittorrent, Transmission, Deluge, SABnzbd, NZBGet
- Media servers: Plex, Jellyfin, Emby
- Sources: any Torznab or Newznab indexer, or Prowlarr or Jackett
- Moves your setup from: Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, Prowlarr, Bazarr, Seerr, Overseerr, qBittorrent, SABnzbd
Open Settings > Move from other apps, add each old app's address and API key (or a backup zip), pick what comes over, run Try it, then Move. You can undo a move later.
HolyArrs only reads your old apps and changes nothing in them, so you can run both side by side until you trust it.
Keys and passwords stay behind; you type them in again or import them from a file. Custom formats, tags and history don't come over. Media files never move. Step by step: Move from other apps.
- Downloading by itself. HolyArrs connects to qBittorrent, SABnzbd and the others. It doesn't replace them.
- AI or MCP features. Not in 1.0.
- Phone and TV apps. Not built. The web app works on a phone.
- Music in Explore is still being built.
What's next is on the roadmap. You vote, I build. Post ideas on r/HolyArrs.
Do I keep qBittorrent or SABnzbd? Yes, for now. HolyArrs connects to the downloader you already run. A built-in downloader is planned for a later release.
Can Sonarr and Radarr keep running while I try it? Yes. HolyArrs reads them once and never changes them.
Is it free? Yes. It's free and open source.
Everything below is reference. The full guides live at docs.HolyArrs.com.
Pulling holyarrs/holyarrs:latest gets the right image for your machine.
On a NAS? See Unraid, Synology and other NAS boxes.
Images live on Docker Hub as holyarrs/holyarrs.
name: holyarrs
services:
  holyarrs:
    image: holyarrs/holyarrs:latest
    container_name: holyarrs
    environment:
      - PUID=1000
      - PGID=1000
      - TZ=America/New_York
    volumes:
      - /your/local/path:/config
      - /path/to/movies:/movies #optional
      - /path/to/tv:/tv #optional
      - /path/to/music:/music #optional
      - /path/to/downloads:/downloads #optional
    ports:
      - 6262:6262
    restart: unless-stoppeddocker run -d \
  --name=holyarrs \
  -e PUID=1000 \
  -e PGID=1000 \
  -e TZ=America/New_York \
  -p 6262:6262 \
  -v /your/local/path:/config \
  -v /path/to/movies:/movies `#optional` \
  -v /path/to/tv:/tv `#optional` \
  -v /path/to/music:/music `#optional` \
  -v /path/to/downloads:/downloads `#optional` \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  holyarrs/holyarrs:latest
Container settings go in compose. Everything else is set in the app.
Each one is written <outside>:<inside>. Change the left side only.
More variables (reverse proxy, URL base, save path): Environment variables.
Put FILE__ in front of any variable to read its value from a file, such as a Docker secret:
environment:
  - FILE__HOLYARRS_ALLOWED_HOSTS=/run/secrets/holyarrs_hosts
PUID and PGID must match the user that owns your media folders. Find them with:
id youruser
# uid=1000(youruser) gid=1000(youruser)
HolyArrs never changes the owner of your media or download folders. Give that user write access to them, because HolyArrs makes folders and moves files.
Open http://your-server:6262 and make the owner account right away. There is no default password. Until you make it, whoever opens HolyArrs first becomes the owner.
The setup that opens next asks for your folders, a downloader and a Source. Guide: First run.
The four optional mounts are the easy way to start. The cost: each mount is its own filesystem inside the container, so every import is a full copy.
Want instant moves that take no extra space? Mount one parent folder with downloads and Library folders inside it, and give your downloader the same mount at the same path. Guide: Folders.
Use a named volume for /config. Media folders can stay host folders. Guide: Install.
holyarrs.key in your config folder is what opens your stored passwords and keys. Backups don't include it, so keep a copy somewhere else. As the owner, open Settings > Backups and choose Download key kit. See Backups.
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d
If the new version changes how data is stored, HolyArrs makes a backup first. To go back to it: docker exec holyarrs /holyarrs restore --pre-update, then docker restart holyarrs. Never remove /config during an update. See Updates.
- The owner account is made at first visit. There is no default password.
- Stored passwords and keys are encrypted with holyarrs.key.
- The image has no shell inside it.
- Don't forward port 6262 on your router. Use a VPN such as Tailscale, or a reverse proxy with HTTPS.
- Report security problems privately: SECURITY.
The image has no shell, so docker exec -it holyarrs /bin/bash won't work. HolyArrs' own commands do:
- Follow the log: docker logs -f holyarrs
- Check your setup. Every line says OK, WARN or FAIL, and each WARN or FAIL says how to fix it:
docker exec holyarrs /holyarrs doctor
- Locked out of the owner account: docker exec -i holyarrs /holyarrs reset-owner
- Version number: docker inspect --format '{{ index .Config.Labels "org.opencontainers.image.version" }}' holyarrs
More: Troubleshooting.
Read CONTRIBUTING, then Architecture and Setup. Open an issue before a big change.
On your first pull request a bot asks you to accept a short licence agreement (CLA.md). One click, once.
HolyArrs is free and open source under the GNU AGPL-3.0.
Want to build it into a closed product? Email support@HolyArrs.com for a commercial licence.
HolyArrs is free, but it isn't free to run. Every install talks to a metadata server I pay for every month. Sponsors cover that, and buy more hours for the things you vote for.
Built by CoderLuii.
If HolyArrs saves you from running six apps, a star helps other people find it.

HolyArrs is free and open source under the GNU AGPL-3.0.
Want to build it into a closed product? Email support@HolyArrs.com for a commercial licence.
HolyArrs is free, but it isn't free to run. Every install talks to a metadata server I pay for every month. Sponsors cover that, and buy more hours for the things you vote for.
Built by CoderLuii.
If HolyArrs saves you from running six apps, a star helps other people find it.

articles.title: M John Harrison becomes first science fiction author to win the Booker prize
articles.body:
Eighty-one-year-old M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, a postapocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast, becoming the oldest winner in the award’s history.
Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said that while plenty of previous winners had dabbled in science fiction, Harrison’s was “the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world”. She called it “a historic win, for a writer whose decades of work are lightly worn on every page”.
Harrison, who has been publishing for six decades, overtakes Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she shared the prize in 2019 for The Testaments. He received the £50,000 award and trophy at a ceremony in London on Monday evening.
The End of Everything, Harrison’s first Booker nomination, is set a few decades from now, years after a disaster nobody can properly account for. Set on the Kent coast, the novel sees Phillip Tennent and his ageing aunt Marnie attempting to survive alongside the looming threat of the mysterious iGhetti: vast, shape-changing beings whose origins and intentions are never explained. At 198 pages, it was the shortest book on the shortlist.
Mary Beard, chair of the judges, said the decision was unanimous, reached after a full day of discussion. “It’s a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile – and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism,” she said. “One main point of the book is that if, or when, such an apocalypse comes it will be incomprehensible. And the old rules won’t matter either … This is the politics of now seen through the lens of the future.”
Harrison, born in Rugby, Warwickshire, in 1945, sold his first story in 1965 and spent most of the 1970s running the books pages of the speculative fiction magazine New Worlds. Alongside his novels he has written five short-story collections and the “anti-memoir” Wish I Was Here (2023). Climbers took the Boardman Tasker prize for mountain literature in 1989, Nova Swing the Arthur C Clarke award in 2007, and The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again the Goldsmiths prize in 2020. Once a keen climber and fell runner, he sat on the Booker judging panel in 2022.
This year’s shortlist included two former winners: Marlon James, the bookmakers’ favourite, for The Disappearers, and Douglas Stuart for John of John. Elizabeth Strout’s The Things We Never Say, Luke Kennard’s Black Bag and Rebecca Perry’s debut May We Feed the King completed the list. Each shortlisted author receives £2,500.
Writing in the Guardian on his inspiration last week, Harrison described The End of Everything as “a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend”, with aliens who arrive “as incomers from another dimension, paralleling the gentrification of places like the UK’s south-east coast”. He admitted to passing on to the reader “some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters”, but said he hoped the issues were transparent – among them “the collapse of rationality that comes with Trumpism and the internet”.
His win marks a rare moment of mainstream recognition for a writer long revered by his peers but at the margins of literary fiction. On BBC Radio 4’s Front Row last month, Harrison said he had been “working for 40 to 50 years to shift the balance, both as a novelist and as a critic”, adding: “Why shouldn’t a well written [work of] SF be considered to be literary fiction?”
Even admirers concede the book is not an easy read. In a rave review for the Guardian, Michel Faber said it “exposes the terrifying insecurity of life right now”, but warned that “it won’t be for everyone”.
The win is timely in the age of AI. Beard noted that the “i” in iGhetti hints “at something digital, but you can’t be sure”, while Wood described the book’s post-apocalyptic landscape as “Large Language Model-dotted”.
The judging panel also included Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, authors Patricia Lockwood and Raymond Antrobus and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu. They considered 163 books published in the UK or Ireland between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026.
It is the first Booker win for Serpent’s Tail, an imprint of the independent publisher Profile Books, and its fifth nomination. Hungarian-British author David Szalay won last year with Flesh; other recent winners include Samantha Harvey’s Orbital, Paul Lynch’s Prophet Song and Shehan Karunatilaka’s The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida.
- The End of Everything by M. John Harrison (Profile, £16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

articles.title: Queens Public library under ransomware attack e-borrowing suspended
articles.body:
All Queens Public Library locations are closed on Wednesday, November 11 in observance of Veterans Day. 
We thank all veterans for their service to our country.
We are open as scheduled but experiencing a significant network outage affecting all locations.
This disruption, the result of a ransomware attack, impacts the following services:
- Queens Public Library website
- QPL Mobile App
- Public Computers at most open locations
- Digital Media Services
The following services have been restored:
- Free Wi-Fi access at all open locations
- Check-out and return machines
- Public Computers at seven locations: Central Library, Far Rockaway, Flushing, Glen Oaks, Hunters Point, Jackson Heights, and Kew Gardens Hills
All QPL locations remain open as scheduled. However, certain virtual and in-person programs may be impacted. Please check with your local branch.
You can continue to borrow and return books and other materials at all locations. During this outage, however, renewals are unavailable. As a reminder, customers are not charged late fines on borrowed materials.
Check this page for updates. You can also check our social media channels:
You may call (718) 990-0728 for assistance.
We apologize for any inconvenience and ask for your patience and understanding as we manage this challenge. Our team is working diligently to restore full access. Please note it will take some time before the Library’s network and systems are restored.

articles.title: Toyota brand Scion is back and it's going to sell a kei truck in America
articles.body:
When Toyota first introduced the Scion marque in 2003, it had one primary goal – sell cars to the younger generation. Its cars were cheaper and available in fun colors with fun names like “High Voltage Yellow” and “xPRESSO.” When I was a kid in the early 2000s, I often dreamed of one day owning a tC in Black Cherry Pearl and enjoyed lovingly calling xBs “toaster cars.” Over half of new Scions sold were to people under 35, and the tC boasted the youngest average buyer age in the entire industry at a sprightly 29. Their sales numbers peaked in 2006, but dropped nearly 75% by 2010. After sustained financial struggle, Toyota retired the marque in 2016. But now, a decade later, everyone’s favorite toaster brand is seemingly back.
Today, Toyota announced the official revival of Scion, but instead of being a quirky and budget-conscious line, they are becoming Toyota’s cornerstone of curiosity. Now called “Scion by Toyota,” it is being launched as a “freedom lab” where drivers can, and are encouraged to challenge conventional ways of thinking about mobility through design, vehicle concepts, and features.
“Okei,” let’s go.
Their first production vehicle is the KEI-01, an ultra-compact utility truck, otherwise known as a kei truck. Toyota will be using its existing manufacturing infrastructure in Indiana to “produce” them for sale in the American market. “Produce” is in quotation marks because the KEI-01 is quite literally a rebadged Toyota Pixis, which is a rebadged Daihatsu Hijet Jumbo Cab. Based on its initial imagery it is seemingly also still right-hand drive, and there’s no word on if a LHD variant will be available in the future.
With its friendly little 660cc engine and CVT transmission, the KEI-01 was certified to meet American low-speed vehicle safety standards, meaning it has a limited top speed of less than 25mph and is only legal on roads with a posted speed limit of less than 35mph. This makes it not really usable as a daily driver, but keeps it in this beautiful sweet spot where it has a shocking number of commercial and agricultural uses.
The KEI-01 has a 600-pound payload (which means cargo and passengers) and a three-way fold-down cargo bed, making it a well-equipped workhorse for use on farms and in warehouses. It’s only about 5 feet wide and 11 feet long, which makes it great for use as a delivery or work vehicle in dense, urban areas like New York City. Believe it or not, it also has 4WD, which means it can traverse uneven terrain in more rural areas with ease. And don’t worry if it’s hot outside, because heat and air conditioning are standard.
It’s worth noting that, while Kei trucks are currently sold new in the U.S. as “mini trucks” through independent distributors, this one is sold directly by Toyota. Before you rush to your local Toyota dealer to place a deposit, I’m going to have to burst your bubble a bit. Initially, the KEI 01 is only going to be available in a low-volume, niche pilot program entirely focused on fleet usage beginning in late 2027. Depending on performance and owner feedback, availability of the KEI-01 may eventually be expanded, but no further information is available from Toyota at the time.
The Hybrid Side-By-Side
Two other mobility concepts accompany the KEI-01 in the Scion by Toyota lineup, the SxS Concept and the BXE Concept.
The SxS Concept was unveiled at the 2025 SEMA Show as a purpose-built side-by-side all-terrain vehicle (click here for our coverage). Developed by Toyota North America, the off-road concept is outfitted with a turbocharged four-cylinder from the Tacoma making in the realm of 300hp. You won’t have to worry about your turbo spool scaring away local fauna, as it is equipped with a “Silent Mode,” which allows the driver to switch from the boisterous internal combustion system to a much more civilised fully electric driving mode. Unlike the KEI-01, the SxS Concept is still just that – a concept, with no current plans to have a version available to the public.
Last, but not least, is the BKE Concept. The BKE concept is entirely focused on personal mobility in the outdoors, filling the gap between the utility of the KEI-01 and the pure performance of the SxS Concept. Its small form factor and rugged tires make it an ideal off-roader for traversing narrow paths while being portable enough to stow away when not in use or easily tote around in the back of a car.
Top graphic image: Toyota

articles.title: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
articles.body:
Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
[LWN subscriber-only content]
Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms.
Synaptics and Displaylink
The dock that he was trying to support is a Dell device that connects to a system via USB 3 and allows users to connect multiple monitors and other devices to their computer. It provides its DisplayLink Manager (DLM) software for Linux for the devices via an APT repository for Ubuntu.
The company only provides DLM software in binary form, and only for x86-based platforms. The software is proprietary, but the company does maintain an open-source, out-of-tree kernel module that is included with DLM, the Extensible Virtual Display Interface (EVDI) project. It provides a driver that's compatible with Linux DRM and allows users to manage their docked displays with standard tools used for display settings, such as xrandr or GNOME and KDE Plasma's utilities.
A short article explains why the company has not released source code for DLM: the software uses a proprietary graphics technology called DL3 to create a compressed stream of the various channels (e.g., USB, DisplayLink video, audio) over a communication channel (USB 3 in this case) and decode it again for output to the user's devices.
Unfortunately, the vendor-supplied software did not work well for Lothian. I spoke and chatted with him via Signal while writing this article; he said that the driver kept crashing under Linux, so he decided to use his Claude subscription to try to develop a new driver and support software.
Vino
He posted the first
patch series for Vino—his Rust-based DRM/KMS driver—to the kernel's
dri-devel list as an RFC on June 17. Lothian noted that it was in an
incomplete state, and asked for help with a blocker that
he had run into trying to communicate with the dock's control plane. "
If you have
knowledge of the DisplayLink DL3 control-plane engagement sequence, or ideas for
isolating a whole-bus timing/ordering property a per-channel diff cannot see,
help would be very welcome.
" He received feedback from a few developers, including guidance
from Danilo Krummrich to rework the driver to use the Rust KMS bindings, but no advice
specific to the problem he was trying to solve.
Lothian also opened an issue on the EVDI GitHub repository on June 17. It explained the work he'd done so far, outlined the approach in trying to reverse-engineer the DL3 protocol, provided links to his GitHub repository with the Vino code, and asked for clarification on a few issues. There was no reply to his issue.
He also reached out to Łukasz Spintzyk of Synaptics directly by email; his correspondence with the company between July 5 and October 7 is available in this PDF compiled by Lothian. He noted that he had found a few bugs in EVDI and opened a pull request (that went unreviewed for several months), and also asked for assistance where he was blocked on Vino. On July 20, he received a reply, not from Spintzyk, but from Michal Lukaszek of Synaptics:
The reason I'm writing is that DisplayLink is not an open standard. The protocol, codec, and other technologies used by DisplayLink devices are proprietary to Synaptics and are protected by a substantial portfolio of patents in a number of jurisdictions, including the UK.
From what you've published, it appears that the VINO project is progressing beyond interoperability work and toward implementing technology that we believe is covered by those patents. While many developers understandably focus on avoiding copyrighted source code, patent law is different. An independently written or clean-room implementation does not necessarily avoid patent infringement if it implements patented inventions.
Lukaszek said it was entirely possible that Lothian was unaware of the
"
intellectual property landscape surrounding DisplayLink
", so he wanted
to make him aware now rather than "
have the situation become more formal
later
". Lothian lives in Scotland and has a ".co.uk" email address, which
explains why the email made reference to the UK.
Cease and desist
On August 17, Andrew Bateman, an assistant general council of
intellectual property for Synaptics, sent a cease-and-desist notice. The letter stated that Lothian had not
"
substantially responded
" to Lukaszek's communication, and had continued
with "
public statements and further development activities
". It included
an appendix with a list of 125 patents that "
cover fundamental aspects of
DisplayLink's architecture and operation
", but did not specify which patents
might be infringed by the work.
Synaptics included a list of eight demands it expected immediate compliance
with, including ceasing development of "
any software or other
implementation that infringes any Synaptics patent
", withdrawing submissions of
materials "
made to Linux kernel maintainers, mailing
lists, code-hosting platforms, package maintainers, distributions, or any other person or
organization
", and to identify in writing every location "
in which the
relevant materials have been published, submitted, stored, or
distributed
". It also demanded that he provide Synaptics with a signed
confirmation, by August 28, that he had complied with its demands.
Lothian, instead, posted version
three of his Vino work for the DisplayLink docks to the dri-devel list on
August 26. He said that the previous two versions had "
never lit a
panel
", but the new work could control three generations of DL3 docks
without any vendor software. There were no substantive reviews of the patch set
posted to the list, though there were some automated reviews from Sashiko.
On August 27, Lothian responded to Bateman and asked him to elaborate
on the patents that Synaptics thought were being infringed. "
A claim chart
mapping the relevant claims to the relevant code would make it much easier for
me to understand and properly respond to your concerns.
"
He also expressed confusion about Synaptics's position that his work was
being treated as patent infringement. Synaptics is a member of the Open Invention Network (OIN), which
was created to help open-source
developers and vendors deal with the threats of expensive patent litigation. It
holds a large, cross-licensed portfolio that serves to provide patent protection
to individuals, open-source projects, and large vendors alike. Lothian said that
he was now an OIN licensee as well, and he thought that it was supposed to
"
reduce exactly this sort of patent problem around Linux and open source
software
".
He asked Bateman to explain how Synaptics claims "
interact with our
respective OIN commitments
", and expressed a desire to sort things out with
Synaptics constructively. "
I don't think a public dispute between Synaptics
and an individual open source developer would be particularly helpful for either
of us, especially within the Linux and open source communities
".
Lothian did not think he could "
reasonably provide the signed undertaking
"
Synaptics had demanded by August 28 without understanding which patent
claims it was alleging. He asked for an extension to the deadline. There was no
response from Bateman, so Lothian sent a follow-up email on
September 18. He said he was concerned there was no acknowledgment to his 
last email, and wondered it was safe to assume he could continue his work. He
had been running the Vino driver himself for quite a while, and was eager to
move it upstream without having patent threats hanging over the work.
Bateman responded the next day and said that he should be concerned:
As you previously requested, we have been documenting your ongoing patent
infringement by mapping your Vino driver to specific claims of our DisplayLink
patents. I will provide this claim mapping documentation to you within the next
two weeks. I will also be sending to you our demand for substantial monetary
compensation to recoup the cost and effort required to create such documentation
of your infringing acts. I previously gave you the opportunity to stop your
infringement, but you decided to push back and not heed my warnings, and so now
we are escalating as we deem appropriate.
The letter continued to claim that Lothian would be "
single-handedly
eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by
educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our
proprietary technology
". He said that DisplayLink is not a member of OIN,
and none of its technology is licensable through OIN or any other
organization.
Bateman sent a follow-up
letter, dated October 5, that included two claim charts for UK patents: GB2484736B ("Display control device") and GB2485613B ("Image generation"), both filed in 2010
and published in 2012. He reiterated Synaptics's demands from its previous
letter, and said that the deadline was now October 11; failure to comply
would result in the company seeking "
monetary
compensation from you in the amount of US$25,000 to recoup the costs and effort required to
create the attached documentation of your infringing acts
". That amount
would be increased by $25,000 each week until the company's demands were
complied with.
Lothian responded the next day, by email, to say that he was on
vacation, and would not be back home until October 13. He asked for an extension
of the deadline to return home and go through the claim charts "
ideally with
someone qualified to help me read them
". Bateman replied
that Synaptics would agree to extend the deadline to October 18, though no
further extensions would be granted. He reiterated that "
DisplayLink is not a
member of OIN
" and none of its technology was licensable through OIN.
OIN to the rescue?
Synaptics is a member of OIN, and is listed in the community directory. In addition to joining OIN, Lothian had reached out to the organization to try to solicit its help and has been in communication with some of the staff there. OIN indicated that it would look into the matter and see if he had any protection as an OIN member. That process took longer than Lothian hoped, though OIN did eventually provide its conclusion.
OIN's portfolio covers a wide range of software that matches its Linux System
Definition, but it does not cover everything that might be implemented for a
Linux system. In particular, its definition specifies that codecs ("
a
component of a program capable of performing transformations of a video, still
image or audio data stream or signal
") are not covered unless specifically
mentioned in this
list of components.
I spoke briefly to OIN CEO Keith Bergelt on October 23, shortly after OIN staff informed Lothian of the result of their research. Bergelt said that OIN's conclusion was that, since codecs are explicitly not covered by OIN's Linux System Definition, its protections did not extend to Lothian's attempted kernel contributions. OIN had recommended that Lothian reach out to a lawyer in the UK, and provided a recommendation.
Status
Unfortunately, that referral did not pan out, Lothian said. He has not given up
entirely, but he has taken down the GitHub repository to comply with Synaptics's

"

articles.title: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
articles.body:
Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
[LWN subscriber-only content]
Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms.
Synaptics and Displaylink
The dock that he was trying to support is a Dell device that connects to a system via USB 3 and allows users to connect multiple monitors and other devices to their computer. It provides its DisplayLink Manager (DLM) software for Linux for the devices via an APT repository for Ubuntu.
The company only provides DLM software in binary form, and only for x86-based platforms. The software is proprietary, but the company does maintain an open-source, out-of-tree kernel module that is included with DLM, the Extensible Virtual Display Interface (EVDI) project. It provides a driver that's compatible with Linux DRM and allows users to manage their docked displays with standard tools used for display settings, such as xrandr or GNOME and KDE Plasma's utilities.
Nobody covers the Linux kernel like LWN; be in the know with
a one-month trial subscription, no credit card needed.
A short article explains why the company has not released source code for DLM: the software uses a proprietary graphics technology called DL3 to create a compressed stream of the various channels (e.g., USB, DisplayLink video, audio) over a communication channel (USB 3 in this case) and decode it again for output to the user's devices.
Unfortunately, the vendor-supplied software did not work well for Lothian. I spoke and chatted with him via Signal while writing this article; he said that the driver kept crashing under Linux, so he decided to use his Claude subscription to try to develop a new driver and support software.
Vino
He posted the first
patch series for Vino—his Rust-based DRM/KMS driver—to the kernel's
dri-devel list as an RFC on June 17. Lothian noted that it was in an
incomplete state, and asked for help with a blocker that
he had run into trying to communicate with the dock's control plane. "
If you have
knowledge of the DisplayLink DL3 control-plane engagement sequence, or ideas for
isolating a whole-bus timing/ordering property a per-channel diff cannot see,
help would be very welcome.
" He received feedback from a few developers, including guidance
from Danilo Krummrich to rework the driver to use the Rust KMS bindings, but no advice
specific to the problem he was trying to solve.
Lothian also opened an issue on the EVDI GitHub repository on June 17. It explained the work he'd done so far, outlined the approach in trying to reverse-engineer the DL3 protocol, provided links to his GitHub repository with the Vino code, and asked for clarification on a few issues. There was no reply to his issue.
He also reached out to Łukasz Spintzyk of Synaptics directly by email; his correspondence with the company between July 5 and October 7 is available in this PDF compiled by Lothian. He noted that he had found a few bugs in EVDI and opened a pull request (that went unreviewed for several months), and also asked for assistance where he was blocked on Vino. On July 20, he received a reply, not from Spintzyk, but from Michal Lukaszek of Synaptics:
The reason I'm writing is that DisplayLink is not an open standard. The protocol, codec, and other technologies used by DisplayLink devices are proprietary to Synaptics and are protected by a substantial portfolio of patents in a number of jurisdictions, including the UK.
From what you've published, it appears that the VINO project is progressing beyond interoperability work and toward implementing technology that we believe is covered by those patents. While many developers understandably focus on avoiding copyrighted source code, patent law is different. An independently written or clean-room implementation does not necessarily avoid patent infringement if it implements patented inventions.
Lukaszek said it was entirely possible that Lothian was unaware of the
"
intellectual property landscape surrounding DisplayLink
", so he wanted
to make him aware now rather than "
have the situation become more formal
later
". Lothian lives in Scotland and has a ".co.uk" email address, which
explains why the email made reference to the UK.
Cease and desist
On August 17, Andrew Bateman, an assistant general council of
intellectual property for Synaptics, sent a cease-and-desist notice. The letter stated that Lothian had not
"
substantially responded
" to Lukaszek's communication, and had continued
with "
public statements and further development activities
". It included
an appendix with a list of 125 patents that "
cover fundamental aspects of
DisplayLink's architecture and operation
", but did not specify which patents
might be infringed by the work.
Synaptics included a list of eight demands it expected immediate compliance
with, including ceasing development of "
any software or other
implementation that infringes any Synaptics patent
", withdrawing submissions of
materials "
made to Linux kernel maintainers, mailing
lists, code-hosting platforms, package maintainers, distributions, or any other person or
organization
", and to identify in writing every location "
in which the
relevant materials have been published, submitted, stored, or
distributed
". It also demanded that he provide Synaptics with a signed
confirmation, by August 28, that he had complied with its demands.
Lothian, instead, posted version
three of his Vino work for the DisplayLink docks to the dri-devel list on
August 26. He said that the previous two versions had "
never lit a
panel
", but the new work could control three generations of DL3 docks
without any vendor software. There were no substantive reviews of the patch set
posted to the list, though there were some automated reviews from Sashiko.
On August 27, Lothian responded to Bateman and asked him to elaborate
on the patents that Synaptics thought were being infringed. "
A claim chart
mapping the relevant claims to the relevant code would make it much easier for
me to understand and properly respond to your concerns.
"
He also expressed confusion about Synaptics's position that his work was
being treated as patent infringement. Synaptics is a member of the Open Invention Network (OIN), which
was created to help open-source
developers and vendors deal with the threats of expensive patent litigation. It
holds a large, cross-licensed portfolio that serves to provide patent protection
to individuals, open-source projects, and large vendors alike. Lothian said that
he was now an OIN licensee as well, and he thought that it was supposed to
"
reduce exactly this sort of patent problem around Linux and open source
software
".
He asked Bateman to explain how Synaptics claims "
interact with our
respective OIN commitments
", and expressed a desire to sort things out with
Synaptics constructively. "
I don't think a public dispute between Synaptics
and an individual open source developer would be particularly helpful for either
of us, especially within the Linux and open source communities
".
Lothian did not think he could "
reasonably provide the signed undertaking
"
Synaptics had demanded by August 28 without understanding which patent
claims it was alleging. He asked for an extension to the deadline. There was no
response from Bateman, so Lothian sent a follow-up email on
September 18. He said he was concerned there was no acknowledgment to his 
last email, and wondered it was safe to assume he could continue his work. He
had been running the Vino driver himself for quite a while, and was eager to
move it upstream without having patent threats hanging over the work.
Bateman responded the next day and said that he should be concerned:
As you previously requested, we have been documenting your ongoing patent
infringement by mapping your Vino driver to specific claims of our DisplayLink
patents. I will provide this claim mapping documentation to you within the next
two weeks. I will also be sending to you our demand for substantial monetary
compensation to recoup the cost and effort required to create such documentation
of your infringing acts. I previously gave you the opportunity to stop your
infringement, but you decided to push back and not heed my warnings, and so now
we are escalating as we deem appropriate.
The letter continued to claim that Lothian would be "
single-handedly
eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by
educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our
proprietary technology
". He said that DisplayLink is not a member of OIN,
and none of its technology is licensable through OIN or any other
organization.
Bateman sent a follow-up
letter, dated October 5, that included two claim charts for UK patents: GB2484736B ("Display control device") and GB2485613B ("Image generation"), both filed in 2010
and published in 2012. He reiterated Synaptics's demands from its previous
letter, and said that the deadline was now October 11; failure to comply
would result in the company seeking "
monetary
compensation from you in the amount of US$25,000 to recoup the costs and effort required to
create the attached documentation of your infringing acts
". That amount
would be increased by $25,000 each week until the company's demands were
complied with.
Lothian responded the next day, by email, to say that he was on
vacation, and would not be back home until October 13. He asked for an extension
of the deadline to return home and go through the claim charts "
ideally with
someone qualified to help me read them
". Bateman replied
that Synaptics would agree to extend the deadline to October 18, though no
further extensions would be granted. He reiterated that "
DisplayLink is not a
member of OIN
" and none of its technology was licensable through OIN.
OIN to the rescue?
Synaptics is a member of OIN, and is listed in the community directory. In addition to joining OIN, Lothian had reached out to the organization to try to solicit its help and has been in communication with some of the staff there. OIN indicated that it would look into the matter and see if he had any protection as an OIN member. That process took longer than Lothian hoped, though OIN did eventually provide its conclusion.
OIN's portfolio covers a wide range of software that matches its Linux System
Definition, but it does not cover everything that might be implemented for a
Linux system. In particular, its definition specifies that codecs ("
a
component of a program capable of performing transformations of a video, still
image or audio data stream or signal
") are not covered unless specifically
mentioned in this
list of components.
I spoke briefly to OIN CEO Keith Bergelt on October 23, shortly after OIN staff informed Lothian of the result of their research. Bergelt said that OIN's conclusion was that, since codecs are explicitly not covered by OIN's Linux System Definition, its protections did not extend to Lothian's attempted kernel contributions. OIN had recommended that Lothian reach out to a lawyer in the UK, and provided a recommendation.
Status
Unfortunately, that referral did not pan out, Lothian said. He has not given up
entirely, but he has taken down the GitHub repository to comply with Synaptics's
demands. For now, he may continue working on some of the components that are not
affected by the patent claims, but the work on Vino will not be submitted
to the kernel. "
Vino itself has to remain local until this is sorted out, I
just can't afford to defend myself against Synaptics.
"

replied to the pull request on October 7. Lothian told me he does not
intend to follow up on the comments: "
You can't threaten to sue me and then
say 'can you update your pull request?'
"

It is an unpleasant reminder that, while much of the current conversations in open-source communities are concerned with LLM-driven development, software patents still pose problems for free-software developers and users.

articles.title: AMD's Zen 6 Family: Feeding the Beast
articles.body:
Hello you fine Internet folks,
Today we’re looking at AMD’s next-generation Zen 6 CPU core family. We’ll explore the changes from Zen 5 and what the differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c tell us about AMD’s approach to microarchitecture.
Hope y’all enjoy!
Overview
From a bird's eye view, Zen 6 is the natural evolution of Zen5, with the expansion of many OoO structures and iterative improvements found throughout the core.
Digging in deeper however tells a different story, with AMD heavily re-working several parts of the core, reminding me of the changes from Zen 1 to Zen 2.
At a high level the changes AMD made to the integer schedules stand out, returning to a layout reminiscent of Zen 3 and Zen 4.
Branch Prediction
Zen 5 had the best direction predictor of any core we have measured and Zen 6 seemingly builds upon that same direction predictor.
The biggest difference we do see is in what happens once the direction predictor gets overwhelmed. Both cores hit that wall in about the same place and past it, the predictor is left guessing at random data, so the time per branch mostly reflects how long the core takes to recover from a wrong guess. 
That plateau sits at roughly 3.5 to 4 ns of extra time per branch on Zen 5 and roughly 3 to 3.5 ns on Zen 6 so Zen 6 is paying less for each branch it gets wrong, which speaks to AMD reducing the latency of a branch mispredict compared to Zen 5.
Zen 6 has also improved the ability of the core to do 2 branches per cycle with Zen 6 able to do 2 branches per cycle within the L1 instruction cache.
When the footprint exceeds the L1i, then it falls to just a single branch per cycle for the rest of the BTB except for the 64B test which goes up to 4 cycles per branch for the L2 BTB.
When comparing the BTB of Zen 6 to Zen 5, Zen 6 appears to have focused on improving the speed of the BTB compared to beefing up the capacity.
The accuracy of Zen 6’s Branch Predictor Unit is very similar to Zen 5’s while also being faster which is a good thing considering that Zen 5 already had a very accurate Branch Predictor.
Instruction Fetch
Zen 6 carries forward the same dual decode cluster schema that Zen 5 introduced but, unlike Zen 5 where a single thread could only effectively use a single decode cluster, now with Zen 6 a single thread can use both decode clusters.
Outside of the L1i, Zen 6 looks very similar to Zen 5’s behavior on the instruction side of things.
Execution Engine
The execution engine of Zen 6 is overall very similar to Zen 5, but there are some important differences to be mindful of.
On the integer side, Zen 6 brings back Zen 4’s NOP pairing behavior, retiring up to 16 NOPs per cycle. Zen 6 also comes closer to theoretical peak throughput for simple integer instructions than Zen 5, sustaining 5.96 64-bit adds per cycle against Zen 5’s 5.25 with the same six ALUs.
AMD has reduced the number of integer multiply units from three to two, with PDEP and PEXT throughput also falling from three instructions per cycle to two. According to AMD, Zen 5’s third integer multiply unit did not justify its area cost.
On the vector side, the floating-point units are unchanged, with Zen 6 still handling two 512-bit FADDs, FMULs, or FMAs per cycle. The change is in VNNI, where Zen 6 doubles the number of units from two to four and our 512-bit VNNI test goes from 1.99 to 3.88 instructions per cycle, with Zen 6c matching it. VNNI instructions are useful for operations like calculating the inner loop of quantized inference as well as for video codecs using them for video filters as well.
Moving over to the other notable change, Zen 5 could already perform four per cycle, but our test shows only two of them could be vector loads, regardless of if they were 256 or 512 bit loads. Zen 6 raises 256-bit loads to four per cycle on both cores while leaving 512-bit loads at two, so both widths now reach the same 128 bytes per cycle which matters because most shipped vector code still targets AVX1/2.
The Out of Order Engine: Where Zen 6 and Zen 6c Split
In the past the difference between the Classic cores and the Dense cores in terms of the architecture were, for all intents and purposes, functionally identical with the biggest changes being in the number of cores on a CCD and the amount of L3 cache per core. With the Zen 6 family, that has changed.
Starting inside of the core, the changes occur after micro-op dispatch and seemingly end after the load queue.
The main differences between Zen 6 and Zen 6c lie in the capacities of their out-of-order structures. Several of these structures are larger on Zen 6c, allowing it to keep more work in flight and absorb more latency than Zen 6. The reorder buffer grows from 576 to 640 entries, the integer register file from 288 to 352, the vector scheduler from 138 to 180, and the load queue from 280 to 330.
The differences suggest that AMD is specializing the two designs. Zen 6 appears tuned for high frequency, while Zen 6c has more capacity to tolerate comparatively high memory latency.
Zen 6 and Zen 6c use 12-core and 32-core CCDs, respectively, but both provide 4 MB of L3 cache per core. That gives the 12-core CCD 48 MB of L3 cache and the 32-core CCD 128 MB.
L3 latency has increased from about 47 cycles on Zen 5 to 55 cycles on Zen 6 and 66 cycles on Zen 6c. The larger caches and greater number of mesh stops likely contribute to the increase. In nanoseconds, Zen 6’s higher clock hides most of the increase, at 10.7 ns against 10.3 ns on the Zen 5-based EPYC 9355P, while Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger CCX put it at 16.4 ns.
Moving over to bandwidth, we see that Zen 6 fixes Zen 5’s odd L2 bandwidth behavior, where a core pulled only about 42 bytes per cycle across most of the L2’s capacity, in Zen 6 the read path now reliably delivers 64 bytes per cycle. The rest of the cache hierarchy is largely unchanged in bandwidth per cycle.
Load/Store
Store-to-load forwarding is seemingly unchanged from Zen 5 and is where the behavior of Zen 6 and Zen 6c re-unify.
A 32-bit load from the same address as a 64-bit store completes with effectively zero latency which lets Zen 6 handle two dependent store-load pairs per cycle. Loads fully contained within the store complete in 7 cycles regardless of alignment with partial overlaps costing 14 cycles, matching Zen 5.
SPEC CPU 2026 Performance
The EPYC 9686F is near the top of our estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 results. It roughly matches the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, AMD’s highest-end client CPU from the previous generation, in integer rate and beats it in floating-point rate. At a matched 4.1 GHz, the 9686F leads the 9950X3D2 by about 4% in integer and 11% in floating point, despite the X3D part’s much larger L3.
The EPYC 9996 is no slouch either. It roughly matches the previous-generation EPYC 9575F in single-threaded performance, despite running at lower clocks and having four times as many cores. It also edges out NVIDIA’s Vera in integer and leads it by about 20% in floating point.
The EPYC 9686F leads on almost every subtest and finishes about 18% ahead of the EPYC 9996 in both suites. It scores 6.20 versus 5.25 in integer and 10.6 versus 8.99 in floating point, with some of its largest leads in 714.cpython, 766.femflow, and 772.marian.
Against the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F, the 9996 scores 5.25 versus 5.13 in integer and 8.99 versus 9.01 in floating point while running about 900 MHz slower. The 9996 also edges out the 9686F in 721.gcc and 765.roms, two subtests where the 9686F’s higher clock provides no advantage.
Top-down breakdowns of pipeline slots on the two Zen 6 chips show where the 9686F’s lead comes from. The integer-rate profiles look almost identical in core-bound subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, 710.omnetpp, 735.gem5, and 753.ns3, retiring slots account for nearly the same share on both chips, with differences of less than one percentage point.
Memory-heavy subtests show larger gaps. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 37.9% to 50.0% of pipeline slots in 729.abc, from 19.0% to 34.1% in 723.llvm, and from 24.8% to 33.2% in 708.sqlite. The share of retiring slots falls accordingly. Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger shared L3 cache may help explain its lower memory-stall share.
The floating-point profiles look similar for most subtests. The retiring share in 731.astcenc, 772.marian, and 767.nest differs by about one percentage point or less, and 709.cactus spends over half its slots stalled on front-end bandwidth on both chips.
The larger gaps again appear in memory-heavy subtests. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 42.5% to 55.3% of slots in 765.roms, from 60.9% to 67.6% in 749.fotonik3d, and from 17.8% to 33.8% in 782.lbm. These are also tests where the 9686F’s higher clock helps least: it trails the 9996 in 765.roms, roughly ties in 749.fotonik3d, and leads by about 11% in 782.lbm, despite clocking up to roughly 29% higher.
Running the 9686F at 4.1 GHz to match the 9996 removes the clock advantage, and the overall picture flips: the 9686F scores 4.92 and 8.64 at that clock, putting Zen 6c about 6.7% ahead per clock in integer and 4% in floating point. At the same clock speed, Zen 6 and Zen 6c look almost identical in core-bound integer subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, retiring slots account for 67.3% of the total on the EPYC 9686F versus 67.6% on the EPYC 9996.The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow.
The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.
The clearest difference is in frontend latency stalls, which account for a much larger share of slots on the 9686F in subtests with large codebases. In 727.cppcheck, that share is 35.2% versus 16.6% on the 9996; in 721.gcc, it is 25.8% versus 10.0%. With clock speed matched and both designs sharing the same frontend, those stalls most likely reflect differences in the cache and memory hierarchy.
The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow.
The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.
Final Words
The Zen 6 Family improves upon its predecessor in various ways, an upgraded frontend allows one thread to utilize both decoders, while a faster branch predictor makes it more forgiving on misses, all tied together with larger OoO structures allowing it to better hide memory stalls. All of this coming together to provide a generational uplift from Zen 5.
However, I think the more interesting change is the split between Zen 6 and Zen 6c. The classic and dense cores now differ within the out-of-order engine, with Zen 6 appearing tuned for higher clocks and Zen 6c providing more capacity to absorb latency. The shared foundation is still clear, but those differences make the choice between them more dependent on workload behavior.
The performance results are encouraging as well with the estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 scores, the EPYC 9686F leads the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F by about 21% in integer and 18% in floating point. The EPYC 9996 roughly matches the 9575F despite running about 900 MHz slower which are strong results for both core designs.
AMD’s answer to the classic-versus-dense question used to be the same core at two densities but now with Zen 6 it is two cores, each shaped for where it will run. That now leaves me wondering what AMD will do with the Zen 7 Family and if we will see even more specialization of the same basic core design or if we will see a larger split of the designs.
