Loads fully contained within the store complete in 7 cycles regardless of alignment with partial overlaps costing 14 cycles, matching Zen 5.
SPEC CPU 2026 Performance
The EPYC 9686F is near the top of our estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 results. It roughly matches the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2, AMD’s highest-end client CPU from the previous generation, in integer rate and beats it in floating-point rate. At a matched 4.1 GHz, the 9686F leads the 9950X3D2 by about 4% in integer and 11% in floating point, despite the X3D part’s much larger L3.
The EPYC 9996 is no slouch either. It roughly matches the previous-generation EPYC 9575F in single-threaded performance, despite running at lower clocks and having four times as many cores. It also edges out NVIDIA’s Vera in integer and leads it by about 20% in floating point.
The EPYC 9686F leads on almost every subtest and finishes about 18% ahead of the EPYC 9996 in both suites. It scores 6.20 versus 5.25 in integer and 10.6 versus 8.99 in floating point, with some of its largest leads in 714.cpython, 766.femflow, and 772.marian.
Against the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F, the 9996 scores 5.25 versus 5.13 in integer and 8.99 versus 9.01 in floating point while running about 900 MHz slower. The 9996 also edges out the 9686F in 721.gcc and 765.roms, two subtests where the 9686F’s higher clock provides no advantage.
Top-down breakdowns of pipeline slots on the two Zen 6 chips show where the 9686F’s lead comes from. The integer-rate profiles look almost identical in core-bound subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, 710.omnetpp, 735.gem5, and 753.ns3, retiring slots account for nearly the same share on both chips, with differences of less than one percentage point.
Memory-heavy subtests show larger gaps. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 37.9% to 50.0% of pipeline slots in 729.abc, from 19.0% to 34.1% in 723.llvm, and from 24.8% to 33.2% in 708.sqlite. The share of retiring slots falls accordingly. Zen 6c’s lower clock and larger shared L3 cache may help explain its lower memory-stall share.
The floating-point profiles look similar for most subtests. The retiring share in 731.astcenc, 772.marian, and 767.nest differs by about one percentage point or less, and 709.cactus spends over half its slots stalled on front-end bandwidth on both chips.
The larger gaps again appear in memory-heavy subtests. Moving from the EPYC 9996 to the EPYC 9686F, backend memory stalls rise from 42.5% to 55.3% of slots in 765.roms, from 60.9% to 67.6% in 749.fotonik3d, and from 17.8% to 33.8% in 782.lbm. These are also tests where the 9686F’s higher clock helps least: it trails the 9996 in 765.roms, roughly ties in 749.fotonik3d, and leads by about 11% in 782.lbm, despite clocking up to roughly 29% higher.
Running the 9686F at 4.1 GHz to match the 9996 removes the clock advantage, and the overall picture flips: the 9686F scores 4.92 and 8.64 at that clock, putting Zen 6c about 6.7% ahead per clock in integer and 4% in floating point. At the same clock speed, Zen 6 and Zen 6c look almost identical in core-bound integer subtests. In 750.sealcrypto, retiring slots account for 67.3% of the total on the EPYC 9686F versus 67.6% on the EPYC 9996.The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow.
The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.
The clearest difference is in frontend latency stalls, which account for a much larger share of slots on the 9686F in subtests with large codebases. In 727.cppcheck, that share is 35.2% versus 16.6% on the 9996; in 721.gcc, it is 25.8% versus 10.0%. With clock speed matched and both designs sharing the same frontend, those stalls most likely reflect differences in the cache and memory hierarchy.
The floating-point profiles also look similar in several subtests at matched clocks. Both chips spend over half their pipeline slots stalled on frontend bandwidth in 709.cactus. Their retiring shares differ by about two percentage points in 722.palm and 766.femflow.
The 9686F still spends a larger share of its pipeline slots stalled on memory. Backend memory stalls account for 50.3% versus 42.5% on the 9996 in 765.roms, 24.9% versus 17.8% in 782.lbm, and 63.3% versus 60.9% in 749.fotonik3d. Zen 6c’s 128 MB L3 cache is likely serving more of these requests than Zen 6’s 48 MB cache, reducing the need to access main memory.
Final Words
The Zen 6 Family improves upon its predecessor in various ways, an upgraded frontend allows one thread to utilize both decoders, while a faster branch predictor makes it more forgiving on misses, all tied together with larger OoO structures allowing it to better hide memory stalls. All of this coming together to provide a generational uplift from Zen 5.
However, I think the more interesting change is the split between Zen 6 and Zen 6c. The classic and dense cores now differ within the out-of-order engine, with Zen 6 appearing tuned for higher clocks and Zen 6c providing more capacity to absorb latency. The shared foundation is still clear, but those differences make the choice between them more dependent on workload behavior.
The performance results are encouraging as well with the estimated single-threaded SPEC CPU 2026 scores, the EPYC 9686F leads the Zen 5-based EPYC 9575F by about 21% in integer and 18% in floating point. The EPYC 9996 roughly matches the 9575F despite running about 900 MHz slower which are strong results for both core designs.
AMD’s answer to the classic-versus-dense question used to be the same core at two densities but now with Zen 6 it is two cores, each shaped for where it will run. That now leaves me wondering what AMD will do with the Zen 7 Family and if we will see even more specialization of the same basic core design or if we will see a larger split of the designs.

articles.title: Blender 5.3 released with Gaussian Splat support
articles.body:
Watch the Recap Video
Make a Splat
Gaussian Magic
Point of View
Radiant Future
More About Shading
CYCLES
Divide and Shine
CYCLES
A diamond
in the Rough
CYCLES
Gone with Denoise
NVIDIA DLSS brings near-final render quality to the viewport, making lighting and look development faster and more responsive while virtually eliminating flickering between frames during animation playback.
Find it in the Denoise panel under Render properties, Sampling.
DLSS denoising requires NVIDIA driver version 620 or newer.
EEVEE
Lights Meet Material Nodes
Lighting to Your Liking
A Wider Perspective
EEVEE can now render panoramic cameras, supporting all types of projections, from equirectangular and cubemap formats to various fisheye models and mirror ball.
The current implementation has a few limitations: depth of field, raytracing, and volumetric temporal reprojection in the viewport are not yet supported.
More in EEVEE & Viewport
COMPOSITOR
Side Effects
You can now stack Effects on your scene just like you would modifiers or constraints.
Applying compositing effects has never been easier.
One-click, Bloom!
Choose from built-in effects such as Bloom, Chromatic Aberration, Film Grain, and Vignette, as well as effects from online asset libraries or your own custom compositor node groups.
Internally, each effect is its own node group, with its output passed on to the next effect.
You can further customize effects at any time in the Compositor editor.
COMPOSITOR
Bundle Up
17 Geometry Nodes are now supported in the Compositor, bringing a range of new capabilities across bundles, math and logic, and utility operations.
This includes bundle support with Get Bundle Item, Store Bundle Item, Combine Bundle, Typed Bundle, and Separate Bundle.
Math and logic nodes such as Boolean Math, Compare, Float to Integer, Integer Math, Matrix SVD, Combine Transform, and Separate Transform. Plus utility nodes including Hash Value, Random Value, Is Viewport, Import Text, and Bone Info.
Play Fast
Playback is now up to 2x faster on GPU, particularly when playing back EXR sequences.
The interactive compositor now supports playback caching. It can be enabled from the sidebar, Options panel.
Anisotropic Kuwahara is now up to 10x faster on Apple GPUs, 2x faster on NVIDIA GPUs, and 25-30% on CPU.
More in Compositor
Study the artwork
Blender splash artwork source files are available for you to play with!
CORE
Blender, meet projects.
Until now, Blender’s preferences (such as asset libraries) were shared across all projects, and it was up to users to keep related files and resources organized.
Blender now supports projects, giving you a way to group related files, share resources, and manage settings across an entire project, whether you’re working alone or as part of a team.
Everything
Everywhere
All In a Project
Projects support custom variables that can be used throughout a project, such as a character’s name or a frequently used file path.
Per-project asset libraries and color management configurations are also supported. You can even set up a custom splash screen for your project, providing quick access to its files and other recent projects.
Add-ons and other extensions per-project will follow in future Blender versions.
Projects are entirely optional, most of the time you’ll probably work without one.
ASSETS
Asset Libraries ♥ Extensions
Asset libraries can now be shared as extensions! Just like add-ons or themes.
Browse hundreds of public domain assets available on the Extensions platform via the Get Extensions tab and install them directly from within Blender.
GREASE PENCIL
Drawn to Select
Draw Mode now has its own selection tools: Tweak, Lasso, Box, and Circle. Select strokes and adjust them right where you draw.
Move, rotate, scale, duplicate, copy, paste, and delete strokes using the usual shortcuts, or access all these actions from the new Stroke menu.
Carve Diem
Meet the new Carver tool in Draw Mode.
It cuts shapes using proper Boolean subtraction, creating clean cuts in strokes and fills based on a lasso selection. Holes are created automatically when needed.
When a shape has both a stroke and a fill, carving a hole into it also creates a stroke around the hole. Fills that are split apart become separate shapes, making them easy to sculpt further.
One Tool to Fill Them All
The Fill tool can now fill multiple regions at once.
Simply draw a path across multiple regions to fill them all as a single shape, with no gaps or borders in between.
Ramp It Up
Gradient fills now use a ColorRamp input instead of being limited to just two colors.
Flip Out
Mirror the camera view horizontally with the new Flip View operator to evaluate the composition from a different perspective and spot asymmetry or visual imbalances.
This only affects the viewport display. It does not change the camera object’s transform or the final render, which remains unchanged. Use the operator again to restore the original orientation.
Flip View has no shortcut assigned by default, but you can assign your own through the right-click menu or add it to Quick Favorites (Q) for easy access.
I/O
USD Collection Importer
Collections can now be associated to importers.
Similar to the Collection Exporters introduced in Blender 4.2 LTS, Collection Importers make it easy to re-import data with a single click, without having to navigate menus or adjust settings repeatedly.
Configure them through the Importers panel under Collection Properties. Settings are stored in .blend files, making them easy to share and preserving them across Blender sessions.
Only the USD importer is supported in Blender 5.3.
See all USD, Alembic, glTF, OpenEXR, and other I/O changes.
VIDEO SEQUENCER
Cut to the chase
The Video Sequencer gets a full ripple editing framework, a rewritten blade tool, and a long list of editing, interface, and performance improvements, including initial OpenTimelineIO support.
Ripple,
Shuffle,
Overwrite
Welcome Ripple editing to Blender 5.3!
This new overlap mode automatically moves strips forward or backward as edits are made, maintaining timeline continuity without the need to manually close gaps.
Ripple, Shuffle, and Overwrite modes are now consistently used across editing operations. Switch between them while moving strips using R, S, and V.
Making Waves
Complete the ripple workflow with these handy operators:
Ripple Add: Hold Shift while dragging and dropping strips to insert them using ripple behavior, automatically making room in the timeline.
Ripple Trim: Trim selected strips at the playhead and automatically close the resulting gaps. Use Shift+Q or Shift+W to trim from either side.
Ripple Delete: Delete selected strips and move subsequent content back to close the gaps. Use Shift+X.
Cutting Edge: Blade 2.0
Splits are now visualized as a line when using Blade and as a region when using Box Blade. Tooltips display frame values at the split location, while a real-time preview shows the frame beneath the cursor.
Press and hold C in the timeline to temporarily activate the Blade tool.
Release it to switch back to the previously active tool.
But wait, there’s more: Hardware decoding, thumbnail support for Scene and other strips, OpenTimelineIO import and export, and much more.
USER INTERFACE
Search. Sort. Scribble.
Sorted Out
Arrange your objects freely with custom sorting in the Outliner. Finally.
Switch back to alphabetical order from the header popover.
Plus improvements to filtering, drag-and-drop behavior, and hierarchy management.
Side Quest
Sidebars in all editors now support search, making it possible to find any property or operator, even inside tabs created by add-ons.
Press Ctrl/Cmd + F while hovering the sidebar and start typing right away, or through the context menu of the tabs and panels.
To clear the search, press Alt/Option + F.
Mark it Down
The Blender UI now supports rendering basic Markdown formatting.
In node editors, write markdown directly in the new Comment node, or in regular layouts for scripts/add-ons through the label_markdown widget. Another handy widget for long strings is label_multiline, it behaves just like labels but allows text to wrap.
But wait: IME support, improved tooltips, box-select gesture, browsable node editor context paths, better Attribute Viewer overlay, Curve widget selection, and more!
What’s Next?
Blender on tablets, texture layers, animation layers? Show your support for upcoming development projects and help shape the future of Blender.
BUT WAIT, THERE’S MORE
Plus hundreds of bug fixes, code cleanups and refactors.
See the full list of changes.
CREDITS
Blender is a community project.
Learn more on how you can contribute to Blender.
List of developers who contributed to Blender 5.3 and all-time contributors.
Splash artwork: OVERGROWN, by Blender Studio
Cycles diamonds render by Chris Tyler. Butterflies specter shader by Cartesian Caramel. Grease Pencil drawings by Vivien Lulkowski from Blender Studio, Cowboi and Storm by Blender Studio.
Huge thanks to everyone involved! 🧡
The Blender team. November 10, 2026

articles.title: Meet the Sad Wives of AI
articles.body:
If i had to listen to another minute of my husband talking about Claude Code, I might have actually died. It was 11 pm in Berkeley, California, where I was home alone with our 10-month-old daughter, and 2 am in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where he was visiting for his newish job in AI. “JUST LOOK AT THIS!” he shouted. The FaceTime camera zoomed toward a laptop sitting on a hotel bed. “SEE?!”
See what, I thought. I wanted to shower. I still had to take the dog out.
“ARE YOU LOOKING?” he shouted again. I wasn’t. I was looking at our real baby. But that’s the thing. There are two babies in this household now: the small human one and the large language model. Both demand constant attention. Both keep us up at 2 am.
Is this a Sophie’s choice kind of situation? Please. I’d kill the AI baby in an instant.
There’s a strange and under-discussed side effect of the AI boom: what it’s doing to family dynamics. By which I mean: how it’s potentially destroying family dynamics. I’m sure this applies to all kinds of families, gay or straight, rich or poor, with any AI-pilled members. The technology is coming, has come, for us all. But for the purposes of this story, I mostly spoke to white-collar heteros in the Bay Area, because that’s where a certain psychological crisis seems most acute. Often it goes like this: He works in AI, and she does everything and anything else. Other times, it’s bleaker: He desperately wants to work in AI—or feels he must work in AI—and she wants him to do literally anything else.
Either way, the men go in and the women want out. How many? It depends on how you define “working in AI.” About 71 percent of “AI-skilled workers,” according to one report, are men, and there are roughly 35,000 open AI roles in the US at any given moment. Broaden that to include investors and you’re adding thousands more. Broaden it further to include every man who has mentioned to his wife that he is “looking at some opportunities in the space”—and we’re in the millions. Conservatively, that means hundreds of thousands of spouses, partners, and girlfriends, holding down the fort while someone mansplains the singularity to them. There are, in other words, a lot of us, and more of us are surfacing—gasping for air and a single conversation that doesn’t involve LLMs—by the day.
There’s a name for our ranks. I call us the sad wives of AI.
First of all, I’m sorry. AI is already the only thing most people talk about here, and it’s even worse for the sad wives.
One of them moved from New York for her husband’s career. He cofounded an AI company; now he’s head of design at another. “He’s so passionate about it,” she says. “I go along to get along.” That is, when she can remember what it is he does, exactly. “My eyes glaze over a bit. I tend to check out. I forget.” She does say his company is at the forefront of … something. Mostly, she’s tired. “I did not expect how homogenous it would be,” she says. “In New York, I had a friend who’s a teacher, a friend who’s a nurse, a friend in fashion, a friend in finance—and none of us talked about our jobs when we went out. Every time I go out in San Francisco, it feels like I’m at a work happy hour. I don’t get it.”
In a way, it can’t be helped. Most days it feels like every billboard in the city is about AI. Every. Single. One. “I’m on the edge,” another AI wife tells me, “while my husband drives by and is like, ‘Oh wow, that’s my company’s billboard.’ Cool. Great.” She, like almost every sad AI wife I talk to, doesn’t want me to include the specifics of her situation. Marriages, social standings, and finances—anything to protect the equity!—are on the line.
Some of the sad wives are obscenely rich; others are struggling. But the more I talk to them, the more I hear the same lines, the same complaints, the same clichés. The hours. The obsession. The sense that missing this moment would mean, for their AI-pilled spouses, missing the most important technological shift of a lifetime. “They really want to ride the wave,” one AI wife says. Another: “He’s always depressed about something.”
Yana van der Meulen Rodgers, the chair of labor studies and employment relations at Rutgers University, has a blunt take: What’s happening in Bay Area households isn’t just a lifestyle story. It’s a labor market story. The AI boom, Rodgers says, is creating a “perfect storm” of forces reshaping household dynamics, playing out along predictably gendered lines.
The story is older than Silicon Valley, of course. Every major technological boom has produced the same figure, the person who gives everything to the wave. During the industrial revolution, it was the factory worker. During the Gold Rush, it was the men who left their families and headed west. During the dotcom boom, it was the founders sleeping under their desks in SoMa. Now, it is the person who is building, building, always building—vibe coding at midnight, constantly upgrading their models—convinced that stopping for five minutes means missing everything. Economists call this the “ideal worker.” Rodgers calls it a trap. “Someone who works many hours, giving all of themselves to this new force,” she says. “That means less time at home for the partner, less time for care work.”
Though things keep changing, some analyses suggest that women are about 20 percent less likely than men to use generative AI. “It’s a function not of gender per se,” Rodgers suggests, “but of the occupations that women hold.” Women are disproportionately represented in jobs—education, health care, social services—that right now use AI less. The result could be a compounding disadvantage. Over time, it means less access to the boom’s financial rewards, more responsibility for the domestic labor it generates.
And what happens when it doesn’t work out for the men? Many, if not most, won’t make it in AI, a lucrative but volatile business. “With job loss comes some depression,” Rodgers says. “Within the household, if one person is going through adverse mental health effects around job loss or uncertainty, the other naturally becomes the support person.” The cruel irony, for some sad wives, is that the moment their husband does leave AI, whether by choice or by force, there’s no relief. Now he’s home. Spiraling. Now she’s managing that too.
It was nearing the end of my therapy session. I had been rambling for 50 minutes about the mental load, the changing hormones, whether my postpartum depression could really just be traced to the fact that it took longer than anticipated to fit back into my jeans. Then my therapist interrupted and asked what exactly my partner did for work again. “Oh,” I said. “Well, he’s head of AI at his company.”
What she said next, I had to write down. Her client base, she allowed, is almost entirely women—women whose husbands, more often than not, are in some way professionally adjacent to AI. And it’s affecting their relationships. The pressure to keep up means zero boundaries at home. The very masculine energy of it all. And the constant fighting, which is about something bigger than them. He’s off in another world, a world of prompts and benchmarks and epiphanies, while she’s firmly in this one.
The resentment builds quietly. Several of these sad wives, my therapist added, have turned down job opportunities in AI themselves. Not because they weren’t qualified, but because it’s hard to raise kids and disrupt civilization at the same time.
Princess Diana famously said there were three people in her marriage. For the sad wives of AI, the third is a chatbot. I spoke to a few other family therapists, and they agreed with mine: The phenomenon is getting worse. “It’s a lot of tech wives,” one said, sighing. “A lot of tech wives.”

None bit.

They have podcasts and Senate hearings and magazine profiles and probably a group chat with the president. They’ve been talked to—and I can’t stress this enough—enough.
On an unseasonably warm evening, I met up with two friends at a wine bar. Both are partnered with men somewhere on the AI spectrum—tangibly building it, wildly chasing it, or simply unable to shut up about it. We ordered something orange and natural, the kind of wine that signals you have opinions.

It’s so existential. I think about it and then I get depressed.
Yeah. Don’t think about it!
We thought about it for the next two hours.
Every night, it’s just existential dread.

Maybe we’ll just go back to the Stone Age.
One friend has started lobbying for her family to become Outdoor People. The kind who go into the wilderness and disconnect. For a whole week, no access. Just don’t tell Claude.
A pause.
Do we want dessert?

They’re both building walls of resentment.”
Which—we know already. But then Balajadia tells me two surprising things. The first is that some sad wives of AI don’t want to talk to her about their husbands. Why? “I’ve already worked through this with my chat,” they say. By which they mean … ChatGPT. Yes. Not only is AI driving a wedge between couples. It’s also become a primary tool for attempting to salvage their marriage.
Balajadia isn’t impressed. “They’re not having great outcomes,” she says. “It’s not going to challenge you. You end up being validated. Then both of you don’t move the needle in conflict.”
It gets worse. ChatGPT subsequently, in some situations, helps these sad wives explore the possibility of cheating. Some of them, Balajadia says, get “validating messages,” such as: “Yes, it makes sense that you’re seeking attraction elsewhere because your partner’s not giving it to you. He’s emotionally unavailable.” She pauses. “That’s probably not a great idea. You probably should address the stuff that’s coming up in your marriage, not go have sex with someone else.”
Some wives, it must be said, have uncomplicated relationships with AI. One tells me it has “supercharged” her life—wedding planning, caring for aging parents, housekeeping, veterinary advice. While her husband is focused on how AI will change the economy, she’s interested in how it will change her. Optimize her, really. “There’s just not enough hours in the day if I don’t try to gain efficiencies in some things.” In fact, she’s just vibe coded something or other. Maybe one day he’ll be a sad AI husband.
Or robots will fix everything. Another wife tells me that her husband, who founded an AI startup, is convinced they will have a household robot within the decade. “Maybe after we have kids, I’ll be like, ‘Bring a robot in,’” she says. “Right now, I can’t wrap my mind around it, though maybe people felt that way about washing machines.” This in response to the question I ask everyone: Has any part of the AI boom made things better at home? Could it ever?
The responses are generally uninspiring. Most of the time, the closest thing to a silver lining any sad wife can offer is that AI has given them something new to talk about at dinner.
Each time it’s the same pattern: a generation (of men) convinced this is their moment, and everyone else trying to figure out where they fit. A bubble. And bubbles, as anyone who was here in 2001 can tell you, tend to burst. One AI wife—the one who drives past billboards for companies her husband has backed—puts it simply: “Half of our income is dependent on AI doing well.”
Mine too. More than half, to be frank.
Flying home from that same trip to Massachusetts, my husband found himself watching the screen of the passenger next to him. It was playing Train Dreams, a movie about a man who leaves his family for logging and railroad work in the American West, a century ago. Even without sound, he got a little emotional. “Is that what I’m doing right now?” he asked me later.
The man in the film ultimately loses his wife and young daughter. He’s filled with regret for much of his life.
“But I’m doing it for our daughter,” my husband assured me. And: “I’ve always wanted the things I’ve worked on to be necessary.”
I thought about that for a while. Then I asked him to take the dog out.
What Say You?

Often it goes like this: He works in AI, and she does everything and anything else. It’s a labor market story. The AI boom, Rodgers says, is creating a “perfect storm” of forces reshaping household dynamics, playing out along predictably gendered lines.
The story is older than Silicon Valley, of course. Every major technological boom has produced the same figure, the person who gives everything to the wave. During the industrial revolution, it was the factory worker. During the Gold Rush, it was the men who left their families and headed west. articles.title: PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery
articles.body:
David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI), used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem about quantum computing.
“I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch. “In a few months, like, why would you even put out a paper?”
The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the two researchers who posed the problem, writes that he doesn’t quite understand the proof but that he believes it’s correct because it was autoformalized in Lean, a coding language for math, and explained by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared the solution.
The solution appears to close the door on one avenue quantum computers could follow to solve certain difficult problems at high speed, but not all of them. “It’s a negative result that allows people to know, okay, we’re no longer looking there,” Turturean said.
More broadly, it reflects the upheaval in the scientific world caused by AI problem-solving.
“A proof of full [Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture] was one of the last remaining open problems in quantum query complexity that everyone seemed to agree was centrally important,” Aaronson, who described himself feeling satisfied, awestruck, disappointed, and fatigued by the news, wrote. “I was surprised, honestly, to see it missing from OpenAI’s Mathocalypse dump a few weeks ago. Surely they tried it, so was it really so much harder than all the problems that were solved?”
That’s a point in favor of PSI’s model, which is to solve scientific problems with specialized model harnesses and scaffolding.
“An effective kind of research system should have lots of things related to harnesses, lots related to tools, memory systems, simulation infrastructure,” PSI CEO Matt Pines told TechCrunch. “You want to be able to really go after a problem at breadth and depth, and be able to consider a wide range of potential alternatives.”
For now, the company’s revenue comes from using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating the variables of heat, power, water, sound — “where the performance of that site as well as its impact on the community are a direct function of its physics.” The long play, however, is converting theoretical physics breakthroughs into actual technologies.
“Six to nine months ago, when I was talking to investors, like I had to sort of stretch to validate that conditional, right? Like, ‘no, no, no, trust me, pretty soon, theoretical physics is going to be mostly the domain of machines,’” Pines said. “And it’s not there yet, but it’s on its way.”
Still, while AI has claimed important solutions in fields like mathematics and computer science where it’s possible to express them in validated code, doing so in less abstracted disciplines like the life sciences or physics has proven more difficult. Last week, the startup Discovered Materials released a $1 million grand challenge for researchers using AI to understand problems like superconductivity and heat dissipation.
“At the end of the day, physics is different than math because it’s the real world … nature gets a vote in your models of reality,” Pines said. He said the startup is focused on understanding how to take computational results and validate them with experiments in the most efficient way possible.
“If it’s a true fact of nature, that’s a trick that you can exploit,” Pines said. “You could build a device out of it, right? The AI suggests an idea; it allows you to do something in the world you weren’t able to do before … and so each of those are kind of loops that PSI is building.”
As “neolabs for science” become a pathway for potentially groundbreaking science, the participants are still figuring out what the standards are for this new world. Because PSI had to hold its result until Anthropic’s model was nearly ready for release, they were able to share it with relevant researchers to better understand it.
“As an academic, we wanted to play our role in doing things the right way,” Jim Halverson, a professor at Northeastern University who advises PSI, said. He’ll be attending a summit at MIT next week where leading physicists will try to hash out a response to the new pace of science. “Best practices are still emerging … We figured that transparency is a good way to go, and contacting experts is a good way to go.”
“We had some time to sit on it … and it was the first time that I actually took one of my AI-elicited solutions on print, and I read through it, and I was like, okay, how can I make this … be presented more naturally for a human?” Turturean, who said the academic community will expect him to be able to explain the result, told TechCrunch. “And I think it also made me realize, oh my God, the weight of what AI can do.”

articles.title: AI is an information gateway. Audiences still don't want it making their news
articles.body:
In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.”
As it turns out, I was right. In new research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered.
For our new report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,” we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.
The use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw.
Many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries said they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.
Despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) said they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment.
Conversational AI as a friction-reducing information intermediary
Our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more quickly.
“Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) said they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024.
We looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%).
Using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year. But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.
Many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust.
At the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) said they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources.
As AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable.
Persistent attitudes: People’s views on generative AI in journalism and news
As in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly.
People across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed.
This also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest.
Zooming out
Our findings raise several important questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI.
First, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context.
Second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also shows that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them.
Third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models.
The differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a new dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued, there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried.
Expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily users and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.
This doesn’t matter just for people’s individual choices around whether and how to make use of AI in their own lives. It also matters where AI is adopted and governed through collective decisions — in public services, for example — that apply to those who do not use it.
Felix Simon is the research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and a research associate at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) at the University of Oxford.

articles.title: 'C:\> FORMAT C:' – relax, it's just a screen saver
articles.body:
FakeDOS 2.0 · Screen saver for macOS
The most realistic DOS since DOS.
Leave your Mac alone for a few minutes and it becomes a 1990s PC: an AWARD BIOS counts through 32 MB of RAM, a VGA prompt starts blinking, and then a ghost begins to type. It boots. It crashes. It dials. It lies convincingly.
C:\> TYPE README.TXT
What is this?
Welcome, traveller. You have just discovered FakeDOS, a macOS screen saver that simulates a pixel-perfect DOS machine. And more.
Leave your Mac alone for a few minutes and something beautiful is going to happen: the screen fills with the warm 80×25 glow of a VGA text mode, an AWARD BIOS POST clicks through memory, and a friendly blinking C:\> prompt appears.
Perfect for
- A conference room that does not need Slack popping up
- Pretending to be a 12-year-old running Landmark Test
- Tricking a co-worker into thinking you have lost it
- Actually getting people to leave you alone
Features
Five boot modes
The Ghost Writer
Leave the prompt idle and a ghost starts typing commands by itself. It alternates between operating systems in an endless loop of simulated productivity.
- Many DOS commands, boot linux, some Linux commands, boot dos, repeat
- Realistic typing speed with human-like typos
- Press any key to take over and the ghost vanishes
Landmark speed test
Type FDOS or LANDMARK at the prompt to see how fast your imaginary Pentium thinks it is.
Pure nostalgia, zero benchmarking.
Pentagon mode
Type PENTAGON at the prompt. We cannot tell you what happens.
ACCESS DENIED. CLASSIFIED.
This is not a real DOS.
- OKYour files are safe.
- OKYour disk is safe.
- OKYour Mac is safe.
- OKYour network is safe.
Absolutely nothing useful happens here.

When you type FORMAT C:, FakeDOS shows a terrifyingly realistic format sequence, complete with percentage counter and head/cylinder display, but your actual drive is perfectly untouched. When you type DEL *.*, nothing gets deleted. Ever.
It simulates. It pretends. It lies convincingly.
But it never, ever touches your real system.
Not a terminal. Not an emulator. Not connected to the Pentagon. Probably.

- DIR
- List files in current directory
- CD
- Change directory
- TYPE
- Display file contents
- COPY
- Copy files
- MOVE
- Move files
- DEL
- Delete files (fake!)
- REN
- Rename files
- MKDIR
- Create directory
- TREE
- Show directory tree
- CLS
- Clear screen
- CHKDSK
- Check disk
- FORMAT
- Fake format (scary!)
- MEM
- Show memory map
- VER
- MS-DOS version
- DATE / TIME
- Current date and time
- BOOT
- Switch to DOS / Linux / C64
- LM
- Landmark speed test
- PENTAGON
- CLASSIFIED
- ???
- CLASSIFIED
- EXIT
- Quit FakeDOS
Arrow keys scroll through the command history.
Download FakeDOS
Downloads since launch 0000000
Psst... the boss thinks C:\ is empty. Type DIR anyway. Some files in the root directory were never meant for office hours.

- Drag FakeDOS.app into /Applications.
- Double-click to launch. It installs itself as a menu-bar icon.
- Click the menu-bar icon to configure or start manually.
- After the configured idle time (default: 5 min), FakeDOS takes over fullscreen.
- Type EXIT to return to your real desktop.

articles.title: Mathematicians Are Like Luddites
articles.body:
Stretching an analogy real far
Mathematicians are like Luddites. Yes, the actual weavers, not just the slur against people who are against technology. They were weavers in general: weavers, knitters, and cloth finishers defending the value of their skill and lifestyle.
Etymology
Maybe astrology for men, but just as fun.
The Proto-Indo European root tek-/tekō/*tek/: to plait/to weave.
Text: words and letters woven together.
Context: that which is woven together (con-*).
Textile. Subtle: the underlying (sub) thread.
Subtext. not etymologically a duplicate of “subtle” but sure feels like one.
Technology: from the word tekne, which means “craft”. Weaving is an old craft, about 20,000 years old. Flint knapping and fire making are older, and damned hard, but weaving has a combination of freedom and skill.
We talk about ideas as though we were handling fabric because, for a very long time, making fabric was one of our most sophisticated skills .
History of Weavers
Master weavers in the Tudor era had to work crazy fast. I don’t recall the exact number, but it’s a combination of speed and skill that isn’t really matched today. Especially in the speed aspect, done by hand.
The raw material, (the text) of weaving, has always been really really time consuming to make. And producing it was necessary to do anything further with it.
Until the Jacquard loom and its cousins, ironically maybe the first true programs. So the computer came for weavers before computers even existed, and Jacquard inspired Babbage.
The Luddites were skilled weavers. The automated looms suddenly collapsed one aspect of their skill, previously inextricably tied to the production of the raw material.
They did not react well to that disappearing, and sought to destroy the machines. But their position in society now ran against economics and therefore the wheel of progress, and their interests became less and less relevant.
When they started destroying, the response was brutal. Troops came in and shot many of them, as did factory owners.
Later, the whole industry sublated. Because the literal raw material of weaving, the cloth, became so cheap, made to measure and prefabricated (off the rack) clothing became possible and soon common. The design aspect of the art was still valuable. This is basically the province of a fashion designer now. But fashion design scales (that’s what a fashion line is), and most of the jobs disappeared. The few that remained are maybe even more prestigious and better paying, but much fewer.
History of Mathematicians
For most of history, mathematics was a hobby of the rich. Later, when basic arithmetic became more widespread, it gained a lower skilled class: “human computers” and scribes (long) before that. Ordinary computation was relegated to them. Abacuses and the like help diffuse this. But abstract math has always had a big cliff blocking further progress and learning into it.
Mathematicians have always had to do computation, but it was not their self conception of their main job after a point. Especially in the 1900s, the research center of math unmoored itself from most other sciences. Leaving a more and more insular group, essentially high priests and sometimes hierophants.
Until the machines have really taken off recently.
Mechanization in both fields
Leibniz worked on a mechanical calculator in the 1670s. He wanted to automate work so “excellent minds” wouldn’t really need to argue, but just “calculate”. Later, de Prony’s large table-making project divided labor into a few people choosing methods, a supervisor group turning the methods into instructions, and god knows how many performing arithmetic. Babbage described this organization in 1832, explicitly comparing it to a cotton mill.
Mechanization has changed both fields, in similar ways. The raw material of math is the proof, and the raw material of weaving is the cloth. Now both are cheap to make. Definitions are harder to launder, but I expect AI will succeed at that too within a year.
While machines are not generally intelligent, the few that are at the frontier of both industries (esp math because ai is a lot better at the virtual than the physical world right now) have greater position than ever. Certainly they can do way more than before by using these tools.
In any case, both math and weaving have changed.
Weaving underwent its own reorganizations. Patterned cloth required skill long before Jacquard, and there was still a high skill ceiling even as tools improved. His mechanism, demonstrated in 1801 and developed commercially around 1804–05, used punched cards to determine which warp threads rose. btw this is where the gpu warp term comes from. A design could be encoded and repeatedly executed aka mechanized.
The British Luddites did not simply rise against the Jacquard loom. Different textile workers opposed different machines and employment practices. In 1808, before the named Luddite disturbances, a Royton handbill protested Parliament’s rejection of a minimum-wage bill. In Arnold in 1811, framework knitters destroyed 63 frames belonging to unpopular hosiers. Yorkshire croppers were skilled cloth finishers threatened by shearing machinery; Lancashire weavers faced power looms. These people already used machines. The dispute was about which machines, under whose control, on what terms, and with what effect on the value of their work.
Mathematicians have tried to stem the tide in some ways, saying that they didn’t want the machines to do their work. Recently they had some declaration (I’m not gonna look it up) about “human mathematics” but economics is against this desire too. And so progress’s wheel rolls (and crushes). Math, against common mathematician belief, is valuable. Really, really valuable. It was just too damn hard to use usefully (until now). The AI galaxy brain is redeeming math’s commercial value, which is why normal people would care. Normal people interact with math through its fruits, and if you took a math paper and turned it upside down and had them read it, it wouldn’t be any less confusing.
The analogy to fashion designers is that the machine can synthesize or spin up new “cloth” so quickly now, leaving people at least for a while at a higher level.
This loops back to the idea of technology and tekne, the Greek conception of arts, or skills that can be improved. Craft is mechanistic and teleological. The machines can grind through the mechanistic aspect, but its teleology is still up for grabs. For now.
The analogies collapse as AI advances because of its meta-aspect, inserting itself into the workflow at every level. I think the order of what AI masters is the human tech tree, turned backwards. So I expect weaving and fashion design to fall after math, but I very much believe they will. AI will supply its own teleology.
Some people at the very highest end still have a position because they can simply use the tools, especially for math, in a way that others can’t because they can just read the outputs. And hardly anyone can do that. And while the AI might produce stuff that outstrips them, they’re still a lot less outstripped than other people, giving an even smaller group of this already small group an exalted position. But I expect it to pop like a bubble in the end, and for the end to be a very finite amount of time away.
The craft itself is greater than ever, for both. Or more like for 1.5. One of my old obsessions was tailoring, and watching the old tailors die is pretty depressing. Ready-made clothing transformed the mass market, though bespoke tailoring survives, but only for the best.
So, yeah you should be mad as a mathematician. You have (had) a meaningful position with respect to status and salary, at least among people you cared about. The scarcity behind that is dissolving. And that sucks.
More literal and metaphorical cloth will be produced than ever, but it’s rly different.
It’s not likely to ratchet backwards, leaving math in this new state.

articles.title: After 7 months, Glasswing overwelms maintainers with underwhelming findings
articles.body:
Key Takeaways:
- Seven months into Project Glasswing, VulnCheck has tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic, roughly 0.5% of all CVEs published this year, with only two identified as exploited in the wild. Of Anthropic’s 37,966 reported findings, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public and just 217 have been marked fixed.
- Since September, Anthropic has added nearly 12,000 findings while recording just 15 additional fixes, widening the gap between discovery and remediation.
- Roughly 1,654 findings (4.4%) have been marked as duplicates, nearly eight times the number fixed, and another 419 have been withdrawn.
- Anthropic’s claimed true positive rate has risen from 90.8% to 94.2%, raising questions about how it accounts for duplicates and withdrawn findings.
- Anthropic’s OSS Scanner shifts validation work to maintainers, with curl rejecting 19 of 34 published reports as vulnerabilities, confirming six as low severity and leaving nine awaiting assessment. Also putting Anthropic's true positive rates into question.
We're seven months into Anthropic's flagship Project Glasswing, and it's time for another update on the results. I've been tracking the project to see whether its claims are overhyped or grounded in reality.
As we all recall, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing on April 7th, claiming, "We have identified thousands of additional high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we are working on responsibly disclosing to open source maintainers." What surprised me was how little evidence the project offered, which made me wonder whether this was more of an overhyped marketing campaign.
That said, we shouldn't overlook that AI is an effective tool for finding vulnerabilities. But that story goes well beyond any single frontier model's capabilities.
If you're just catching up, this builds on my earlier posts:
- Tracking CVEs Attributed to Anthropic Researchers and Project Glasswing - April 15
- Observations on Anthropic's Vulnerability Disclosure Ledger - June 9
- 1H-2026 State of Exploitation Report - July 28
- The Anthropic Glasswing Receipts Are Starting to Trickle In - September 8
So let's look at the results…
Tracking Anthropic-Discovered Vulnerabilities
I started tracking Anthropic's discovered vulnerabilities on April 17th, shortly after launch, in an open source repo called Anthropic Credited CVEs. The goal was to see whether Anthropic's claims lived up to the hype. This was before Anthropic launched its own disclosure ledger, which is only updated in infrequent bulk batches.
My repo tracks every vulnerability attributable to Anthropic using CVE records, GHSAs, Linux kernel commits, and Anthropic's own ledger. I also manually audit advisories to catch CVEs that might otherwise get overlooked.
After seven months, I've tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic. That's an average of just 63 per month. Out of the 93,450 CVEs published this year, that's only about 0.5% of all CVEs.
For comparison, Anthropic's own public ledger lists just 217 fixed vulnerabilities, so I've tracked more than twice as many as Anthropic has disclosed itself.
The Danger Narrative Isn't Adding Up
You may recall that Glasswing launched with the message that we'd entered the Mythos era of vulnerability discovery. But are these vulnerabilities actually useful to attackers? To find out, I've been tracking Anthropic-discovered CVEs against VulnCheck KEV. So far, only 2 of the 442 have been exploited in the wild, just 0.45%. (CVE-2026-61500 and CVE-2026-26980)
Anthropic's Ledger Continues to Underwhelm
When Anthropic first launched its ledger in May, it reported 23,019 findings and a 90.8% true positive rate. As of its most recent update on November 2nd, there are 37,966 findings and just 217 fixes. That looks like a staggering failure to me, but let's take a closer look.
Of the 37,966 findings Anthropic reports, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public. Just 217 of those have been marked fixed. The more glaring number is that 4.4% (1,654) of the project's findings have already been marked as duplicates, 7.5x more duplicates than fixes. On top of that, 419 findings have been withdrawn. It seems odd that the ledger now claims a 94.2% true positive rate, up from 90.8% at launch, when more findings have been withdrawn or marked as duplicates than fixed, likely a feedback loop missing to the triage rates listed as “True Positives”.
The trend since my September update is even more telling:
In two months, Anthropic added nearly 12,000 findings and fixed just 15 more. Duplicates went from two to thousands, which is exactly what I warned about in September: the longer findings sit, the more likely someone else finds and fixes them first. I don't know how anyone can read these numbers as anything but damning.
You may also notice a correction in my visual. There appears to be a bug on Anthropic's ledger that inflates the number of findings marked as disclosed. Check for yourself using the "disclosed" filter.
Anthropic's Pivot to OSS Scanner
Having humans triage every finding clearly didn't scale, and Anthropic has said as much. In its OSS Scanner launch post on October 8th, Anthropic said it had found more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities but had manually reviewed only about 6,000, and that it remains "bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings." It had also already sent nearly 5,000 unverified reports to maintainers who asked for everything in bulk.
So with the Glasswing open source initiative hitting a wall, launching a self-service OSS Scanner that projects can opt into makes sense. Maintainers can now request a scan and triage the findings themselves. Anthropic is upfront that these reports are "fully model-generated, without human review or triage" and that "it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid."
In other words, the triage bottleneck didn't go away. It moved to the maintainers. If the true positive rate is really as high as Anthropic claims, that shouldn't be a problem.
curl Gives Anthropic's OSS Scanner a Reality Check
Three days ago, Daniel Stenberg, who maintains curl, announced that the project had received a batch of 45 vulnerability reports from Anthropic. Anthropic rated only one as medium severity and the rest as low. Daniel is moving them over to GitHub at a deliberate pace "to soften the impact for the team," with plans to have them all published by the end of the week. This gives us a rare look at what Anthropic's findings look like once a maintainer actually validates them.
Of the 34 reports published so far, 19 have been marked as not a vulnerability, 6 have been confirmed as low severity, and 9 are still awaiting assessment. That puts the false positive rate at 55.9% so far, and only 17.6% of findings have been confirmed, all of them low severity. That's a lot of work dumped on open source maintainers for a small handful of low-impact bugs, and when a maintainer has to pace reports just to protect his team, that says plenty about the burden.
This also isn't new for curl. Back in May, Daniel wrote that five Mythos findings boiled down to a single confirmed vulnerability.
It's a far cry from the 94.2% true positive rate Anthropic currently claims on its ledger. It also undercuts the "high- and critical-severity" framing Glasswing launched with. In September, I found that Claude rated 91.5% of ledger findings as critical or high, while maintainers rated only 51.3% that way. I'm curious whether other open source projects are seeing the same thing.
curl took a bold move by deciding to publish low and medium vulnerabilities findings publicly as issues for full transparency and we encourage other open source maintainers to follow their lead.
Takeaways After Seven Months
AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile.
About VulnCheck
VulnCheck is helping organizations not just to solve the vulnerability prioritization challenge - we’re working to help equip any product manager, CSIRT/PSIRT or SecOps team and Threat Hunting team to get faster and more accurate with infinite efficiency using VulnCheck solutions.
We knew that we needed better data, faster across the board, in our industry. So that’s what we deliver to the market. We’re going to continue to deliver key insights on vulnerability management, exploitation and major trends we can extrapolate from our dataset to continuously support practitioners.
Are you interested in learning more? If so, VulnCheck's Exploit & Vulnerability Intelligence has broad threat actor coverage. Register and demo our data today.

Daniel is moving them over to GitHub at a deliberate pace "to soften the impact for the team," with plans to have them all published by the end of the week. This gives us a rare look at what Anthropic's findings look like once a maintainer actually validates them.
Of the 34 reports published so far, 19 have been marked as not a vulnerability, 6 have been confirmed as low severity, and 9 are still awaiting assessment. That puts the false positive rate at 55.9% so far, and only 17.6% of findings have been confirmed, all of them low severity. That's a lot of work dumped on open source maintainers for a small handful of low-impact bugs, and when a maintainer has to pace reports just to protect his team, that says plenty about the burden.
This also isn't new for curl. Back in May, Daniel wrote that five Mythos findings boiled down to a single confirmed vulnerability.
It's a far cry from the 94.2% true positive rate Anthropic currently claims on its ledger. It also undercuts the "high- and critical-severity" framing Glasswing launched with. In September, I found that Claude rated 91.5% of ledger findings as critical or high, while maintainers rated only 51.3% that way. I'm curious whether other open source projects are seeing the same thing.
curl took a bold move by deciding to publish low and medium vulnerabilities findings publicly as issues for full transparency and we encourage other open source maintainers to follow their lead.
Takeaways After Seven Months
AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile.

VulnCheck is helping organizations not just to solve the vulnerability prioritization challenge - we’re working to help equip any product manager, CSIRT/PSIRT or SecOps team and Threat Hunting team to get faster and more accurate with infinite efficiency using VulnCheck solutions.
We knew that we needed better data, faster across the board, in our industry. So that’s what we deliver to the market. We’re going to continue to deliver key insights on vulnerability management, exploitation and major trends we can extrapolate from our dataset to continuously support practitioners.

articles.title: What objective is reasoning solving?
articles.body:
There’s an intuitive but simplified picture of reasoning: let a model think for longer, and it’ll be more likely to be correct. This aligns well with our human intuition: spend more time and effort on thinking and it’s more likely that we’ll arrive at a correct answer.
But this picture doesn’t seem to explain everything. During RL training, models learn to write longer chains of thought, and they get more accurate as they do. Yet if you take a trained model and force any one chain to run longer, it helps for a while, then stops helping.1 Sometimes the answer even gets worse, as if it’s overthinking.2 If a chain of thought were truly converging toward some optimum, more steps shouldn’t make it worse. So is it really the length of each chain that helps at inference time? Or is it something more subtle?
This post is my attempt to clarify this confusion (mostly for myself) by looking at reasoning as pathfinding through token space. We’ll see that RL maximizes the probability of finding a path from $x$ to $\Scal_x$, but individual paths are not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer. As a bonus, this perspective clarifies some odd observations about reasoning models, like unfaithful chains of thought and reward hacking.
Reasoning as pathfinding#
Ask a reasoning model the same math problem ten times and you’ll get ten different chains of thought. Rather than thinking of reasoning as one mysterious process heading toward an answer, let’s think of it as pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses one of them with each sample.
Consider the problem: “what’s $1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots + 10$”? One solution is to add the numbers one at a time: 1, 3, 6, 10, and so on up to 55. Another way is to pair them from the outside in: $1 + 10$, $2 + 9$, $3 + 8$, $4 + 7$ and $5 + 6$ each make 11, and five pairs of 11 make 55. Both of these paths land on the correct answer, 55.
We can think about reasoning as following this general pattern. We are given a starting point, the prompt, which we’ll call $x$. We want to find a path $z$ that starts from $x$ and ends at a correct answer $y$. To tell whether a path lands in the right place, we assume we have a verifier $r(x, y)$ that returns 1 if $y$ is correct and 0 if it isn’t.
So given a starting point $x$, we want to find a path of tokens $z$ that lands in the set
$$\Scal_x = \{y : r(x, y) = 1\}.$$
The figure at the top of this post sketches this picture. Each gray line is a sampled path: it starts from the prompt on the left, meanders in token space by sampling $z$, with some of these paths landing in $\Scal_x$.
Since many paths land in $\Scal_x$, the success probability adds up over all of them. Let $\pi(z \mid x)$ be the probability that the model generates the path $z$ given the prompt $x$, and $y(z)$ for the final answer at the end of $z$. The probability of success is the probability of generating each path, times the probability that path lands in $\Scal_x$, summed over every path:
$$p_x = \prob{\text{a path lands in } \Scal_x \mid x} = \sum_{z} \underbrace{\pi(z \mid x)}_{\text{samples path } z}\; \underbrace{\prob{y(z) \in \Scal_x \mid z}}_{\text{path } z \text{ lands in }\Scal_x}.$$
The second factor is just 1 if the path lands in $\Scal_x$ and 0 if it doesn’t, so we sum only the probability of paths that land in $\Scal_x$:
$$p_x = \sum_{z} \pi(z \mid x)\, \ind{y(z) \in \Scal_x} = \sum_{z \,:\, y(z) \in \Scal_x} \pi(z \mid x).$$
We’ll call $p_x$ the success probability. Maximizing this probability means our model will be more likely to sample a path that lands in $\Scal_x$.
Note that there are two ways of increasing this probability. Either the model can sample multiple paths to the same answer, each with a small probability, or the model can sample a single path to the answer with a very high probability. The success probability doesn’t care which one we get, but in practice we might want to prioritize specific paths or ensure diversity in the samples3.
How do we boost our success probability?#
Best-of-$k$ sampling#
The simplest way to pathfind is to have the model $\pi$ keep sampling paths $z$ until one lands in $\Scal_x$.
Since we assumed we had a verifier, we can do best-of-$k$ sampling, which samples $k$ paths and looks for a success. Each path misses with probability $1 - p_x$, so all $k$ miss with probability $(1-p_x)^k$, and the success probability rises from $p_x$ to
$$\prob{\text{at least one of } k \text{ paths lands in } \Scal_x \mid x} = 1 - \underbrace{(1-p_x)^k}_{\text{all } k \text{ paths miss}}.$$
This is a guaranteed axis of compute-scaling. As long as $p_x > 0$, the success probability increases monotonically as we sample more paths, so spending more compute on more samples always helps, as seen early on by Brown et al. 2024. However, the scaling here is over the number of samples rather than the length of the paths (thinking longer).
Train the model to generate better samples#
So far the model was fixed, so $p_x$ was fixed too. Can we change the model to increase $p_x$ itself?
Here’s a simple way to do this. Collect many prompts whose answers we can check. For each one, sample some paths from the model. We keep the paths that land in $\Scal_x$, and train the model on the ones we kept. Then repeat. Each round, we train the model to put more weight on the successful paths that it sampled. This loop is called rejection-sampling fine-tuning, and STaR was an early version of it for reasoning.
RL with a verifiable reward, which is how today’s reasoning models are trained, turns out to do almost the same thing. Let $\pi_\theta$ be the model with weights $\theta$. Then since $r(x, y(z)) = 1$ exactly when $y(z) \in \Scal_x$:
$$ \begin{aligned} p_x &= \sum_{z \,:\, y(z) \in \Scal_x} \pi_\theta(z \mid x) \\ &= \sum_{z} \pi_\theta(z \mid x)\, \ind{y(z) \in \Scal_x} \\ &= \sum_{z} \pi_\theta(z \mid x)\, r(x, y(z)) \\ &= \ev[z \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)]{r(x, y(z))}, \end{aligned} $$
meaning the expected binary reward is exactly the success probability $p_x$.
Computing the gradient of the success probability via the log-derivative trick, we arrive at
$$\grad_\theta\, p_x = \ev[z \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)]{r(x, y(z))\, \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z \mid x)},$$
which is exactly the policy gradient, also called the REINFORCE estimator. Now estimate this gradient with $N$ sampled paths $z_1, \dots, z_N$. The paths that failed have $r = 0$ and disappear, while the paths that land in $\Scal_x$ have $r = 1$. If $M$ of the $N$ paths succeed, the estimate is
$$\grad_\theta\, p_x \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i \,:\, \text{landed}} \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_i \mid x) = \underbrace{\frac{M}{N}}_{\text{success rate}} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{M} \sum_{i \,:\, \text{landed}} \grad_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_i \mid x)}_{\text{log likelihood of the successful paths}}.$$
This gradient involves two terms: the empirical success rate $M/N$ and the average log likelihood of the successful paths.
In other words, a step of REINFORCE with a binary reward is a step of rejection-sampling fine-tuning on the model’s own sampled paths, scaled by the current success rate $M/N$.
This also explains the first observation from the intro, that chains of thought get longer during RL training. Each step pulls the model toward the paths that landed, so if the paths that succeeded tended to be longer than the ones that failed (e.g. because they include backtracking behavior, gather more feedback from the environment, or just dumb luck), the model will learn to write longer paths.
Amortization and generalization#
During RL training, we spend a lot of compute to search for good paths and then we train the model to generate those paths directly. Once trained, the model can produce the answer without spending all this extra compute on sampling multiple paths. This is called amortizing the search: we pay for it once during training, so we don’t have to pay for it every time we ask the model a question.4 Since we train a single model on many prompts, the model can potentially generalize to new prompts it has never seen.
The figure below shows this for four prompts, each with its own $\Scal_x$, and switches between the model before and after training. During training, we sample paths from every prompt, keep the ones that succeed, and SFT on them. The percentages show the empirical rate of success given each prompt. The hollow prompt is new and not seen before by the model, but the model generalizes to this new prompt after training. As the new prompt gets further from the training distribution, its accuracy drops (try dragging it!).
Revisiting some observations about reasoning#
Once we see a reasoning model as a distribution trained to land in $\Scal_x$ given any $x$, a few odd facts about these models become clear.
Chains of thought are not guaranteed to be faithful#
Our verifier above only checks whether the answer is correct. The reward is 1 if $y(z) \in \Scal_x$ and 0 otherwise, so the intermediate tokens $z$ are just a way for the model to get to the answer. Nothing requires those tokens to be true, or to explain the answer that follows, though of course these are often correlated due to the model’s pretraining.
If we want meaningful chains of thought, we need to adjust the rewards or the training objective.
Reward hacking comes from both the verifier and the sampler#
We also assumed the verifier is never wrong, that $r(x, y)=1$ if and only if $y$ is actually the correct answer to $x$. But in practice the verifier can be imperfect. Then $\Scal_x$, the set of answers the verifier accepts, isn’t the same as the set of correct answers: it can include wrong answers and leave out correct ones. This misspecification opens up regions of $\Scal_x$ that the model might learn to land in even though it’s not what we intended.
Thus reward-hacking comes from an imperfect verifier, which fails to capture what we truly want, as well as an imperfect sampling procedure which fails to stay away from these shortcut regions.
In the figure below, the dashed circle is the set of correct answers and the red ellipse is $\Scal_x$. The ellipse stretches back toward the prompt, so its wrong answers are the easiest to reach, and after training most paths land there.
This visualization also shows why scaling up RL (generating more samples and longer samples) makes reward hacking more likely. The more extensively we “fuzz” the verifier, the more likely we’ll find a path that lands in the misspecified region of $\Scal_x$. Once the model finds this shortcut, training pushes the model towards similar behavior.
So what objective is reasoning solving?#
Reasoning isn’t actually solving any objective at all. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer. It’s only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success.
RL training directly raises the success probability $p_x$, by spending a lot of compute on searching for successful paths and then training the model to reproduce them. Thinking longer helps because training taught the model to use the extra tokens, not because generating more tokens is intrinsically better. The cost of sampling during RL is amortized into the weights. At inference time the model is likely to succeed with a single sample, but any individual sample is not guaranteed to succeed.
- Muennighoff et al. 2025 forced a model to keep thinking by appending “Wait” whenever it tried to stop. Accuracy rose at first, and then flattened. ↩︎
- A neat example is Gema et al. 2025 which found tasks where longer reasoning resulted in worse accuracy. ↩︎
- We might revisit this in a future post. ↩︎
- This idea of using expensive search to find a better answer and then training a network to output the answer cheaply, shows up outside language models too. AlphaZero runs a tree search at every move of self-play and trains its policy network to prefer the moves that were found (expert iteration is the same idea). Physicists and weather forecasters do it with simulators: they run an expensive hand-crafted simulation to get an answer, then train a neural network to predict that answer directly. ↩︎
