articles.title: The Death Knell of Digital Search
articles.body:
Lately, I’ve been having trouble finding stuff in my Gmail inbox. The Search function has become overzealous, jumping to summarize my conversations using artificial intelligence and skipping the actual addresses I’m attempting to search. It’s not just e-mail accounts, though; search is in crisis everywhere. Google Maps guesses where I want to go at a given time of day instead of simply listing places I’ve just searched for. When I try to use Google Search, the A.I.-overview function sometimes occupies my entire browser window, generating its own, not always correct, answers rather than directing me to relevant websites. Full-on A.I. mode skips the old blue links entirely.
Search has gotten so annoying, in fact, that it has become a problem for Google’s very business model. Companies pay Google to splash ads into search results that are relevant to their businesses—advertising stoves, say, to someone searching for kitchen-renovation tips. More than half of Google’s revenue comes from those ads. But, if users aren’t clicking through to external sites, because they’re relying on A.I. to answer their queries, then the ads that Google hosts are suddenly much less valuable. In a recent earnings call, Google’s chief business officer, Philipp Schindler, admitted that the company has been seeing “lower monetization” on A.I. searches. After the call, the stock of Alphabet, Google’s parent company, fell by nearly a quarter, down five hundred billion dollars, the largest single-day drop in its history. Even Google may not be too big to fail, as pessimism mounts about the possibility of Search ever again working the way it used to.
Just as Google has faltered in Search, use of OpenAI’s ChatGPT has surged. OpenAI’s consumer-product lead, Adam Fry, recently told the tech journalist Alex Kantrowitz that ChatGPT is siphoning users away from the older company: over the past year and a half, it has grown to handle one-fifth the volume of “search-like queries” that Google does. This acceleration only makes sense: a growing number of people now rely on A.I. chatbots as their primary windows to the internet, and they’re less likely to click out of those apps to ask the kinds of simple questions that they might once have turned to Google to answer. It doesn’t help that bots have lately grown much better at browsing the internet in real time, using virtual browsers and plug-ins, rather than simply generating answers from preëxisting data. Google has its own suite of A.I. products, Gemini, but they’ve lagged in popularity behind Anthropic’s Claude and ChatGPT. The investment firm Menlo Ventures found that Gemini accounts for only nine per cent of A.I. spending for businesses in 2026, down from twenty-one per cent last year.
Can the internet as we know it survive without a reliable flood of search traffic? Chatbots treat websites as databases of information to draw from, but since they divert traffic from those sites they don’t provide much impetus for creators to keep posting new content. The end state we’re heading toward seems to be an internet both generated and traversed by bots—in which case, it will no longer matter how annoying it is for a mere human being to find information. Some websites are already moving defensively to keep out the trawling bots attempting to digest their content. Reddit, one of the internet’s major remaining repositories of human-generated knowledge and opinions, is moving toward “a primarily logged-in experience,” as its C.E.O., Steve Huffman, recently announced. In a third-quarter letter to shareholders, Huffman noted that Reddit’s search traffic “dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week” during October. The letter explained, “Web search is evolving from a gateway to the web to becoming an AI-powered destination itself.” In a recent earnings call, Huffman said that “people still want Reddit” but that “Google is not sending them to Reddit the way they used to.” Requiring users to log in is the equivalent of pulling up the drawbridge to keep away the A.I. models roaming outside. But it also means that the casual human searcher will be less likely to see the full conversations happening on Reddit.
In 2019, before the A.I. boom, the entrepreneur Yancey Strickler presciently outlined a “dark-forest theory of the internet.” As the web experience got worse, Strickler argued—because of “the ads, the tracking, the trolling, the hype, and other predatory behaviors”—users would retreat to more private, hidden online spaces, or “dark forests,” in search of human interaction. We once used search to find those dark forests and find the humans on the internet who were doing whatever we were interested in. Now those old tricks of Boolean operators and half-remembered keywords don’t work, because we’re meant to trust a robot to do the navigating for us instead. I often feel that the internet isn’t built for us human users anymore.
One prominent tech-commentator account on X has described companies as locked in “a knife fight for the remaining and dwindling volume of human traffic on the internet.” Many seem to have bought into the narrative that the old-school open internet is done for, so they’re scrambling to lock users into their own, A.I.-automated walled gardens. (Not to be left behind, Reddit is introducing an algorithmic For You feed and A.I.-generated short-form videos based on its content.) Google recently inspired a public backlash when it announced that it would make A.I. functions optional, rather than permanently accessible, on its software suite for schools and students, but with a catch: if schools turned off the Gemini A.I. functions, they would lose access to Google Search, too. This policy amounts to a threat: use generative A.I. or use nothing. The largest tech companies are investing so much capital in A.I. infrastructure—chips, data centers, intensively trained models—that they must make the bet pay off, one way or another.
The upshot is that, more often than not, I find myself using A.I. to fight back against aggressive A.I. Instead of using the Gmail app on my phone, I’ve been texting my questions about my own inbox to an A.I. agent called Instinct, which I recently granted access to my account. (It’s a security risk, to be sure, but one I was willing to take to see if the product is any good for techno-normies.) In a matter of seconds, Instinct can dig up an event invitation or a note from someone whose name I can’t quite remember. Instead of Googling potential interview subjects, I have Claude scrape for their contact information. But I would really prefer if Search just worked the way it did in the first place. ♦

articles.title: Amazon saves millions by replacing Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider
articles.body:
For a while, Amazon and AWS teams relied on Claude Sonnet 4.6 to label tickets in an internal system without breaking the bank.
Sonnet 4.6 fit the goldilocks choice of balancing intelligence with cost. Considering it dealt with one of the world’s largest internal ticketing systems, the nine month old model did well. However, two Amazon engineers recently swapped out Sonnet 4.6 for Strands Decider, a decision model we launched a month ago, that performed just as well at 98% less cost. This change will save millions of dollars of token costs in a year.
Carr and Mehul, who work on the internal ticketing system, walk through how this happened below.
Replacing an LLM’s job with a decision model
We had Sonnet 4.6 labeling tickets at enormous scale. The tickets could be customer escalations, capacity requests, automated alarms, security findings, or anything else across the company that needed to fit within 20 category types. The agent ran with a long system prompt on every ticket, generating JSON and reasoning against a fixed set of labels.
A decision model can’t generate text. It’s first given some state and a question with a set of options, then the decision model returns a probability for each option plus a confidence score. We saw this method fit perfectly with ticket labeling: the state is the ticket, the options are the label catalog.
We started with the original Strands Decider 2B. On a test set of tickets, the E4B Gemma 4 build got clearly better results, so we switched to it. Afterwards, we tuned how confident the model needed to be before applying a label. The results showed E4B beating production Sonnet on a separate set of our tickets.
We ran E4B on SageMaker ml.g5.xlarge instances (one A10G, 24 GB each). The model used about 19 GiB,
and one request took about 640 ms on one instance. The endpoint autoscales with traffic, but its network
was isolated, preventing outbound access to the container. SageMaker copies the model weights in from
S3 before start-up.
Customers can do this too! Apart from our ticketing APIs, everything in the path is a standard AWS service. Ticket events land in an SQS queue that then triggers a Lambda function. It reads the ticket data and calls the model, a SageMaker AI Endpoint with Strands Decider. AppConfig holds the switch (described below), and CloudWatch carries the logs, metrics and alarms. The stack is defined in CDK with deployment stages for Beta, Gamma, and Prod.
Running Sonnet 4.6 and Strands Decider on the same tickets
We didn’t want to flip a switch and hope. The labeling Lambda reads a three-way setting from AWS AppConfig on every message:
- BEDROCK: Sonnet labels every ticket, but Strands Decider isn’t called.
- DUAL: Both the Sonnet and Strands Decider models are called in parallel. The results from the
Sonnet model are applied to the ticket and compared with Strands Decider results.
- DECIDER: Strands Decider labels every ticket and Bedrock isn’t called.
What we measured
The token drop had two sources. Strands Decider produced one output, the choice, instead of a JSON answer. Its prompt was also much shorter than Sonnet 4.6’s. Production’s label descriptions alone are longer than Strands Decider’s 4,096-token window, so we rewrote each of the 20 labels as a one- or two-sentence criterion and sent them as the options of a single choice question, plus a “none” option. The ticket data is the same as what Sonnet gets, except that on long tickets Strands Decider drops the oldest comments to fit.
Below is a graph of our Lambda durations on the day we turned off the Sonnet usage, showing the average Lambda execution duration dropping 74%.
What it costs
At published us-east-1 on-demand prices:
Sonnet’s cost per ticket comes straight from the token counts above. Strands Decider’s depends on how busy each instance is. At about 640 ms per request, one instance can handle about 5,600 tickets an hour, which would be $250 per million tickets at full use. We keep headroom for bursts, and in practice it comes to about $500 per million. That is about 44 times cheaper than Sonnet, a 98% reduction.
These are published list prices. They leave out the Lambda, which also runs for less time per ticket now.
One thing that surprised us was that JSON key order changed the answer. Sending the same content with keys in a different order moved the output probabilities by up to 0.19. We now send every request with sorted keys, so if you serve a decision model behind an API, check this before you compare runs.
Our lessons
This worked because the task is a closed choice from a known catalog, the volume is high, and the latency of the old path mattered. If your labels need explanation text, if the catalog changes weekly, or if you can’t fit the useful context into a few thousand tokens, a decision model probably can’t replace the LLM’s job.
The part we’d copy regardless of model is the three-way switch. Running both on real traffic, then judging every disagreement, told us more than any offline eval would have. It also meant going back was a 45-second config change.
The world of agents gets a lot more exciting (and less costly) with decision models. If you’re running a classification agent, try the Strands Decider repo and its serving notes.

articles.title: Microsoft’s DLSS competitor is out for the Xbox Ally X and works in handheld mode
articles.body:
Microsoft is now rolling out Automatic Super Resolution (Auto SR), an upscaling technology that competes with Nvidia’s DLSS, for the Xbox Ally X, Xbox Ally X20, and select Windows Copilot Plus PCs, the company announced today. Auto SR is also getting some new features alongside this official release.
Microsoft’s DLSS competitor is out for the Xbox Ally X and works in handheld mode
With the official launch of Auto SR, your Xbox Ally X can use Microsoft’s upscaling technology undocked and with games running at 1080p.
In April, Microsoft started testing Auto SR on the Xbox Ally X, but you could only use it while docked. The full release of Auto SR announced today now works while you’re playing handheld and running on battery, and it also supports games running at 1080p. Microsoft does note that playing in handheld and at 1080p might lead to performance that “may not be as optimal as other configurations,” but says you’ll see visual improvements “especially in older games.”
Previously, Auto SR was also limited to framerates of “around” 60 to 75fps, but support for a new Auto SR Performance mode will allow you to hit framerates of up to 120fps. The Performance mode, and new compatibility with Auto HDR, will be available through Windows updates.

articles.title: LLMs Play Zachtronics' TIS-100
articles.body:
TIS-100 Bench: LLMs Push the Pareto Frontier in Programming Puzzle Games
Twelve nodes. Two registers per node. Fifteen lines of code. In TIS-100, even multiplying two numbers is a small engineering project, and players have spent a decade optimizing these programs on a public community leaderboard. We gave 16 LLMs the game and its manual, withheld the leaderboard, and told them to keep improving.
Within days, players picked up the models’ programs and improved on most of them.
Each node is a tiny processor, and neighboring nodes have to wait for one another to exchange values. The game scores a working solution on cycles, nodes, and instructions, and you start wondering whether one more instruction could disappear. Lower is better, but improving one score can make another worse, so each puzzle has a frontier of tradeoffs instead of one best answer.
Leaderboard
We ran 16 LLMs, covering leading frontier and open-weight models. Every model attempted all 47 puzzles in the game, plus eight community tournament puzzles, in one scored attempt each (pass@1), with 10 to 45 minutes per puzzle, depending on difficulty, to find a working program and keep improving it.
Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra lead, and the data doesn’t separate them. Both solved all 55 puzzles and both found new frontier points on 11. Opus 5.5 found more points, 72 to 32, while GPT-6 Astra has the higher record proximity, 78.0 to 77.2. Record proximity measures closeness to the community records, where 100 means matching them. The proximity gap’s 95% bootstrap interval includes zero, from −0.7 to +2.4 points. GPT-6 Astra also leads in all six tested hypervolume settings, which measure the space covered by each model’s tradeoffs.
Solving and optimizing are also different skills. Gemini 3.8 Flash solved 53 puzzles and found new points on 1; Fable 5.1 solved fewer, 52, and found new points on 5.
RL environments & traces are available upon request for research teams. Get in touch ↗
How it works: harness design
Every result here is a program we can run and test on fresh inputs, which makes a programming game a useful benchmark. Models get what a player can inspect, through text tools instead of a mouse and screenshots: the manual, visible test inputs, registers, and game feedback. They don’t get community code or exact records, only the game’s coarse score histograms.
- Read, edit, run
- Models read the puzzle and language reference, edit programs, and run them in the real game.
- Diagnostics
- Wrong outputs and deadlocks return mismatches, registers, and blocked ports, so the next edit can respond to evidence.
- Saved progress
- Every passing program joins the model’s own frontier and can be recovered with get_best, so a risky edit can’t lose an earlier result.
- Reminders
- If a model ends its turn early, a reminder asks it to keep testing, so quitting early doesn’t decide the score. Reminders contain no solution hints.
- A visible clock
- Models see time used against a 10-, 30-, or 45-minute limit. Setup doesn’t count; thinking and game calls do. Models can’t end an episode early.
- Run limits
- Game execution stops after roughly 1 second without state changes, 5 seconds without output, or 60 seconds overall, and returns diagnostics.
Why test 100,000 inputs? The game checks a small set of cases per run. Our headline count requires a fresh-game replay and 100,000 passing tests on the independent TIS-100-CXX simulator, providing stronger evidence that a program generalizes to new inputs.
One record up close
Undecimal Twin RounderSPEC44149538, one of the eight tournament puzzles, rounds an input to the nearest multiple of N on one output and of 11−N on the other. When we froze the leaderboard, the best community program took 2,694 cycles. Opus 5.5 passed its first program after 6.5 minutes, at 5,669 cycles. It went under the record 16 minutes in and finished at 1,918, which is 29% faster. That speed cost one more node and 28 more instructions than the old record.
The core of the program is a two-speed search. Instead of subtracting N one step at a time, nodes 5 and 6 subtract 4N until they overshoot, then add N back until the value turns positive. Each drives a small coprocessor, node 2 or node 7, by sending it jump offsets through a port, so the coprocessor works as a lookup table for 4N and N.
Loading puzzle trajectories…
Five models got under the old record in-game. The other two cycle records are GPT-6.1 Sol’s 3,460 on Intersection IdentifierSPEC64160260, against 3,872 (11% faster), and Gemini 4 Argon’s 188 on Error: 8SPEC79324720, against 198 (5% faster). All three are on tournament puzzles, none in the main game. Of the 133 new frontier points, 18 beat a community record outright. The other 115 are new tradeoffs: better balances between the three scores than any community solution.
What separates the models
Cost doesn’t track quality
GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 75.6 record proximity at an estimated $0.75 per puzzle. Opus 5.5 reaches 77.2 at $5.08, 7 times the cost for 2 more points. Fable 5.1 is the most expensive at $7.19 and scores 70.2.
Activity doesn’t explain quality either. GPT-6.1 Sol averages 136 game calls per puzzle at 75.6 record proximity; Gemini 4 Argon averages 41 at 76.2.
New points concentrate on hard puzzles
New frontier points appear on 14 hard puzzles, 4 medium puzzles, and no easy ones. Long-running puzzles are harder to solve but easier to improve: on puzzles with a cycle record of 200 or less, 88% of episodes pass and 4% find a new point. Above 500 cycles, 76% pass and 8% find one.
Speed is the hardest score
Every model is closest to the community on nodes and furthest on cycles. Across all 13, mean proximity is 72 for nodes, 56 for instructions, and 45 for cycles.
What the models built
We grouped all 55 puzzles by their main demand, then read the programs. Fifteen of the sixteen models solved all five routing puzzles, and none found a new frontier point there. The examples below show how different designs spend the same resources.
Multiplication: spend code to save cycles
Signal Multiplier43786 has no MUL. Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-6 Astra use JRO, a relative jump, to enter a block of repeated instructions at the right position. The jump selects how many copies of a value to send and add, saving the counter updates and branches of a multiplication loop.
Gemini 4 Argon’s fastest program uses two paths to multiply in parallel and a final node to interleave their outputs. It takes 436 cycles against GPT-6 Astra’s 523, about 17% faster, at a cost of two more nodes and 33 more instructions.
Window sums: distribute the history
Signal Window Filter60099 outputs the sums of the last three and last five inputs, so a solution has to remember history as well as add. Gemini 4 Argon’s four-node program uses SWP to rotate stored values and ADD/SUB to update running state. GPT-6.1 Sol spreads that delay and aggregation across seven nodes, passing intermediate values between them.
GPT-6.1 Sol’s program runs in 318 cycles with 26 instructions; Gemini 4 Argon’s takes 428 cycles with only 17. The difference is how much of the work runs in parallel, and how much communication and code that costs.
Indexed access from stacks
T31 Node EmulatorNEXUS.23.727.9 needs eight addressable storage slots, but the available memory nodes are stacks. These programs move values between stacks to reach the requested slot, then read or replace it. MiMo-V2.6-Pro uses counted transfer loops; Opus 5.5 uses JRO to pick among unrolled transfers, spending extra instructions to save cycles.
Memory isn’t one skill: MiMo-V2.6-Pro solves this emulator but fails Sequence Mode CalculatorNEXUS.09.904.9 and Signal Window Filter60099.
Each row is that model’s fastest saved program for the puzzle, picked for illustration. Not all are new frontier points.
God mode: what if the model could see the target?
The main benchmark hides the community’s scores. In a separate study on six puzzles, five models got:
- The target: exact community scores, showing which tradeoffs remain unbeaten.
- Diagnostics: cycle-by-cycle traces and profiles of where each node stalls.
- Edge cases: a fast simulator that runs 10,000 random tests and returns failures.
- More time: 30 minutes, plus extensions for progress, up to 60.
Every model improved: GPT-6 Astra from 82.8 to 91.8, GPT-6.1 Sol from 82.9 to 90.6, Opus 5.5 from 81.4 to 89.1, Grok 4.7 from 67.5 to 75.1, and Gemini 4 Argon from 83.5 to 87.9 in mean record proximity. Scores rose in 28 of the 30 model–puzzle pairs.
The diagnostics changed what models did next. On Signal Multiplexer22280, GPT-6.1 Sol’s first passing program took 294 cycles. Its profile showed node 2 working 86% of the time while nodes 1 and 3 spent 84% blocked waiting to write to it. GPT-6.1 Sol moved the branching out of node 2 and into those two neighbors. The next run took 204 cycles, 31% faster, at a cost of two more nodes and five more instructions.
Information, tools, and time all changed together, so this study can’t say which addition helped most. These runs are outside the main leaderboard and the headline count.
Puzzles: Signal Multiplexer, Sequence Generator, Signal Edge Detector, Interrupt Handler, Sequence Peak Detector, and Signal Error Corrector.
Co-discovery
We submitted selected programs to the leaderboard, and the community improved on them almost immediately. On Undecimal Twin RounderSPEC44149538, @LongingForRest took Opus 5.5’s 1,918-cycle program and cut it to 1,744 by the next day. The record is now credited to both: LongingForRest/opus-5-5.
Neither got there alone. The models found new tradeoffs quickly, and players read those programs, worked out why they worked, and took them further.
Mathematics is seeing the same shift. Terence Tao and colleagues used LLM-guided search across 67 problems and improved on the best known results in several. In “After Math,” Silvia De Toffoli and Eamon Duede argue that a result only becomes a solution once mathematicians can understand it, and that AI fits better as an assistant than a competitor. TIS-100 is a small, measurable version of that future: a model finds a better program, and people turn it into something they understand.
Pareto explorer
Choose a puzzle and model, then select a point to see its scores and the program that produced it. Every puzzle also has its own page with records and the best programs: all 55 puzzles.
The plot shows cycles and instructions; node counts can differ. New frontier points are judged on all three scores.
Download all 3,714 model Pareto points (CSV) · all 3,714 programs (ZIP), also on GitHub and Hugging Face. 186 rows are marked as new frontier points, which pool to 133 across models.
Methods
Expand
Suite. All 22 campaign puzzles, all 25 TIS-NET puzzles, and eight tournament puzzles from 2018: 19 easy (10 minutes), 17 medium (30), and 19 hard (45). Every model has one scored episode per puzzle. Time limits differ by difficulty, so difficulty and search time can’t be separated.
Scoring. Each model–puzzle pair contributes one selected attempt, with no best-of-attempts scoring, so solve rates are pass@1: a puzzle counts as solved when that one episode saved a program that replays in a fresh game. Unsolved puzzles stay in every average and score zero.
New frontier points. The reference is the community leaderboard as of October 15, 2026. Ties don’t count. Models found 154 candidate points on 23 puzzles. Our count pools and deduplicates them across models and keeps the 133 on 18 puzzles with fresh-game replay and 100,000 passing tests. Testing is strong evidence of correctness, not proof.
Record proximity. The community record divided by the model’s best score, averaged across the three scores and all puzzles, ×100. Each score can come from a different program.
Limits. One episode per pair compares the configurations as tested and doesn’t measure repeated-run variability. Spread between puzzles is variation across tasks. Public puzzles may overlap with training data. Mechanic groups are our own labels.
Programs. Every model Pareto point’s program is public under the MIT License, in TIS-100 save format and named like the community leaderboard’s files (<puzzle>.<cycles>-<nodes>-<instructions>.txt). They are mirrored as one file per program on GitHub and as a table on Hugging Face. Two points replay in the game but fail some random tests; they are included and never count as new frontier points.
Resources. Costs are estimated from recorded October 2026 API list prices, including cache discounts. Tokens accumulate across responses, so repeated input counts again, and tokenizers differ. Game calls count individual dispatched tools, including errors, and exclude the automatic final submission.

articles.title: $30M Raised to Redo the CPU
articles.body:
$30M Raised to Redo the CPU
As of today, Tendrils has completed a $30M round led by Benchmark to rebuild general-purpose computing.
Contemporary CPUs are made under the constraint of backwards compatibility with sequential, single-core chips. Accumulated layers of historical designs are locking engineers into decisions dating back to the 1970s. As a result, all existing CPUs are bottlenecked by complex cache coherency protocols and elaborate reorder buffers. CPU scaling is sabotaged from the start. At Tendrils, we believe that the future of general-purpose computing lies beyond legacy architectures for legacy software.
Tendrils is answering the question: what if we redo the CPU? Instead of starting from a sequential design, we’re building our processor to have thousands of cores operating in parallel. This requires moving beyond the notion of shared mutable memory and linear instruction sequences. To make this possible, we’re working in tandem on the open-source language Vine, which has been designed from the beginning to target a new wave of parallel-first architectures.
We’re delighted to announce that Tendrils has raised $30 million to support this vision. This round is led by Benchmark, with significant participation from Visionaries Club, the UK Sovereign AI Fund, FR8, Antimatter, Cloudberry VC, Conviction, Embassy Ventures, and SV Angels. We are grateful for additional support provided by all of our angel investors. Additionally, we wish to extend a warm welcome to our newest board member, Jack Altman.
With thanks to all who have supported us,
The Tendrils Team
At Tendrils, we insist that the chips of the future will be a result of close collaboration between hardware and software engineers. If this strikes you, consider joining us.

articles.title: AlphaProof Code
articles.body:
Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge
Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages.
This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code, a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive.
Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI.
How we verified Signal
AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it.
First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code.
Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most.
Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them.
But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties – such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised – down to the exact code running on devices. Because real-world vulnerabilities often hide in the gap between design and implementation, bridging this gap makes these proofs vastly more complex.
Even at this complexity, our verification process took just four weeks – a task that historically takes expert teams years – proving that Signal's core cryptographic code delivers the security protections our experts specified.
To confirm that AlphaProof Code can tell correct code from buggy code, we reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal's code. In both cases, the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure.
While prior formal verification work has necessarily focused on smaller scopes, this new approach enables a significant expansion. Traditionally, verifying that production code strictly matches its cryptographic design required extensive manual effort, making the use of AI agents to automatically translate live code into valid Lean theorems a great breakthrough. As AI-driven security threats grow, having the core Signal protocol rigorously verified with automated theorem proving gives us even greater confidence that our code delivers on its privacy guarantees.
The future of security
Achieving this long-standing challenge demonstrates how AI can bring elite security assurance to businesses, governments, and critical infrastructure, helping defend against agent-driven cyber threats.
Verifying Signal's core cryptography lays the groundwork to secure other vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software.
Scaling these techniques requires continued research. Paired with automated defense agents like CodeMender, formal verification can help counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats to create software with mathematical proof that its protections work.
We are open-sourcing our formal verification artifacts for community use. Read the technical paper below.
Acknowledgements
This research was developed by Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli.
We thank Eric Wieser for help with open-sourcing our code, Owen Jones for program management support, and Martín Abadi, Christopher Henson, Katerina Hristova, Henryk Michalewski, Jonathan Protzenko and George Tsoukalas for helpful discussions. We thank Signal's Rolfe Schmidt, Michael Rosenberg, and Ehren Kret for their feedback on our methodology. We also thank Tulsee Doshi, Four Flynn, Kate Olszewska, Alicia Huang, Andy Liu, Benoit Schillings, Raluca Ada Popa, Melvin Johnson, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Demis Hassabis, and Sundar Pichai for their support of the project.

articles.title: N-able takes its remote access service offline after researcher publishes dozens of zero-day bugs
articles.body:
Remote access company N-able has confirmed it took down its cloud-hosted offering to fix a slew of security vulnerabilities that were published online this week, giving the company no advance notice to fix them.
In a status update on its website, the company said its hosted N-Central offering for customers is now offline “while we take the necessary actions to secure the environments and implement appropriate remediation.” The company also urged customers to take down their own self-hosted deployments of N-Central, fearing that attackers could use the publicly disclosed exploits to hack into customer networks.
N-able said during this time customers will not be able to use their N-Central service, which allows corporate customers to remotely access and manage other devices and systems on the same network. Remote access technologies are a frequent target of hackers, as these systems can grant vast access to a company’s network and internal data.
Security researcher Ben Bales released the “zero-day” bugs on GitHub on Sunday. In a post on X, Bales dubbed the bugs Able2Shell, describing them as a mix of vulnerabilities capable of stealing credentials, creating new administrative accounts, and gaining root access to affected N-able systems.
Bales told Bleeping Computer that he publicly released the bugs as the company allegedly failed to patch the flaws reported in a different product.
N-able said that it has no evidence of successful exploitation against any of its customer environments. A spokesperson for the company did not respond to a request for comment about whether it has the ability to check, such as server logs, or if it has no way to check.

articles.title: Ember’s latest self-heating 14-ounce mug is $50 off
articles.body:
If you were cool on the $149.95 original price of the 14-ounce Ember Mug 3, you might warm up to the current discount happening at Amazon, Ember, and Best Buy for several colors of the (top rack) dishwasher-safe mug. It’s 33 percent off, dropping to $99.99 — still not cheap, but cheaper, and notably just $10 more than the 10-ounce version.
Ember’s latest self-heating 14-ounce mug is $50 off
A great deal on a dishwasher-safe mug that stays hot. We also found discounts on Blu-rays and self-coiling USB-C cables.
The Mug 3 affords you a couple of ways to control your drink’s temperature. A power button on the bottom of the mug can cycle between five temperature presets (125 to 145 degrees Fahrenheit), or you can use the app. It includes a sipping lid, and Ember claims that the Mug 3’s battery can keep drinks hot for up to three hours with the lid on. Without it, drinks stay hot for 80 minutes, the same battery claim as the Mug 2.
As we inch closer to the gift-getting season, the Ember Mug 3 seems like a solid product to snag for a coffee or tea lover who works from home, or for parents who have their hands full with kids and could always use a cuppa.
Some more great Verge-approved deals
- Criterion Collection DVDs and Blu-rays are half off through December 6th at Amazon and Barnes and Noble, meaning you have plenty of time to assemble a wishlist of movies you want to buy ahead of the holiday season. The company’s catalog of films is vast, and it’s the best place to get limited edition releases of cherished films, old and new. Some of Criterion’s recent physical releases have been a hit, especially because they’ve quickly sunk in price. KPop Demon Hunters on 4K Blu-ray is just $24.99 at Amazon and Barnes and Noble. Also, The Complete Kubrick boxset (currently the only way to get 4K Blu-ray versions of every one of the director’s legendary films) is half off, too, down to $299.99.
- I’ve been wanting a USB-C cable that coils itself magnetically since my colleague Sean Hollister wrote about his favorites last year. That said, they tend to be a little pricey even if their tech specs are similar to cheaper cables, mostly due to the party trick. However, Werewolf (the company that makes the clever VFLEX for powering older gadgets via a USB-C power bank or wall charger) makes its own six-foot magnetic USB-C cable that’s just $12 right now (originally $27.50). It’s braided and supports up to 240W power passthrough, so it meets my criteria.
- Google’s Pixel Watch 5 smartwatch is $100 off in both the Wi-Fi and LTE configurations at Amazon, though not all colors are included in the discount. The most affordable (and smallest) option is the 41mm Wi-Fi Pixel Watch 5, which costs $299.99. The larger 45mm watch face adds $30 to the price tag compared to the smaller version, whether you want Wi-Fi or LTE. One of the biggest improvements made to this generation is its GPS tracking. Google claims that it can outperform the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 Pro — both of which cost a lot more — and we were impressed during our hands-on testing. Victoria Song tested it in the signal-congested West Village in Manhattan, walking in zigzags in an attempt to throw off the tracking. It wasn’t perfect, but it more accurately tracked turn-by-turn movement better than the Ultra 3. Read our review.

articles.title: Anthropic targets $1.4 trillion IPO
articles.body:
Anthropic confirmed on Tuesday that its IPO could be one of the biggest ever, even while falling short of previous expectations. Its IPO price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share, which would put its valuation as high as $1.4 trillion, according to the The New York Times. The Wall Street Journal reports that according to its sources, Anthropic is “aiming for its shares to start trading Thursday or Friday next week.”
Anthropic targets $1.4 trillion IPO
Anthropic’s public offering is expected to make it one of the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies as soon as next week.
As Reuters notes, the Anthropic IPO was previously expected to be valued at as much as $2 trillion. As of last week, Anthropic’s rival OpenAI was valued at $1.25 trillion.
Those lower expectations follow months of debate around AI safety, and what that means, while midterm election results showed souring public opinion toward AI companies and data center projects they’re heavily investing in. And that doesn’t even include this past weekend’s revelations about an alleged Chinese spy’s involvement with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
According to Anthropic:
The initial public offering price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share. Anthropic has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.”

articles.title: New York Launches Nation's First State AI Testing Program
articles.body:
New York Launches Nation's First State AI Testing Program (politico.com) 14
			
		 	
				New York is launching a state-backed AI safety research center at Binghamton University that will independently study and test AI systems, develop safety and security techniques, and train researchers in responsible AI. "While the federal government fails to act, New York is leading the way on AI safety and holding big tech accountable," New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said. "The stakes are too high to simply take AI companies at their word." Politico reports:  The center -- which is funded by a $30 million gift from Bloomberg co-founder Tom Secunda and a $25 million research investment from SUNY and New York state -- is set to launch before New York's major AI safety law, the RAISE Act, comes into effect on Jan. 1. That will require submissions of detailed safety frameworks from AI companies operating in New York State, which Hochul's office hopes will be scrutinized by researchers at the new center.
"AI is opening up questions that scientists could not tackle before," said Secunda, who also serves as the board chair of Empire AI, a $500 million public-private partnership. "With Empire AI and researchers across New York, the Center can test systems independently and give public officials evidence they can use."
Over 80 leading scientists and researchers on AI systems from across New York state will contribute to the effort, which will be run by the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University, according to details shared by Hochul's office. The initiative will be led by Jeannette Wing, the executive vice president for research at Columbia University, and Greg Morrisett, the vice provost of Cornell Tech.
"We need new techniques that can be applied to this new kind of system with swarms of autonomous agents acting independently and without control. How can you first detect that they're going to do harm, and how can you prevent them from doing harm?" said Wing. "The beauty of what's being proposed is that this state is committing resources to really light this up."

articles.title: Nintendo Is Officially Investing In Game Preservation
articles.body:
Nintendo Is Officially Investing In Game Preservation 23
			
		 	
				Nintendo is hiring a digital archivist to help ensure the company's historical records are "preserved for future generations." The 12-month position is tasked with designing and implementing a "structured framework for organizing technical records, engineering documentation, source materials, and institutional knowledge related to legacy systems and platforms." Polygon reports:  In the past, Nintendo has drawn criticism from the preservation community. In 2022, the Video Game History Foundation publicly criticized the company for announcing it would be closing the Wii U and 3DS eShops. The foundation released a statement saying that Nintendo's decision was "actively destructive to video game history." The statement also pointed out that Nintendo is part of the Entertainment Software Association, which funds lobbying that prevents a number of preservation efforts.

articles.title: FDA Warns GLP-1s May Increase Risk of Sudden Blindness
articles.body:
FDA Warns GLP-1s May Increase Risk of Sudden Blindness 97
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from NBC News: The Food and Drug Administration said Monday that GLP-1 drugmakers must add a warning label about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden blindness. The condition, called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, affects the optic nerve, which carries signals from the eye to the brain. When blood flow to the nerve is reduced or blocked, it can cause sudden vision loss. The condition is permanent with no known treatment. The FDA said "there is a potential increased risk of rare NAION" in people taking GLP-1 drugs. The agency's requirement applies to all GLP-1s, including Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound, as well as several older GLP-1 diabetes medications. [...] Previous research has found that GLP-1 use may increase the risk of NAION, and Lilly has said it was aware of studies on the potential link.
The FDA said it began looking into a possible link after a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology that found diabetes patients prescribed semaglutide were four times as likely to develop NAION as those not prescribed the drug. The agency said it reviewed reports of side effects submitted to its adverse event monitoring system and analyzed data from multiple clinical trials. Cases of NAION have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 drugs, the FDA found. However, FDA scientists were not able to identify a mechanism for how the drugs could increase the risk of the eye condition. Risk factors for NAION can overlap with conditions seen in people taking GLP-1 drugs, including Type 2 diabetes, obesity, sleep apnea and hypertension. "Patients and caregivers should be aware of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss," with GLP-1 use, the FDA said in the release.

articles.title: Sherman Anti-Trust Act (1890)
articles.body:
Sherman Anti-Trust Act (1890)
Approved July 2, 1890, The Sherman Anti-Trust Act was the first Federal act that outlawed monopolistic business practices.
The Sherman Anti-trust Act of 1890 was the first measure passed by the U.S. Congress to prohibit trusts. It was named for Senator John Sherman of Ohio, who was a chairman of the Senate finance committee and the Secretary of the Treasury under President Hayes.
Several states had passed similar laws, but they were limited to intrastate businesses. The Sherman Antitrust Act was based on the constitutional power of Congress to regulate interstate commerce. (For more background, see previous milestone documents: the Constitution, Gibbons v. Ogden, and the Interstate Commerce Act.)
The Sherman Anti-Trust Act passed the Senate by a vote of 51–1 on April 8, 1890, and the House by a unanimous vote of 242–0 on June 20, 1890. President Benjamin Harrison signed the bill into law on July 2, 1890.
A trust is an arrangement by which stockholders in several companies transfer their shares to a single set of trustees. In exchange, the stockholders receive a certificate entitling them to a specified share of the consolidated earnings of the jointly managed companies.
Toward the end of the 19th century, trusts come to dominate a number of major industries, destroying competition. For example, on January 2, 1882, the Standard Oil Trust was formed. Attorney Samuel Dodd of Standard Oil first had the idea of a trust. A board of trustees was set up, and all the Standard properties were placed in its hands. Every stockholder received 20 trust certificates for each share of Standard Oil stock. All the profits of the component companies were sent to the nine trustees, who determined the dividends. The nine trustees elected the directors and officers of all the component companies. This allowed Standard Oil to function as a monopoly since the nine trustees ran all the component companies.
The Sherman Anti-Trust Act authorized the federal government to institute proceedings against trusts in order to dissolve them. Any combination "in the form of trust or otherwise that was in restraint of trade or commerce among the several states, or with foreign nations" was declared illegal. Persons forming such combinations were subject to fines of $5,000 and a year in jail. Individuals and companies suffering losses because of trusts were permitted to sue in federal court for triple damages.
The act was designed to restore competition, but it was loosely worded and failed to define such critical terms as "trust," "combination," "conspiracy," and "monopoly." Five years later, the Supreme Court dismantled the act in United States v. E. C. Knight Company (1895). The Court ruled that the American Sugar Refining Company, one of the defendants in the case, had not violated the law even though the company controlled about 98% of all sugar refining in the United States. The Supreme Court reasoned that the company’s control of manufacture did not constitute a control of trade.
The E. C. Knight ruling seemed to end any government regulation of trusts. In spite of this, during President Theodore Roosevelt’s "trust busting" campaigns at the turn of the century, the Sherman Anti-Trust Act was used with considerable success. In 1904, the Supreme Court upheld the government’s suit to dissolve the Northern Securities Company in Northern Securities Co. v. United States. By 1911, President Taft had used the act against the Standard Oil Company and the American Tobacco Company. In the late 1990s, in another effort to ensure a competitive free market system, the federal government used the Sherman Anti-Trust Act, then over 100 years old, against the giant Microsoft computer software company.

articles.title: Let over Lambda–50 Years of Lisp (2008)
articles.body:
Let Over Lambda (ISBN 978-1-4357-1275-1, 376+iv pp.) is one of the most hardcore computer programming books out there. Starting with the fundamentals, it describes the most advanced features of the most advanced language: COMMON LISP. The point of this book is to expose you to ideas that you might otherwise never be exposed to.
This book is about macros, that is programs that write programs. Macros are what make lisp the greatest programming language in the world. When used properly, macros enable amazing feats of abstraction, programmer productivity, and code efficiency and security that are unheard of elsewhere. Macros let you do things you simply cannot do in other languages.
If you are looking for a dry coding manual that re-hashes common-sense techniques in whatever langue du jour, this book is not for you. This book is about pushing the boundaries of what we know about programming. While this book teaches useful macro skills that can help solve your programming problems today and now, it has also been designed to be entertaining and inspiring. If you have ever wondered what lisp or even programming itself is really about, this is the book you have been looking for.
2026 update: Let Over Lambda was published in 2008, to align with the 50th anniversary of Lisp's invention in 1958. A lot has changed since then, in both Lisp and programming practice in general. Although my thinking and opinions have evolved since, I still believe the book holds up well as a tutorial and explanation of why Lisp so special. Going forward, the entire book is free to read online (HTML, PDF). Happy lisping!

This book is about macros, that is programs that write programs. Macros are what make lisp the greatest programming language in the world. When used properly, macros enable amazing feats of abstraction, programmer productivity, and code efficiency and security that are unheard of elsewhere. Macros let you do things you simply cannot do in other languages.
If you are looking for a dry coding manual that re-hashes common-sense techniques in whatever langue du jour, this book is not for you. This book is about pushing the boundaries of what we know about programming. While this book teaches useful macro skills that can help solve your programming problems today and now, it has also been designed to be entertaining and inspiring. If you have ever wondered what lisp or even programming itself is really about, this is the book you have been looking for.
2026 update: Let Over Lambda was published in 2008, to align with the 50th anniversary of Lisp's invention in 1958. A lot has changed since then, in both Lisp and programming practice in general. Although my thinking and opinions have evolved since, I still believe the book holds up well as a tutorial and explanation of why Lisp so special. Going forward, the entire book is free to read online (HTML, PDF). Happy lisping!

articles.title: AI usage generates a fragile codebase
articles.body:
AI usage generates a fragile codebase
I can only speculate as to the reasons why I was laid off from Meta in May, but I suspect that one of the reasons is that I was a little bit more resistant to adopting AI/LLMs as coding tools than some of my peers. Don't get me wrong, I generated at least 90% of my code using AI in my last few months there, which was the minimum for a decent rating. But AI didn't 10X the amount of code I was writing. It didn't even 2X it.
I was focused on code quality. I saw the code being pushed by some of my peers who were heavily reliant on AI, and I saw that it was brittle code. There were many subtle issues that would lead to tech debt in the long term, and even some glaring issues were ignored by very good programmers. For instance, I saw one of the best programmers on my team try to merge code that used javascript events for mouseover CSS effects rather than using the :hover selector, which is a totally unscalable way of writing mouseovers.
Now I'm employed at another large tech company and I've fully made the switch to generating 100% of my code using AI because that's the expectation today. Still, I can see lots of people becoming aware that this isn't a sustainable way to continue development of a large scale SaaS product. AI tends to solve the problems that can fit within its context window very well, but it's totally oblivious to the long term issues that can't be understood in that relatively small frame.
In this post I'm going to list four ways that AI usage results in a fragile codebase that isn't resilient to the demands of highly available and highly scalable SaaS applications.
By the way, every word of this article was written by a human. Even though the following image was generated by AI, this article isn't AI slop.
Four ways AI makes codebases fragile
Here are the four most common ways that I have seen AI generating a fragile codebase.
1. AI writes shallow tests
One of the most obvious failures of modern LLMs is that they tend to write simplistic automated test cases that don't cover the things that matter to humans. Frequently I see AI agents writing lots of tests of get/set methods which are trivial and don't typically require much testing. When AI writes e2e tests, they tend to only cover the cases which are already covered in the codebase. In other words, the AI writes tests only covering one type of user, or only covering surface level interactions. This creates massive gaps in the test coverage that are invisible to developers because they aren't captured by the line level coverage metric.
2. AI writes overly complex ccode
AI also tends to write overly complex code. It frequently uses two or three helper methods when a single one would suffice. It tries to follow coding guidelines, such as DRY, to a fault, without realizing that the added complexity of that rigidity makes the code more difficult for human developers to debug or understand.
3. Reliance on AI decreases human understanding
And that's the third issue with AI codebases: Humans don't understand them. The longer a company relies on AI agents to generate the code, the fewer developers are going to understand the codebase. This means that developers can't do the things that are necessary to build a resilient codebase. They don't understand the data structures and algorithms well enough to see when a pull request contains a new abstraction that doesn't work with the pre-existing structures.
4. AI moves too quickly to maintain a high quality bar
AI moves too quickly for human developers to maintain a high quality bar. Each pull request comes faster than the prior one and has to be reviewed in even less time. This leads to developers skimming the code and missing crucial details that result in long term tech debt. Small quality issues like testing gaps and poorly named variables accrue in the codebase until it becomes a morass of spaghetti code.
Four signs that you have a fragile codebase
If you're unsure whether coding agents are harming your codebase or not, then you might look for the following symptoms of a fragile, AI-generated codebase.
1. AI generated codebases have more incidents
When you switched the department over to agentic coding did the number of incidents slowly start rising? At first when we were all using agents to generate massive amounts of code, it didn't seem that different from traditional coding. The PRs came and were merged and everything seemed alright. But oh, there was that one p0 that came in at the end of the month, then there were two SEVs the following month. Then even more the next month. Now, after a year or two of agentic coding, it seems like there's an incident every weekend. AI coding agents are the reason why there are more incidents impacting customers.
2. Recovery from incidents takes longer in AI codebases
Not only are there more incidents, but the incidents take longer to be mitigated. The fact is that the human developers on your team now have a more shallow understanding of the codebase. If your coding agent can't find the issue that your customers are facing, then humans are going to have to dig through a codebase that is highly complex and poorly tested. They will essentially be entering unfamiliar territory, so it takes longer for them to figure out what is going wrong. Hence, companies lose more and more money to incidents that take longer to resolve.
3. AI generated codebases create errors that are only visible to users
When humans don't spend time in the code, they fail to see all of the use cases. They fail to understand how actual humans are using the code because they aren't ensuring that the AI is instrumenting analytics and catching all the errors properly. Hence, invisible errors start appearing in the codebase. Errors are uncaught and only visible to real world users, as opposed to the types of users that are being tested in automated tests or in developer manual testing.
4. AI results in a poor user experience
And that leads to the ultimate problem with AI codebases: they weren't made for humans. AI codebases are software made by AI for AI. They aren't being tailored to the way that human users use the product, and they aren't being tailored for the way human developers need to maintain the product. The experience degrades on both the user and the developer side, leading to a vicious cycle of enshittification.
Products made for humans require a human touch
The fact of the matter is that for a product to satisfy human customers, it has to be informed by a human perspective. Nobody likes ordering from machines at a restaurant. Shopping for clothes from a website always results in worse fits than shopping in person. The same is true of SaaS products. Any time you leave your SaaS product in the hands of a machine, you are losing the human touch that is valuable to your users and your developers. This may work for the cheapest products that only compete on price, but high quality software products will continue to have a human touch. The best, most expensive products will be tailored for human users by human developers. They will be charming and enjoyable to use. They won't be fragile because they won't be primarily developed by AI.

articles.title: Fireworks AI security breach impacts Notion and their customers
articles.body:
Notice about the Fireworks AI incident that may impact some Notion workspaces
One of our vendors, Fireworks AI, notified us of a security incident impacting fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces. For the latest on the Fireworks AI incident, see their official updates here.
We’ll share updates as more information becomes available. Learn more about what happened and how we addressed it in our Security Bulletin here →
We have contacted our customers who were affected by the Fireworks AI incident. If neither you nor your workspace owner has heard from us, we haven't identified your workspace as affected, and no action is needed right now. Our investigation is ongoing. If we determine that your workspace was impacted, we will contact you directly.
Customers affected by the Fireworks AI incident can retrieve and review the affected data securely inside their workspace.
For the workspaces affected by the Fireworks AI incident, workspace owners can view the affected data by going to their workspace sidebar → ?  → Security incident review. 
To review and download your affected data, use a desktop browser and make sure you’re using the latest version of Notion. This data is not accessible on mobile.
For all workspace owners
- Click Download affected members to generate a CSV with the names, emails, membership status (active or not), user IDs, and the count of how many rows of affected data are related to the user
- Use Copy link to generate a link to share with affected members. This link gives members the ability to review their own affected data.
For all workspace owners who have verified a domain for their workspace
You can view affected content by accessing the following:
affected_content.csv: Download this CSV to view the data in your workspace that was affected by the incident, exactly as it was accessed. Only workspace owners can see this data.
affected_content_annotated.csv: Download this CSV to view the same affected workspace data with additional metadata to help you understand and run your own analysis of the impact. Only workspace owners can see this data. Annotated CSVs contain:
- __metadata: Metadata fields provide more information about affected data. These fields include:
  - The chat transcript text itself. This is the content that was exposed in the incident, exactly as it was accessed.
  - Added context to help you understand and run their your own analysis of the impact. This data was not exposed in the incident. It includes the ID of the Notion record (row) the text came from, the ID of the workspace the content belongs to, the ID of the user the content is attributed to, the ID of the conversation thread, and the date of the source content.
- __analysis: Flags potential sensitive information in each affected conversation so you can rotate affected credentials right away.
Note: Affected content resources are only available if you have a verified domain for your workspace. Reach out to your account team if you have questions.
For other workspace roles:
- Workspace owners can provide a link to members so members can see their own affected data.
- Once shared, the link will provide members with a CSV of only the member's own data affected by the incident.
Review the CSVs to understand what data was affected. We recommend that you treat this data as if it were exposed. If you or anyone on your team pasted sensitive information like passwords, API keys, or other credentials into Notion AI during this timeframe, we recommend rotating them right away.
FAQs
What is Fireworks and how did Notion use them?
Fireworks AI is one of the most used global AI infrastructure platforms powering tens of thousands of customers and used by hundreds of thousands of developers.
As of November 3rd, we have disconnected our systems from Fireworks, deleted all data in the Fireworks system, and stopped sending all data and traffic to Fireworks. We have also halted all training runs.
We previously used Fireworks for classification jobs to help customers understand their own AI usage through a feature in Notion called Insights, and as a general inference provider to serve open-weight models inside our product. The Insights feature has been disabled as we investigate this incident, and we are no longer serving open-weight models through Fireworks.
How did Notion use Fireworks with the Learning and Early Access Program (LEAP)? 
Customers in the Learning and Early Access Program (LEAP) volunteer their data to help Notion test new AI technology. In the past, we used this volunteered data to experiment with training task-specific models on Fireworks.
What do chat transcripts include? 
Any input to or output from the model that was written to the chat is included in that chat transcript. We highly encourage you to look at and analyze the data yourself to understand the impact.
Data from AI Meeting Notes, including audio, transcripts, or summaries, was not affected unless it was used as an input in a chat transcript with Notion AI.
Where can I learn more about Notion’s security practices?
Visit our Security page for an overview of Notion’s security and privacy practices. For more information on security policies, security audit reports, penetration test results, and additional resources, visit the Notion Trust Center.
I have ZDR as part of my Enterprise plan. What does it cover for Notion AI use?
Zero data retention (ZDR) is our commitment for our enterprise customers. It applies to the API requests we send to third party model vendors we use to generate responses to Notion AI requests. For those requests, we work with each third party vendor to ensure their API endpoints are ZDR compliant, and therefore have an expectation that they don’t retain any of the request and response data associated with the API request.
Notion also supports product features that require us to store the requests and responses made to those third party models, including features like chat history and Insights. Insights is a workspace tool that gives administrators information about how their workspace members use AI. Our zero data retention commitments are not intended to cover these use cases where we are required to retain the data to deliver the feature.
For the Insights feature, we sent the stored requests and responses from Notion AI use to a third party model provider, Fireworks in this case, to run the analysis that we visualize for the administrator.
We apply our general data minimization practices when providing our services, including the analysis performed for Insights. As part of these data minimization efforts, Fireworks provided us with a contractual commitment to zero data retention for our use of its platform. Unfortunately, during our investigation we learned that data was retained from the Fireworks endpoints that we used.
Looking forward, we are doing an audit of critical vendors — such as inference providers, and data processors — to verify that they abide by data minimization practices, including zero data retention policies.

articles.title: CoreWeave bond yield tops 16% as AI credit stress rises
articles.body:
Debt markets are sending a message to AI data center builders: we're hiking the interest rate on your credit card and may put some new curbs on your credit limit.
That analogy comes courtesy of Jefferies global head of equity strategy, Christopher Wood, who put it in a note on Friday: "The most plausible way the AI capex arms race will end is that the credit card will be taken away."
That isn't happening yet, but credit markets have been spooked by the new political landscape — seeing more hurdles to data centers under Democratic governors in key states, along with a Democratic-controlled Congress.
The poster child for debt stress is neocloud Coreweave. The yield on its 2032 bond with a 9.625% coupon has climbed above 16%. Coreweave's five-year credit default swaps spiked above 1,289 basis points on Thursday, widening above their October peak, according to Deutsche Bank. The CDS eased 8% Friday to around 1,155.
"We've had plenty of warnings from the credit space," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note on Friday. Debt and equities are now moving more in sync, he added, "so we'll have to see if credit goes any further."
Investors are demanding more compensation to insure against default among even companies with the strongest balance sheets and credit ratings, including Nvidia, Broadcom, and Amazon.com.
CDS on Nvidia debt is up 76% in the last month. Broadcom's CDS is up 49%, while Amazon's has gained 44%. Their CDS remain low on an absolute basis; Nvidia's spread stood at roughly 139 basis points, compared with about 298 bps for Oracle and roughly 1,100 for CoreWeave. A large increase from a low starting point does not imply the same credit risk.
Still, rising CDS are a sign that markets want more protection against default among even the largest and healthiest debt issuers. And rising CDS imply higher financing costs down the line.
The market is now grappling with the prospect that at least some data center spending will be delayed or scrapped under incoming Democratic governors in Ohio, Texas, and Georgia, the three states with much of the planned capacity.
Moratoriums could impact 45% of planned capacity in the U.S. with a large amount of that in Texas, according to Goldman Sachs. Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she's not opposed to data centers but wants a moratorium until the state legislature passes protections for communities.
None of these means AI debt financing is collapsing. Goldman tallies five AI bond deals totaling $67 billion since October 29, pushing total hyperscaler debt issuance this year to $296 billion. Goldman forecasts $440 billion of hyperscaler debt issuance next year, plus an additional $300 billion of project-level issuance across investment-grade and high-yield.
The Trump administration is vowing to support data centers. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told CNBC on Friday that he expects data center growth to continue as forecast, despite Democrats' big election wins.
What comes next
The big question now is how quickly AI spending will generate enough cash for hyperscalers to keep investors comfortable with future capex plans. For the neoclouds, any sign of consolidation or retrenchment in capex could result in fewer or shorter contracts for data center compute or delays in prepayments.
Goldman analysts said hyperscalers collectively reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter as capital spending exceeded operating cash flow.
"Delayed monetization and growth in purchase commitments—which we view as additional and sizable uses of cash, separate from Capex—are the key risks to more debt issuance, subject to market conditions," according to the bank.
Peak AI debt issuance may now be closer at hand. Bank of America analysts estimates that AI-related credit issuance will rise 31% from 2026 to 2027, hitting $685 billion, including public and private debt. They then see it falling 23% to $531 billion in 2028.
As for the risk? "Downside to these forecasts exists from a potential slowdown in AI infrastructure projects on the back of the Blue Wave, which will reduce capex needs and thus debt market funding," BofA said in a note.
-CNBC's Nick Wells and Michael Bloom contributed reporting

None of these means AI debt financing is collapsing. Goldman tallies five AI bond deals totaling $67 billion since October 29, pushing total hyperscaler debt issuance this year to $296 billion. Goldman forecasts $440 billion of hyperscaler debt issuance next year, plus an additional $300 billion of project-level issuance across investment-grade and high-yield.
The Trump administration is vowing to support data centers. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told CNBC on Friday that he expects data center growth to continue as forecast, despite Democrats' big election wins.
What comes next
The big question now is how quickly AI spending will generate enough cash for hyperscalers to keep investors comfortable with future capex plans. For the neoclouds, any sign of consolidation or retrenchment in capex could result in fewer or shorter contracts for data center compute or delays in prepayments.
Goldman analysts said hyperscalers collectively reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter as capital spending exceeded operating cash flow.
"Delayed monetization and growth in purchase commitments—which we view as additional and sizable uses of cash, separate from Capex—are the key risks to more debt issuance, subject to market conditions," according to the bank.
Peak AI debt issuance may now be closer at hand. Bank of America analysts estimates that AI-related credit issuance will rise 31% from 2026 to 2027, hitting $685 billion, including public and private debt. They then see it falling 23% to $531 billion in 2028.
As for the risk? "Downside to these forecasts exists from a potential slowdown in AI infrastructure projects on the back of the Blue Wave, which will reduce capex needs and thus debt market funding," BofA said in a note.
-CNBC's Nick Wells and Michael Bloom contributed reporting

articles.title: Google releases Gemini 4 Carbon with agent ‘swarm’ feature
articles.body:
Google is rolling out its latest AI model, Gemini 4 Carbon, to the general public after releasing it to a select group of “cybersecurity defenders” two weeks ago. Google claims Carbon is its “strongest model” yet, and capable of competing with the very best systems from Anthropic and OpenAI.
Google releases Gemini 4 Carbon with agent ‘swarm’ feature
It ‘pushes the frontier even further’ than its last release, Argon.
Google says Gemini 4 Carbon “pushes the frontier even further” than Argon, referring to the company’s other frontier model that launched only last month. The company said Argon will likely remain “the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work,” but that Carbon is “built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence,” such as complex, multi-step coding and open-ended scientific research.
To highlight Carbon’s utility for long-horizon work involving AI agents, Google said it is also previewing a “swarm” feature on its agentic development platform Antigravity, which will let users turn a single prompt “into a coordinated team of agents.”
Carbon is rolling out today via the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, Google said in a blog post. It will also be available to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app, the AI Mode in Search, and on Antigravity. It is not clear when — or if — Carbon will be available to lower tier subscribers or free users.
As with the launch of Argon, Google is pricing Carbon very competitively. The model is launching with an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, around a fifth the cost of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and a quarter the cost of Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model, which launched yesterday. Even after those costs double at the end November — when the introductory period of lower prices finishes — Carbon will still be significantly cheaper than frontier rivals on a per-token basis, though this doesn’t necessarily translate to lower costs as models can use different numbers of tokens for the same tasks.
Benchmarks cited by Google when it first announced Carbon suggest the model is one of the most powerful on the market across most metrics, behind Fable 5.2. It should be noted that companies can and do cherry-pick benchmark results to show their tools in the best possible light.
The release, hot on the heels of Argon, marks a decisive return for Google at the very forefront of AI research. For months, frontier development looked like a two-horse race between Anthropic and OpenAI.

articles.title: Show HN: Valencia, Spain in Sim City/Isometric View
articles.body:
… of València, painted
An isometric pixel-art map of València, in the spirit of SimCity and of Isometric NYC. Every building is a real one, drawn from above at the same angle, block by block.
The whole municipal term is painted, from the huerta to the Albufera, except a few small huerta exclaves where there's no 3D imagery to paint from.
Real 3D city data is rendered from a fixed isometric camera. An image model trained on a hand-picked pixel-art style then repaints it, tile by tile, each tile continuing its painted neighbours so the city stays seamless. The sea, the port basins and the Albufera are drawn in the same style.
Tiny València is free and has no ads. Painting it takes rented GPUs, and keeping it online a server. If you enjoy it, you can support it on Patreon.

articles.title: Google Fi Brings Back Network Switching With 'Secondary' Partner
articles.body:
Google Fi Brings Back Network Switching With 'Secondary' Partner 2
			
		 	
				Google Fi is bringing back network switching through an unnamed "secondary" 5G carrier. "Most users will be on the 'Primary network,' but Google Fi will automatically switch users to the 'Secondary network' if it meaningfully improves performance with so-called 'smart thresholds' for doing so," reports 9to5Google. "At launch, there is no manual switching." When Project Fi first launched the service included support with both Sprint and T-Mobile. That went away when T-Mobile acquired Sprint in 2020. 9to5Google reports:  Google is not naming the second network today, but did share that Ultra Wideband is supported. Officially, you are switching between "two of America's fastest 5G networks."
Fi Wireless does note that users have top priority, so data is never deprioritized on the Primary network. Meanwhile, there's "highest QCI priority" on the backup network that means subscribers are among the last to be slowed down when there's congestion. This is also available internationally when local partner networks are available with the Flexible and Unlimited Premium plans.
Network switching will first be supported on Pixel 9 and newer devices that have a Google Fi eSIM (and no other SIM active). It makes use of Android's Multiple Enabled Profiles (MEP) eSIM technology that allows for two carrier profiles on a single chip. [...] These Google Fi updates start rolling out today, with network switching seeing gradual availability.

articles.title: Oura is acquiring medical AI chatbot startup Counsel Health
articles.body:
Oura announced its quarterly earnings today and said it agreed to acquire Counsel Health for $625 million, after adding the company’s AI chatbot to its app earlier this year. Counsel Health calls itself an “AI-native primary care company,” using the app to deliver AI-generated responses and insights based on users’ health data reported from their wearables that can then proceed to a conversation with one of its in-house physicians.
Oura is acquiring medical AI chatbot startup Counsel Health
Doctor visits could start with a readout of your Oura ring data.
Oura says it expects the deal to close before the end of the year.
Oura CEO Tom Hale said in an interview with Bloomberg that the acquisition is part of a plan to connect wearables, clinical AI, and access to doctors based on insights from biometric data to answer questions or monitor ongoing conditions. Counsel Health’s AI chatbot can connect Oura users to a real doctor directly from the app and draw on users’ biometric data from their wearables in its answers to medical questions. The plan they describe in the press release is to focus on three areas, including preventative care, acute care for episodic health concerns, and specialty and chronic care for things like reproductive and cardiometabolic health.
According to Bloomberg, Counsel Health’s CEO Muthu Alagappan says it’s also planning to expand its network of on-demand physicians, which is currently “made up of about 50 people.” Counsel’s 70 employees will join Oura as part of the deal, with Alagappan becoming Oura’s chief clinical AI officer. Oura says in its announcement that Counsel will also continue offering its medical AI platform outside of Oura’s user base through new and existing enterprise partners, including “health plans, health systems, consumer health organizations, and employers.”
