Phoronix reports:  Blender now allows importing Gaussian Splats from PLY, SPZ, and glTF files. Also new to Blender 5.3 is NVIDIA DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction support as a new denoiser. Blender 5.3 also brings support for NVIDIA RTX Spark devices.
For the Cycles code in Blender 5.3 the Principled BSDF for shader nodes now supports dispersion. Vulkan 1.1 or newer is required and should deliver better performance than OpenGL.

articles.title: Six Math Essentials by Terence Tao
articles.body:
Terence Tao · original page
In Six Math Essentials, the renowned mathematician and Fields Medalist Terence Tao introduces readers to six central concepts that have guided mathematicians from antiquity to the frontiers of what we know today and now help us make sense of our complex world. This slim, elegant volume explores numbers as the gateway to quantitative thinking; algebra as the gateway to abstraction; geometry as a way to calculate beyond what we can see; probability as a tool to navigate uncertainty with rigorous thinking; analysis as a means to tame the very large or the very small; and dynamics as the mathematics of change.
No errata have been recorded for this book.

articles.title: Show HN: Aircad – Professional drafting and 3D modeling in the browser
articles.body:
Draft, model, and document. Together.
Precision 2D drafting and 3D modeling, with multiplayer editing and an AI agent that drafts, models, and renders alongside you.
Read the docs
- No installs
- Open a browser and start drawing, always on the latest version.
- Pro 2D & 3D drafting
- Precision drafting and solid modeling in one app.
- Version history
- Every change is on record.
- Opens your DWGs
- With their layouts, blocks, and dimensions.
Pro 2D & pro 3D in one app.
2D drafting and 3D solid modeling in one fast, beautiful workspace, from a command line that takes the shortcuts you already know.
Browse every command
- Familiar drafting tools
- Trim, split, extend, stretch, arcs, hatches, blocks, and layers, with command line precision and snaps.
- NURBS-based solid modeling
- Booleans, fillets, shells, lofts, and sweeps.
- Push/pull modeling
- Pick a face and push or pull it with precision.
- Block libraries built in
- Doors, windows, furniture, and plumbing in Imperial and Metric, plus your team’s own blocks, shared in one place.
Powerful AI on your terms.
Ask a question or describe an edit in plain words, and the agent works right in your drawing.
How the agent works
- Help with the whole job
- It drafts, models, and writes commands, and renders your model as an image or right in a viewport.
- Nothing changes without your OK
- Every change arrives as a draft, highlighted in the drawing, for you to apply or discard.
- Right where you work
- Ask from the command line or the Agents panel, with your choice of model. Threads are saved with the file, private to you.
- Entirely optional
- Everything in Aircad works without it. Use it as much or as little as you like.
Always up to date. Every change on record.
One source of truth for every drawing. No emailed copies, no files checked out, no “final_v3.” Every edit is kept with who made it and when.
Sharing and comments in the docs
Multiplayer editing
Share a link and everyone works in the same file, so there's never a stale copy, and you can see who's working where.
- Always the latest revision
- Everyone edits the same file at once, and each change shows up for everyone as it's made.
- Comments on the drawing
- Feedback stays pinned to the spot it's about, not lost in email, so the context is kept as the drawing changes.
- Review is built in
- Comments, redlines, and marked-up PDFs are part of Aircad. No separate review subscription required.
- Control who can edit
- Share with a link, and decide who can edit and who can only view.
A clear record of every change.
Every file keeps unlimited version history, so nothing is lost and any change can be traced back.
- A complete audit trail
- Every edit is kept with who made it and when, in an activity feed for the file.
- Compare any two versions
- See what was added, changed, and deleted, tinted right in the drawing.
- Fork and edit
- Experiment on a fork from any point in the history. The original stays as it was.
- Restore earlier work
- Bring back an earlier version whenever you need it.
Document everything, beautifully.
A drawing set is only as good as its annotation. Dimensions, GD&T, leaders, text, and tables, on layouts with viewports at any scale that print exactly as they look.
Annotation in the docs
- Every dimension type
- Linear, angular, radius, diameter, arc length, ordinate, baseline, and continue. Each follows the geometry it measures, so it stays right as the design changes.
- GD&T and leaders
- Feature control frames on their own or on a leader, and leaders for notes and callouts.
- Text, tables, and title blocks
- Styled text, tables for schedules and parts lists, and title blocks with attributes. Styles keep a whole set consistent.
- Beautiful view styles
- Sections with hatching, hidden line from the model, line weights, shadows, and physically based materials, with a print preview that matches the PDF.
Bring your files. Take them anywhere.
Open DWG and DXF with their layouts, blocks, and dimensions, and bring in Rhino, STEP, glTF, and SVG. Send drawings back as DWG, DXF, or PDF, and models as STL or OBJ.
What each format brings in
Performance
Serious CAD performance.
250,000+ entities in one file. Keep the whole model in one place instead of splitting it across files to keep your CAD responsive.
108 floors. 38,510 editable solids.
- Big models stay smooth
- Pan, zoom, and orbit stay fluid with thousands of solids on screen, and repeated parts and blocks barely add to the load.
- Edits stay quick
- Changing one part updates just that part, so a big file feels as quick as a small one.
- Heavy work runs in the background
- Booleans, edge fillets, lofts, sweeps, and Make2D run off to the side. The drawing stays live, and Esc stops them.
- Views switch without reloading
- Split the screen, change view styles, or turn on print preview, and the model doesn’t load again.
Make the command you wish you had.
Write commands in JavaScript on the same API our built-in commands use: inputs with snaps, live previews, options, and one undo step. Keep them in the file or share them with your team. Or describe the command and let the agent write it.
Read the script APIimport { BRep, Curve, Plane } from "aircad";
export const manifest = {
  name: "Torus",
  kind: "command",
  capabilities: ["document:read", "document:write"],
  inputs: {
    center: { type: "point", prompt: "Pick the center" },
    radius: { type: "length", prompt: "Major radius" },
    tube: { type: "length", prompt: "Tube radius" },
  },
  api: 1,
};
export default async function main(cad) {
  const center = await cad.input.point("center");
  // Draw the ring while the pointer moves.
  const ring = cad.display.show();
  const radius = await cad.input.length("radius", {
    from: center,
    onChange: (r) => ring.set(Curve.circle(Plane.at(center), r)),
  });
  const tube = await cad.input.length("tube");
  return cad.doc.add(BRep.torus(Plane.at(center), radius, tube));
}
- Deep scripting API
- No matter how strange the problem, our scripting API has you covered.
- Live previews
- Draw as the pointer moves; commit on the click.
- Shared through libraries
- Publish commands to your team and keep everyone current.
- Safe by design
- Scripts run in a sandbox with no network access.
Start drawing together.
Bring your next idea to life, together in one team workspace.

articles.title: Anthropic has its own AI-powered office suite now
articles.body:
For years, Anthropic has been known for its focus on enterprise and coding tools that attract high-flying corporate clients, inspiring competing frontier labs — like OpenAI, SpaceXSI, and Meta — to copy its strategies. Earlier this year, Claude Code went through its own particular hype cycle. And now, Anthropic is trying to expand its footprint to other knowledge workers with an AI-powered suite of office tools.
Anthropic has its own AI-powered office suite now
The company is courting white-collar workers ahead of its IPO.
At an event in San Francisco on Tuesday, Anthropic unveiled new tools for non-technical workers who spend a lot of time attending meetings, brainstorming new ideas, and analyzing metrics: Claude Meetings, Claude Sheets, and Claude Whiteboards. The tools allow for Claude to join a meeting, take notes, lay out ideas on a shared whiteboard, edit spreadsheets alongside employees, or turn a presentation into a one-minute explainer video. The new “Artifacts,” or Anthropic’s version of graphical UI, come two and a half years after Artifacts first debuted, and join existing tools like Claude Docs, Slides, Design and Motion.
Claude Whiteboards, Sheets, and Meetings are all now available in beta, with the first two available to all paid plans and Meetings available for Teams and Enterprise subscriptions. The company also announced that Claude Data (formerly known as Claude Dashboards when it was introduced in beta in October) is now generally available to all paid plans.
Nicholas Lin, who works on product at Anthropic, told The Verge in a pre-briefing that Claude Code “changed how engineers work a year ago” — and now, the company is looking to knowledge workers as “the gap we’re hoping to close.”
“I think there’s still a lot of friction when it comes to adopting AI for non-developers,” he said.
The company also unveiled new interactive connectors that allow for users to open apps from partnered companies, such as HubSpot, Adobe, and Atlassian, inside Claude. The company launched Model Context Protocol about two years ago, and its marketplace of tools has grown to more than 9,000 plugin options; now, Lin says, the company is looking to make those connections a lot deeper, so that users don’t have to switch tabs to access the services they use every day and instead just embed them into Claude. For example, with the new tools, people can access a native Adobe PDF editor or a HubSpot marketing campaign tracker inside Claude itself.
The tools follow other AI companies’ offerings in recent years: Google’s Gemini can join meetings and take live notes, and so can OpenAI’s ChatGPT, in some cases, via its “record” feature. Gemini is also well-versed in creating spreadsheets (thanks to Google Sheets), and Google has a lot of different “interactive connectors” for its suite of office tools. At OpenAI’s DevDay last month, OpenAI leaned even further into integrated apps and connectors in order to make its new Dots agents more useful. Anthropic is following in some of their footsteps, plus trying to gain new ground in the AI agent race.
The company is under a lot of pressure to generate more revenue and drive more product engagement ahead of its IPO, as it’s slated to potentially make the most valuable public debut of all time. And although that will turn heads, it also translates to a lot of pressure from investors, who want to see a viable path to profit at Anthropic.
The tools Anthropic debuted on Tuesday are some of the company’s first native products for non-technical knowledge workers. Lin said that although Claude Cowork, one of the company’s other tools for non-engineers, is essentially a wrapper for Claude Code, that tool was aimed at the “technical parts of [Anthropic’s] non-technical audience,” Lin said.
“Now we want to expand that reach toward everybody else.”

articles.title: One of our favorite multi-filament 3D printers is $100 off
articles.body:
If you’re tired of filament jams and clogged nozzles, perhaps it’s time for a new 3D printer. Through December 1st, the Bambu Lab P2S Combo, currently one of the best models that’s easy to use, is discounted. It’s $649 at Best Buy, as well as directly from Bambu Lab. That’s $100 off the list price for the bundle, which includes the Bambu P2S printer and the AMS 2 Pro multi-filament handler for multicolor prints.
One of our favorite multi-filament 3D printers is $100 off
Bambu’s P2S prints quickly and consistently, and automatically swaps between up to four filament colors out of the box.
Bambu Lab P2S Combo
Bambu Lab’s P2S Combo is a 3D printer that can print in multiple colors and automatically dry its materials to help improve print quality. It also features a 5-inch touchscreen, a built-in camera for monitoring prints remotely, and AI-powered tools that can detect printing problems.
My colleague Sean Hollister praised the P2S printer for its consistency and hands-off approach to 3D printing. Automatic bed leveling, including a warning if you forget to reinstall the plate, and a bevy of sensors helps ensure every print goes smoothly. There’s a live camera feed, too, so you can check in on your prints or share a timelapse. On its own, the P2S printer is usually $549, but is also currently $100 off.
The AMS 2 Pro’s filament handler’s fully enclosed setup saves your filament from absorbing moisture and clogging the nozzle or tubes. As a result, you can go weeks between prints and fire one off from your computer without checking on colors or manually swapping filaments. The AMS 2 Pro itself is typically $299, but is currently on sale for $229, and the P2S printer supports up to four AMS 2 Pro units simultaneously.

articles.title: The indie game community is in disarray over AI and Big Walk
articles.body:
Some Independent Games Festival (IGF) jurors published a statement yesterday saying they would not vote for games that use generative AI in “any capacity.” Soon after, the developer of indie hit Big Walk has published a statement saying it “sparingly” used AI in the “final stretch” of the game’s development to “help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs.”
The indie game community is in disarray over AI and Big Walk
Big Walk’s developers said that they used AI ‘sparingly’ to help work through ‘difficult technical challenges.’
According to the jurors’ statement, a copy of which was posted by Austin Walker, while this year’s IGF entries have been “incredible,” there has been “a significant increase” in the number of games “developed with generative AI tools,” leading to “fairly intense discussion and disagreement” with no “universal consensus.” The statement includes a list of beliefs, including that generative AI has “negative effects,” that AI-generated code is “not an exception to these harms,” and that use of AI tools is “not a forgone conclusion in our industry.”
IGF jurors that signed include Telling Lies and Immortality creator Sam Barlow and Celeste composer Lena Raine. The jurors say that the statement doesn’t speak for IGF as an organization or for all IGF jury members, noting that some voiced concern about being able to safely sign “without professional blowback.”
One contentious title was apparently Big Walk, the co-op adventure game from Untitled Goose Game developer House House. In a statement to Aftermath and posted on its website, House House said that “In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.”
House House said its “primary use case” of LLMs was “to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code,” including fixing an issue with shadows by modifying LLM-suggested code. House House noted it turned to the “LLM chatbot” after researching the problem “extensively” and even speaking to an engineer at Unity.
The studio said it disclosed its AI usage as part of its IGF submission, though it has not disclosed AI usage on Big Walk’s Steam page because “the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage.”
“This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal,” House House said. “We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as ‘inevitable’. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.”
House House didn’t have an AI policy in place when it developed Big Walk, which it described as a “failure,” and said it will “work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards.”
Barlow said after we published this post that Big Walk was not the “impetus” for the IGF’s discussion, but it became the “tricky edge case — well what about this minimal use of AI, what about when your favorite game, or team uses it?” Barlow added that “This is not a call to boycott a certain game, or to economically hurt a team — this was about a single award’s show of many and what that award should mean to reflect our ‘indie’ alternative to mainstream and larger scale game development.” Walker also shared a long blog post that’s worth reading about his position on AI and the IGF awards.
Update, November 10th: Added posts from Barlow and Walker.

articles.title: The DRAM interface and the PHY (why a DDR3+ interface must be tuned at boot)
articles.body:
This chapter explains what happens on the wires between the FPGA and the DRAM, and why a DRAM interface must be tuned at boot. It covers the signals, the strobes, the board topology, the leveling procedures, the termination and the reference voltages, then the clocks of the FPGA and the DFI interface between the controller and the PHY.
Each section ends with the part of LiteDRAM that implements the mechanism. The previous chapter, DRAM in a nutshell, explained the commands and the timings; Initialization and calibration gives the exact steps the BIOS runs.
A DRAM interface has two halves. The command and address half goes one way, from the controller to the DRAM, and is shared by every chip of a rank. The data half is bidirectional and split into byte lanes, each with its own strobe. The figure below shows the signals.
A byte lane is 8 DQ, their DQS pair and their DM. Each lane is routed on its own, so each one can arrive at a slightly different time, and each one is tuned on its own.
In LiteDRAM, the pads of the DRAM are a record from the platform file, with fields named after
these signals (dq, dqs_p, a, ba, cs_n). The PHY counts the lanes from it. Two helpers
of litedram/common.py reshape the pads: PHYPadsReducer keeps some lanes only, and
PHYPadsCombiner merges chips with separate command buses into one controller.
SDR memory transfers one word per clock, sampled on the rising edge of the clock that the controller sends. DDR memories transfer two words per clock, one on each edge, and at these rates the clock from the controller cannot be trusted to sample the data: the delays of the board and of the chips are too large.
The data therefore travel with their own clock, the strobe DQS: the side that sends the data also sends DQS, and the receiver samples DQ with it. This is a source-synchronous interface. Both travel the same path, so their delays cancel. The figure below shows how DQS is aligned with DQ.
On writes the controller sends DQS centre aligned, its edges in the middle of each bit. On reads the DRAM sends DQS edge aligned, on the bit transitions, and the receiver delays it by a quarter of a clock. Before the burst, DQS is driven for a preamble, and after it for a postamble, without carrying data.
In LiteDRAM, the DDR PHYs shift the write DQS by a quarter of a clock from DQ, with the means of its FPGA:
- The Artix-7 PHY clocks its DQS serializers from a clock shifted by 90 degrees, sys4x_dqs,
which the target builds (bench/arty.py).
- The PHYs with output delays (Kintex-7 and Virtex-7 HP banks, UltraScale) delay DQS by a quarter of a clock.
- The Lattice and Gowin PHYs take the shifted write clock of the DQS block of their FPGA.
On reads, the PHYs differ:
- The Xilinx PHYs do not use DQS. They sample DQ with their own fast clock, through an input delay that read leveling tunes per lane.
- The Lattice and Gowin PHYs use the DQS blocks of their FPGA, which delay DQS by 90 degrees, capture DQ with it and report when they saw a burst (burst detect).
DDR3 and DDR4 route the clock, command and address pins as one bus that passes by every chip in turn and ends on a termination: the fly-by topology. It keeps these heavily loaded signals clean at high rates, but each chip receives the clock a little later than the previous one. The figure below shows it.
The data lanes are point to point, so their delays do not follow the clock. A chip needs DQS to arrive close to its own CK edge (tDQSS). With fly-by routing the skew between the first and the last chip can exceed a clock period, so each lane needs its own DQS delay.
Write leveling measures that delay. The controller sets the DRAM into write leveling mode with a mode register bit (MR1 bit A7 on DDR3 and DDR4), then sends DQS pulses. The DRAM samples its CK with each DQS rising edge and returns the sampled value on DQ. The controller delays DQS step by step until DQ goes from 0 to 1: DQS is then aligned with CK at that chip.
In LiteDRAM, the PHYs expose write leveling through registers: wlevel_en enables the mode,
wlevel_strobe sends one DQS pulse, and per-lane output delays move DQS and DQ. The BIOS runs the
scan (sdram_write_leveling in liblitedram).
Write leveling needs output delays: the Kintex-7 and Virtex-7 PHYs in HP banks and the UltraScale
PHYs have them. The Artix-7 has none: with one static DQS phase, only some lanes of a fly-by
memory meet tDQSS. Its optional CK phase shift mode (with_ck_phase_shift, DDR3 at 1:4) moves CK
against all the lanes instead (CK phase shift).
Write leveling aligns DQS with CK within one clock period, but a lane can be one whole clock early or late: the DRAM then writes the burst shifted by a few words. Write latency calibration writes a known pattern, reads it back, and moves each lane by whole clocks until the pattern is right.
DQ-DQS training then centres DQ against DQS on writes. It sweeps the output delay of the DQ pins of each lane, writes and reads back a pattern at each step, and keeps the middle of the passing range. It relies on a working read side, which read leveling then refines.
In LiteDRAM, the write latency is moved by write bitslips (wdly_dq_bitslip) and DQ by output
delays (wdly_dq). Each PHY declares which calibrations it supports in its settings
(write_leveling, write_latency_calibration, write_dq_dqs_training, read_leveling); the
BIOS runs only those.
On reads, the controller does not know when the data arrive. The DRAM answers CL clocks after RD, but the board and the I/Os add a delay that differs per lane. Two settings must be found for each lane: a coarse one, which fast clock cycle holds the first word, and a fine one, where in the bit to sample.
The coarse setting is a bitslip: the deserializer output is shifted by whole bits until the words line up. The fine setting is an input delay, from a few picoseconds to about a hundred per step depending on the FPGA (78 ps on 7-Series with a 200 MHz reference). Read leveling writes a pattern, then for each bitslip sweeps the delay and reads the pattern back. The figure below shows such a scan.
The window is the data eye seen through the delay line. A wide window means a robust interface; a narrow one points to a signal integrity or clocking problem. DDR3 and DDR4 can also return a fixed pattern from their MPR (multi-purpose register), so the read side can be tuned before anything has been written.
The PHYs that capture with DQS have one more problem: DQS is not driven between bursts, so the receiver must listen to it only during a read. The FPGA's DQS block opens this gate and reports a burst detect, which read leveling uses to confirm that the read window is right.
In LiteDRAM, each PHY declares its number of delay taps and bitslips in its settings (delays,
bitslips), and exposes them through registers (rdly_dq_inc, rdly_dq_bitslip, and
burstdet_seen on the Lattice and Gowin PHYs). The BIOS runs the scan and prints one line per
lane and bitslip. On DDR4 it reads the MPR patterns, except on registered DIMMs and clamshell
layouts.
At DRAM rates, a signal reflects at the end of a line that is not terminated. The DRAM therefore terminates its own data pins with an on-die termination (ODT): a resistor switched on when the ODT pin is high. The FPGA terminates its inputs in the same way when it receives read data.
DDR3 and DDR4 have two termination values: RTT_NOM, used when the chip is idle or another rank is written, and RTT_WR, used while the chip itself is written (dynamic ODT). The driver strength of the DRAM, RON, sets how hard it drives the read data. All three are set in the mode registers.
In LiteDRAM, the defaults of the table are set by litedram/init.py; a PHY can override them
(rtt_nom, rtt_wr, ron in its settings). With the DRAM DLL off, a DDR3 mode for low
clock rates that the GW5A PHY offers (dll_off), both terminations are disabled.
The ODT pin is driven statically by default. With with_dynamic_odt (DDR3, single rank), the
controller raises ODT only around writes, so the DRAM terminations are off during reads
(Dynamic ODT). The FPGA side termination is part of the I/O standards of the
platform file, not of LiteDRAM.
The resistance of the drivers and terminations of a chip varies with the process, the voltage and the temperature. DDR3 and later chips calibrate them against a precision resistor on their ZQ pin, 240 ohm to ground. ZQCL, the long calibration, runs once at initialization; ZQCS, the short one, corrects the drift from time to time during operation.
In LiteDRAM, the initialization sequence ends with ZQCL (Mode registers and power-up), and the refresher sends ZQCS once per second by default (Refresh). LPDDR4 has no ZQCS: it calibrates with two multi-purpose commands (MPC), start and latch, which LiteDRAM sends at initialization only.
The data receivers compare each input to a reference voltage, VREF, set halfway between the high and the low levels. On DDR3 the board provides VREF on dedicated pins. DDR4 terminates its data pins to the supply (pseudo open drain), so the data swing sits near the top of the supply and the right reference is not halfway. The DRAM generates its data VREF internally, programmed in MR6.
On the FPGA side, the receivers of the read data also need a VREF. Some FPGA I/O banks can set it internally, in steps, instead of using a VREF pin.
In LiteDRAM, the DDR4 initialization writes MR6 with tCCD_L only and leaves its VREF field at zero, the first value of range 1 (60% of VDDQ): the DRAM data VREF is not trained.
The UltraScale+ PHY can set the FPGA read VREF of its HP I/O banks (with_hpio_vref, register
rd_vref, codes 0 to 72). The BIOS does not scan it: the register keeps its build-time value
(hpio_vref_tune) unless software writes it. LiteX issue 2769 tracks the missing BIOS sweep.
An FPGA fabric cannot run at the DRAM clock: a DDR3 at 800 MT/s has a 400 MHz clock and moves data at 800 Mbps per pin. The PHY therefore uses the serializers and deserializers of the FPGA I/Os. The controller runs at a fraction of the DRAM clock, and moves several clocks' worth of commands and data per cycle.
This fraction is the frequency ratio. At 1:4, the controller runs at a quarter of the DRAM clock: the Arty A7 bench target runs its controller at 125 MHz, its DRAM clock at 500 MHz, and its DDR3 at 1000 MT/s. For a DDR memory, the data rate is twice the DRAM clock: at 1:4, eight times the controller clock.
An Artix-7 DDR3 target needs four clocks, generated by a PLL in the board's clock module
(bench/arty.py). The Kintex-7 and Virtex-7 targets need no sys4x_dqs: their output delays shift
DQS instead.
Other families use their own clocking: the ECP5 PHY uses a 2x clock for its I/O gearing and a 4x clock at 1:4, and the Gowin GW5A PHY selects 1:2 or 1:4 with its number of phases. DDR PHYs gives the clocks of each family.
The controller and the PHY meet at a DFI interface, named after the DDR PHY Interface specification. It carries, for each DRAM clock of a controller cycle, one command slot and the data of that clock. Each of these slots is a DFI phase. The figure below shows the phases at a 1:4 ratio.
Two latencies tie the commands to their data. The write latency is the number of controller cycles between WR and the cycle where the controller presents the write data. The read latency is the number of cycles between RD and the cycle where the read data come back valid. Both follow from CL, CWL and the pipeline of the PHY.
The commands do not always start on phase 0. The PHY tells the controller on which phase to issue
reads and writes (rdphase, wrphase), so that the data of a burst fill whole controller cycles.
In LiteDRAM, the DFI interface is Interface of litedram/phy/dfi.py. It follows the structure of
the DFI specification, phases and signal names, without claiming a version of it.
Each PHY fills a PhySettings with its number of phases, its latencies in controller cycles, CL and CWL in DRAM
clocks, and its calibration capabilities. DFIRateConverter wraps a PHY to raise the ratio, with
more phases and narrower data per phase. See Core architecture.
Each PHY is built from the I/O primitives of its FPGA family. The table below summarizes what the LiteDRAM PHYs use; DDR PHYs describes each one.
The 7-Series input and output delays need a reference clock of 200 or 300 MHz, or 400 MHz on the
faster speed grades; their output delays exist only in the HP banks of Kintex-7 and Virtex-7. The UltraScale delays are set in time
units, and the FPGA compensates them for voltage and temperature while en_vtc is set.
Where to go next: Initialization and calibration for the BIOS steps, DDR PHYs for each family, Debugging when a scan shows no window.

articles.title: rVPN – stealth VPN with end-to-end encryption
articles.body:
rVPN is an open-source protocol that carries your traffic safely across the internet, indistinguishable from ordinary HTTPS, so it works even where VPNs are blocked.
We believe privacy should be proven, not promised. Every line is open to read, audit, and run yourself.
curl -fsSL https://assets.rvpn.org/install.sh | sudo bash  A censor watching the wire sees ordinary web traffic on port 443. No tell-tale handshake, no blockable fingerprint. If they probe the server, it answers like a normal website.
A Double Ratchet rekeys every message, so a stolen key never unlocks the past or the future.
Probe the endpoint and it serves a real decoy site. Nothing to confirm, nothing to block.
The core is written in Rust, so entire classes of vulnerability cannot occur.
One TLS connection per flow means hundreds of parallel sessions under load: slow to establish, and a shape worth flagging. Pooled multiplexing carries every flow over a handful of long-lived connections, so the wire stays small and ordinary no matter how busy you are.
Every flow pays a full TCP + TLS + WebSocket + X3DH handshake. A busy client holds hundreds of parallel TLS sessions to one server.
Flows share a small pool of long-lived connections. Credit-based flow control keeps bulk transfers from starving interactive ones, and reconnects resume TLS 1.3 tickets in a single round trip.
Every claim on this page maps to code you can read. Clone the repo, check out a tag, and build the exact binary we ship. Reproducible by design.
Read the whitepaper →
rVPN is free and open under AGPLv3, and always will be. Development is fully funded by PDG Global Limited; sales of the iOS and Android apps, together with donations, contribute towards development costs. The code never closes.
One protocol, every device. Native apps for phone and desktop, a command-line client for your servers, and the source code to port it anywhere we have not yet.
Free, open source, and ready on every platform. The apps are on the stores and the source is on GitHub today.
